   Over the next two days, we closed in on the scout. Their attempts to ditch us got more
   elaborate, but sloppier; they took sweeping detours through the paddy fields, doubled back
   into wilder marshes, at one point even veered off to go through a small village and try to hide
   their trail among the beaten-earth roads and cart tracks there.

   It would have worked better for them if they hadn’t chosen a civilian henge to hide behind.
   The villagers might not be the most observant of people, but they weren’t stupid - a stray
   ninja passing through the village was one thing, but a lone ‘merchant’ with no caravan and no
   hired escort was practically an invitation to gossip. It wasn’t difficult to pick up which
   direction they went, and they’d spent so long walking at a civilian pace to uphold their cover
   story that they lost almost half their lead on us in the process.

   Somewhere between an overcast sundown and a pouring wet midnight on the second night,
   Pakkun reappeared from one of his frequent absences and announced, “They’re sending
   backup for the retrieval. One ANBU, codename Crane, about an hour out. He’ll rendezvous
   with you the normal way.”

   Kakashi slowed to an abrupt halt. I matched him, frowning in concentration as I used my
   chakra to avoid skidding on the slick grass. He didn’t say anything, but his posture was tense
   - though, that might just have been in response to the rain dripping down the back of his
   neck, I know that was making me tense - and his grimace was annoyed.

   “For a scout?” I asked. “But we’re so close. We can’t afford to wait an hour. The rain’s their
   best chance of escaping us, we have to move now.”

   “A scout with unknown combat skills and the ability to summon at least two jounin-level
   allies,” Kakashi corrected. “Given how crucial their information is to the war, sending backup
   isn’t unreasonable.” He sounded frustrated though. I wasn’t surprised; the scout’s combat
   skills might be unknown, but we’d been the ones tracking them for the past five days, and
   however long before that that Kakashi had spent working out they existed and narrowing
   down their location in the first place. Even if they did call the strike team to help them, I
   knew he was strong enough to take all three. Obviously he was strong enough to take all
three. I wasn’t familiar enough with ANBU to know if sending backup like this was standard
procedure or not, but it certainly felt like a dig against him.

“It might not be unreasonable but it’s still not necessary,” I muttered mulishly. “We’re fine.
We don’t need anyone else.”

“Saa,” he said, abandoning his frown to eye-smile at me. I could tell from both his tone and
expression that if I was standing any closer he’d’ve ruffled my hair, and I flattened it
defensively just in case. “Don’t be like that, Sasuke. You like new people.”

“Lies.”

“Hmm, if you say so. How do you feel about pretending to be ANBU?”

I froze, then hastily un-froze myself to hide the reaction. “Uh. What?”

“Only, this is meant to be an ANBU mission. Here, see if this fits.” He pulled something
small and white from seemingly nowhere, and tossed it to me in a lazy underhand throw.
When I caught it I recognised the smooth porcelain and intricate seal work as belonging to an
ANBU mask, but when I turned it over I wasn’t immediately sure what animal the markings
were meant to represent. It had two triangular ears, like Itachi’s did, but where his had a
single stripe down the centre this one had two red markings on each cheek, and a thick
outline around the eye-holes that pulled them back and up in a slanted, angular shape.

A cat, maybe? Why would Kakashi have a random cat mask on him?

“Really?” Pakkun asked, levelling him an unimpressed stare. “Jiraiya knows she’s here.”

“Crane doesn’t,” Kakashi pointed out. “May as well keep up appearances. Ah, but if you’re
wearing the mask, I guess that means I’ll be left as a plain old jounin…” He tapped his chin,
then shrugged. “Oh well.”

The mask. The singular - I nearly dropped it. “It’s your mask? You want me to pretend to be
ANBU Hound?”

He eye-smiled again. And got my hair this time, despite the fact that I could’ve sworn I was
still out of reach.

“You’re a bit short to be Hound just yet. ANBU Puppy, maybe. Though you are thirteen now,
I guess that makes you old enough.”

Twelve, I almost corrected, then blinked, and counted the days.

My birthday had been the day before yesterday. I’d completely missed it. Huh.

Pakkun huffed, shaking his head and breaking me out of my thoughts. “Masks get recycled,”
he told me. “If Crane asks, you’re Hound, not Puppy. If anyone who knows that Hound
hasn’t actually retired asks, blame your sensei.”
I looked between them. Pakkun resigned, Kakashi suspiciously innocent. I was definitely
missing something, and there was more meaning to the mask than just making sure Crane
didn’t know who I was.

I squinted.

“This is a fuck you to Jiraiya,” I decided. Pakkun wouldn’t have mentioned him if he wasn’t
involved, and as far as I knew Jiraiya didn’t usually work with ANBU, which meant: “He
didn’t want you to take me out of Konoha and you’re pissed at him. Your mask, your student,
that’s why you want me to wear it.”

Kakashi’s innocent expression turned uncomfortable. “Ah -”

“Cool,” I interrupted, and put the mask on, flaring my chakra to activate the seals and attach
it to my face. I applied the henge in the same movement, one layer to change my clothes for
Itachi’s dark shirt and pants combination, and another for the armour plates over the top.
When I lifted my hands up to tug my hair free though, I grimaced; the sleeves didn’t look
realistic in the rain. Good enough to fool most people, but wet cloth stuck and pulled in
different ways to dry, and I wasn’t confident enough to mimic it. It wasn’t an issue for the
armour - I added a slight sheen from the water dripping off it, but didn’t need to do anything
other than that - and the pants were close enough to my own that I could get away with it, but
the sleeves would have to go.

“Help me draw the tattoo?” I asked, pinning the second of the familiar two buns in place and
replacing the henged shirt with a sleeveless version instead. “I don’t know what it looks like.”

Kakashi paused, tilting his head and looking at me thoughtfully before answering. “It’s not
for Jiraiya,” he said. Pakkun coughed, and he amended, “It’s not only for Jiraiya. I brought
you with me to keep you safe from Orochimaru, and hiding your identity like this is a useful
defence.”

“From Crane? Do we not trust him?”

His cheek twitched, as though he’d gone to pull a face and suppressed it. “He’s one of the
Hokage’s most loyal. But if there’s any chance of the scout or strike team being able to get a
message back to Sound, I’d rather they not know you’re here.”

It seemed overly cautious to me; with Kakashi and a second ANBU ninja attacking, the
likelihood of anyone escaping was slim to none. I didn’t mention it though, just nodded, and
let Kakashi use a henge of his own to demonstrate what the tattoo looked like for me to copy.

At least, I assume it was a henge. If it wasn’t, then he’d somehow managed to take his arm
out his sleeve to show me his shoulder without taking his flak jacket off. I wouldn’t put it
past him, but also, why.

Either way, I faithfully copied the swirl, and so long as no one looked too closely or tried to
test it with chakra, it should hold up to inspection. That done, we were ready to go again,
doggedly following the scout’s trail before the rain could wash too much of it away - all
taken, we’d only paused for a few minutes since Pakkun had arrived and passed on the
message. Crane was still around an hour out, the scout was less than an hour ahead, and with
the ground beneath us getting steadily as wet as the sky above us, we ran.

Forty eight minutes later Kakashi made a handseal and, I assumed, flared his chakra in
response to a signal I hadn’t picked up. Seventeen seconds after that ANBU Crane flowed
seamlessly out of the darkness and fell into formation beside us. I glanced over enough to
register that he was a few inches shorter than Kakashi, that he was built for speed and
precision rather than power, and that the hair above his white and red mask was wild, black,
and curling slightly in the rain, but other than that, I ignored him.

I blinked, relying on my own mask to hide the action, and slid my eyes back over to him
without turning my head.

His hair was wild, black, curling slightly in the rain, and according to my sharingan, an
illusion.

That in itself wasn’t unusual, if you thought about it. ANBU went to so much effort to keep
their identity hidden, then left their hair exposed for anyone to recognise? No. The hair was
left out so people would remember it, and not focus on the ANBU’s body shape or anything
else that was harder to disguise. What was unusual though was the fact that, without the
sharingan to spot it, I wouldn’t have been able to tell it was a genjutsu at all.

Which. What. I didn’t get fooled by people’s genjutsu. Other people got fooled by people’s
genjutsu, I spotted the little mistakes people made and called them out for being shoddy. It
was my thing. And I get that that sounds arrogant, but. Hair. Hair. Every individual strand
moving like hair was meant to move, and reflecting the light properly given both how little
light there was to begin with and the fact that water made everything harder to get right?

I was in love. It was amazing. The level of detail - I suddenly had a new goal in life, and it
was to find ANBU Crane’s weakness and bribe him with it, maybe a bit of extortion,
whatever it took until he taught me everything he knew. Forget dramatic, reality-defying
scenarios like Kurenai was known to favour, this was the subtlety genjutsu was made for. It
was flawless. It was beautiful. I needed it.

I also felt suddenly self-conscious about the henge I was wearing. It was good, I knew it was
good - other than the shirt it was an exact duplicate of an outfit I’d worn before. I’d had my
sharingan open at the time, I was hardly going to have missed parts of it. Every single hair
though, that was a whole other level. Who had the brain power to calculate where they were
meant to go? I mean, Crane did, obviously, but. How? You couldn’t do it just by copying
someone else with a similar hairstyle. You could try, but you’d have to know them well
enough to mimic their hair in wet, in dry, when it was windy, when they changed direction
while running and the bit sticking up at the back swayed to the left then bounced back -

I might have been staring. I just. Perfect. He was perfect.

And in light of finally seeing how genjutsu was meant to be used, I had a whole new
understanding of what I needed to work on. I’d added a sheen to my armour to account for it
being wet; with my head still stubbornly turned forwards to hide my fascination I studied his
armour and amended the sheen to include water droplets running down the metal, the
darkening of the straps and the way they stretched differently when they were soaked
through, the slight traces of dirt and mud that got kicked up and stuck differently to armour
versus cloth -

I was so caught up in it that it was something of a surprise when Kakashi raised a hand for
attention. His fingers flashed through a series of signals, almost but not quite the ones he’d
taught me before. ANBU sign; I caught a few commands, but I didn’t know them all, and I
fought the urge to tense up.

“Urushi,” he said, voice low and barely audible over the storm. “You’re with Hound. Stay
back, circle the perimeter. If they break free from us, give chase, but only engage if
necessary. Clear?”

I mentally sighed in relief. Those instructions were for my benefit, Urushi had worked with
Kakashi long enough to know ANBU sign. He played along with the pretence though,
ducking his head in a sharp nod to show his understanding.

His nod was clearly the signal. Kakashi and Crane split, vanishing into the night to curve
round in a pincer movement. Pakkun went with Kakashi, and Urushi and I veered off to keep
an eye for the scout trying to escape. We’d reached an area of wetland where the grass was
easily waist high on the dry parts, transitioning to half-submerged reeds as it reached the edge
of the marshy lake. The scout was underwater - probably hoping we’d run over the top
without noticing and leave them behind. The ground around the banks was spongy, semi-
solid and treacherous, with low-lying shrubs growing between the reeds that were little more
than hollow shells of leaves with nothing but water underneath. The rain was coming down in
thick sheets, blocking out the faint moonlight from earlier until even with the sharingan I was
struggling to see far enough ahead to keep track of the others.

I reached blindly in the water for a rock, found nothing but mud, and ripped out a single
woody reed instead.

“Urushi,” I said, handing it to him. I attached a thread of chakra to it, as though in preparation
for kawarimi; I wouldn’t risk switching while he was holding it for fear of ripping out his
teeth, but it would let me know where he was if he went out of my field of view. “Take the far
side. I can follow you through this if you spot the scout and run after them.”

Reed in his mouth and sticking close to the water’s edge so he could water-walk, he went.

As for me, I gave up on my sight, and focussed instead on my chakra. I’d given Urushi a
thread, but the rest of it I spread out as a thin sheet, hovering on the surface of the water and
stretching out as far around the lake as I could go. The vibrations of the raindrops hitting it
were a constant background noise that I didn’t bother to tune out, Urushi’s footsteps a faint
rhythm as he loped steadily to the other side; if the scout was going to try and get past me
over the water, I should be able to feel it as they went past.

For the first half minute, there was nothing. Urushi moved away from the water two thirds of
the way round the lake, leaving me relying purely on the kawarimi thread to keep track of
him. I couldn’t see, hear, or feel Kakashi or Crane.
Then - flute music, high and out of place, cutting unnaturally clearly through the rain. It was
followed very quickly after by one-two-three roars, the crash-thud of something large kicking
off from the ground, and a flare of light from what had to be a lightning jutsu in the distance.

Tayuya. And her summons, but they were too far away for me to identify what they were;
they sounded vaguely human - or humanoid - but I couldn’t tell anything further than that. If
the scout had called Tayuya, Kidomaru was almost certainly there as well. I bit my lip.
Staying back and waiting like this felt wrong on every level, particularly when I knew the
Sound Four in a way that neither Kakashi nor Crane did. Had I even told Kakashi about the
curse seal? I hadn’t - there wouldn’t have been any way for me to know, I couldn’t - but what
if I’d put him in danger by withholding knowledge, what if he was - oh god, the summons ate
chakra, didn’t they? Did they? They did, I think, and Kakashi’s weakness was his small
reserves, he didn’t have enough to spare -

“Get a fucking grip,” I snarled, readying three shuriken in each hand just for something to do.
“He’s Kakashi. He’s not going to die. And even if - even if he was, you can’t go after him.
You promised.” I took a breath. Kakashi was fine. Crane was a genjutsu master the likes of
which Konoha hadn’t seen since they lost the Uchiha, he wasn’t allowed to die until he’d
explained how his illusions worked. I had a job to do, and if I wasn’t allowing myself to get
distracted by how cold I was after an hour of practically swimming through the rain, then I
wasn’t allowed to get distracted by being over dramatic and doubting Kakashi either.

I flexed my fingers, resettled the shuriken into a better hold, and crouched in the grass to
focus on my chakra and wait.

Another half a minute. It crawled; the distant sounds of the battle were both agonisingly slow
and happening too quick to follow. Then - a splash, just on the very edge of the sheet of
chakra I had over the lake, followed by the hard impact of a foot, then the disruption on the
water as the scout exploded out from under it and started running. They vanished from my
senses as soon as they left the lake but Urushi bolted after them, taking the reed with him and
showing me the way. I sprinted, aiming diagonally to intercept them both and sparing just
enough concentration to my feet to ensure I didn’t step in a sink-hole and snap my leg.

The scout was fast and desperate. I was faster. They weren’t trying to hide, too worn out from
the days of pursuit and too far from Kakashi to think they needed to bother. I went low,
streaking through the grass and shifting my henge to camouflage myself against it; by the
time they spotted me I’d already circled round in front of them, Urushi coming up the other
direction and the two of us neatly cutting off their escape.

Her escape. She was tall, leanly muscled with her hair too tightly tied back to grab on to,
missing her right eye. Try attacking from that side then, but it was too obvious a weakness for
her not to have a way to mitigate it. Clothes - short white kimono, circle-patterned obi, black
leggings and standard sandals. Not long enough to restrict movement, not obviously
armoured enough to block more than a glancing blow, but the wide sleeves could be hiding
something. The free ends of the obi were moving oddly. Weighted? Hard to tell. In total I
gleaned very little about her skills or fighting style, and other than noting a lack of any large,
easily identifiable weapons or heavy taijutsu build I didn’t have much to help me face her.
Which I wasn’t meant to be doing in the first place but in my defence, Kakashi had told me
to engage if necessary. Or he’d told Urushi and ANBU Hound at least, it would probably
have looked weird to Crane if he’d done anything else. It was a loophole I was willing to
exploit.

For Kakashi, I tried to be cautious, and my opening move was to throw up a Naruto-esque
wall of illusion clones and duplicate Urushi into an entire pack of snarling dogs. It wasn’t my
usual style, but with the poor visibility she wouldn’t be able to tell the real from the fake and
given that my goal was to herd her back to the others -

“Byakugan,” she spat, right hand held in front of her face so the eyeball on the back of it
lined up with the empty socket in her head. She saw through the illusion and darted for the
gap between me and Urushi without even breaking stride.

I stumbled, staring after her for an endless, free-falling second.

In the back of my mind the new information slotted neatly into place; why Orochimaru had
changed his plans to target Hinata of all people, how the scouts were so good at evading
detection, why there were two strike teams and two scouts and two eyeballs and -

I let go of the kawarimi thread to Urushi and created a new one. It lashed after her, whip-like
and vicious, aiming for her right hand but missing and hooking onto her left instead. When I
switched, I did it with a savage, relentless twist that tore her hand off at the wrist and used it
to replace myself with. The hand landed with an inaudible thump where I’d been standing
and I appeared in a tangle of limbs half on top of her, the shredded stump of her arm
smearing against my chest and the blood mixing with the rain running down my front.

“Give it back,” I snarled, elbow jabbing at her throat and other hand reaching for the
byakugan. “It’s not yours, give it - shit.” I moved with the force of her blow; she had
something sharp along the edge of her forearm, I couldn’t see what but it tore at the fabric of
my jacket and sliced a thin, painful line into the skin of my shoulder below. The distance
gave her the space she needed to break free, and with both of us slick from the rain I didn’t
have a hope of holding on.

She choked out a hysterical laugh, cradling her arm to her chest as she hunched over her
missing hand. “You,” she started, then broke off to laugh again. I recovered my logic enough
to remember the shuriken I’d been holding earlier and flung them at her, but she raised her
good arm and batted them away with a clash of metal on metal. Her other arm was bleeding
heavily, dark rivulets fanning up over her skin where the wide sleeve of her kimono had
fallen down and forming glistening, branching patterns. “You,” she repeated, voice rising to
something high and shrill. “You took my hand.”

“It happens to the best of us,” I said, more to buy time than anything else. I didn’t know
where Urushi was. I didn’t want to risk more shuriken if she was going to deflect them, not
without knowing if he was in the cross-fire, and illusions weren’t going to do shit against her.
The rain put any fire jutsu out of the question - someone better than I was could still manage
them even in this, but I wasn’t better than I was so screw that - and I doubted I’d get her with
kawarimi again (I just ripped off a piece of someone). That left me with taijutsu, my chakra
arm, and the sudden realisation that blood went down her arm but the branching patterns had
been going up -

She whirled on me, right arm flung out and a barrage of silver feathers flying off it towards
me. I flattened myself against the ground; each one looked razor sharp and too deadly for me
to afford to let them hit. “You took my hand,” she shrieked, sending another barrage in a
wide, uncontrolled spray.

I had to move in. I couldn’t stay at a distance, not with that sort of attack and not with Urushi
somewhere unknown. I threaded my fingers with shuriken again and coiled my water-arm in
preparation, readying my chakra for another rapid kawarimi. Why was there nothing to
switch with. Why were there no convenient rocks or twigs or - grass, grass would do. I came
in low, legs bent and already pushing off the ground to leap up inside her guard when I
landed. She spun, swiping at me with the trailing ends of her obi - I was right, they were
weighted, and I dodged instinctively back to avoid them until I knew whether they were
made out of cloth or not.

They weren’t. None of her kimono was; it was made of feathers, jagged metal feathers rising
with her arms like wings, and as the obi lifted behind her the two ends of it divided and
divided again until they fanned out in a mimicry of a peacock tail. If, you know, every feather
of a peacock tail was made of deadly sharpened steel, but other than that it was pretty
accurate. The circle pattern even looked like eyes.

“Bullshit,” I said, backing away from her in shock. “I don’t care how overpowered the curse
seal transformation is, it doesn’t affect your clothes.”

“Die,” was her intelligent and well-reasoned response to that. I tore my eyes away from her
logic-defying kimono to realise that the patterns I’d noticed before had finished spreading
over her skin, turning her face a flat, feather-etched grey and her hair a spiky silver flaring
out like a crest behind her head. She crossed both arms in front of her and brought them
jerking down, firing out a mix of the smaller arm feathers as well as several tail feathers that
flew like fucking javelins - I kawarimid. No. Not happening. I had a moment to adjust to this
new and terrifying development, then I was kawariming again when she sent more - what the
hell, how did they regrow that fast - then ducked under her sweeping tail and grabbed for her
feet with my chakra arm, then had to abandon the movement to dodge feather-death again -

I was getting nowhere. She was driving me back, and I was hamstrung not only by the terrain
working against me and my worry for Urushi, but also by the need to capture her instead of
kill. How much blood had she already lost from her missing hand? If I attacked her like that
again would she even survive? I didn’t have methods of subduing people that didn’t involve
at the very least knocking them out. My best chance was to get close and switch us back to
the lake, but that put me in reach of both her obi-tail and her kimono-wings, neither of which
fit with me continuing through life unskewered and alive.

If I died, Kakashi was going to kill me.

“New plan,” I muttered. She had the byakugan, but from the way she used it I assumed she
needed to hold it in front of her face to make it work, and her hand was occupied with other
things. It wasn’t a certainty but I was confident enough with my guess that the next time she
flung her feathers at me I mimed getting hit, layering a genjutsu over my hip and thigh where
my fake-armour didn’t cover and adopting a limp with a hissed grimace of pain.

I didn’t have to face her head-on. She was exhausted, wounded, and desperate; if I could bait
her into abandoning her defensive position and making a run for it, she’d be far easier to take
down - sneak attacks from behind were much more my style than the relentless assault I’d
been trying to fight her with so far.

At least, they were much more my style when I wasn’t losing my temper over people’s
eyeballs being passed out like trail rations, but we weren’t mentioning that.

I pulled the illusion feather from my thigh, gritting my teeth and making a show of testing
how well it held my weight. Her eyes lit up, exactly as I’d hoped; she fired another barrage
straight for me which I got ready to just about dodge without giving away how uninjured I
actually was -

Someone scooped me up. I think. It happened too suddenly, I didn’t even notice them until I
was already in their arms and being deposited on the ground a safe distance away.

“What the -”

I caught a glimpse of a white mask, the narrow line of the beak on it marking it as Crane’s,
then he was gone again in the fastest shunshin I think I’d ever seen in my life.

“Holy shit,” I mumbled. Without my sharingan, I wouldn’t have been able to follow his
movements. With my sharingan, I could barely follow them - he was running between the
fecking rain drops, all the while maintaining his stupidly perfect henge. It was like what my
kawarimi could one day aspire to be; sure, I got from point A to point B quicker, but with his
shunshin he could slice at his enemy as he went dancing past, and he wasn’t restricted by
finding things to switch with. The man could change direction midair. What was he even
pushing off from. Kawarimi couldn’t change direction midair. Mid-switch. He was better
than me at genjutsu and now better than me at speedy bouncing around a battlefield, if I
wasn’t so determined to make him teach me I think I would’ve hated him on principle.

It was unfair. Also amazing. But unfair.

All of four seconds later, the scout was down. Crane even cauterised her wrist so she
wouldn’t bleed out, pressing a jutsu-heated kunai against the stump in one-two second bursts
until it was sealed. It was an efficient but not widely used method; unless treated
immediately, the burn would be impossible for even a skilled medic to heal, and any medic
who could treat the burn immediately may as well deal with the wound properly in the first
place. Whatever hope the scout had of reattaching her hand was now lost.

Not that she’d’ve been given the chance to reattach it anyway. I tried to dredge up some kind
of horror or guilt at what I’d done to her, but. She had Hinata’s eye. Best I could offer was a
vague sense of nausea if I thought too much about the details - I’d just torn someone's hand
off - but that was easily solved by not thinking too much about the details, so. She deserved
it, and I hoped it hurt, and if that wasn’t the response Naruto would have approved of, then so
what. He wasn’t here. Kiba and Shino would understand.
(It just. Came off. All ragged, not even a clean cut. Literally torn off.)

(Bleck.)

Urushi trotted up while Crane was occupied, still faithfully holding the kawarimi reed in his
mouth.

“Hey,” I said quietly, holding out my hand for him to drop it. “Thank you. You didn’t get
hit?”

He wagged his tail, keeping it low to avoid drawing attention to it, and nosed curiously at the
bleeding hole in my thigh.

“Oh, no, that’s - here. Gone now.” I frowned as I dismissed the illusion. He’d not been
bothered because he’d easily identified it as fake, so how would I make an injury smell like
an injury? I doubted I’d ever have to fool the dogs, but Kakashi wasn’t the only nin with a
sensitive nose. Restricting myself just to visual genjutsu was stupid. I should fix that.

Crane politely made his footsteps audible to announce his presence. I scrambled to my feet,
suppressing a shiver as the lack of adrenalin made me aware again that I was soaked through
and freezing cold.

“You’re a genjutsu user,” he stated. He held his head still, but I got the impression he was
checking for any non-illusion wounds all the same. I nodded - probably unnecessarily - and
fervently hoped my fake ANBU uniform wasn’t as obvious as it suddenly felt like. Thank
god for the mask to hide my face. I didn’t know what expression would be on it, but I was
absolutely certain it would give me away.

All Crane did though was nod in return, pick up the scout’s unconscious body and sling it
over his shoulders, and turn to go back to the lake. “You’re good at it,” he said as Urushi and
I fell in behind him at an easy jog. “My apologies for interfering, I misread the situation.”

I nearly tripped. Should I say thank you? No worries? Did ANBU people say no worries?
Probably not. Definitely not in a high-pitched star-stuck kind of voice. Not that I was star-
struck, but still. ANBU probably didn't completely ignore each other either, so I mumbled
something that almost resembled words and hoped they conveyed the right meaning.
Internally, I was still caught on the casual you’re good at it - was this a positive sign that he’d
be willing to teach me? Not be my teacher, that was still Kakashi, but - I mean, I only wanted
to know the secret of his success and recreate his entire skillset for myself. That wasn’t too
much to ask. Right? Right. What were a few illusions between random ANBU and the
tagalong genin who wasn’t meant to be on the same mission as them but was anyway because
reasons. Entirely reasonable, that’s what.

… I should probably stick to my original plan of bribery, but I was going to take his praise as
a good omen all the same.
The strike team were dead. Fragments of Kidomaru’s hard exoskeleton littered the water
around him, but he himself looked remarkably normal and un-cursed, at least as much as
someone with six arms and a chidori where their heart should be could. Or, evidence of a
chidori. It wasn’t still chidori-ing now. As for Tayuya, she had the sort of neat, brutally
efficient kunai wound that spoke of someone being too distracted by one ANBU to notice the
other sneaking up behind them. It wasn’t dramatic or flashy, and for all we were ninja it was
the sort of tactic that was often frowned on by the idiots who cared more about honour than
practicality, but it was undeniably effective all the same.

There was one other corpse, multiple times larger than a normal human and just wrong
enough to be off-putting without it being obvious why. Ogre, I realised - that was what
Tayuya summoned, she summoned ogres. This one in particular had long hair hanging in a
solid sheet over its face, a black jumpsuit, and an enormous club covered in head-sized metal
studs. It was half-submerged in the marsh, and though I couldn’t quite tell with the way it had
slumped, I got the horrible feeling that it was missing most of its lower jaw. And chin. And -
oh god, please don’t say there was just a gaping void under all that hair. That would be. No.

Moving on.

I hung back while the other two dealt with the bodies. I’d never been taught how to prepare
one for sealing, and in the middle of a rainy battlefield while I was pretending to be someone
competent didn’t exactly seem like the best time to learn. For the sake of completeness
Urushi and I looped round in a quick patrol route to check for surviving enemies, but neither
of us were surprised when we didn’t find any. When I came back Crane was holding out the
scout’s arm (sans the hand, why did he have to choose that one) and pushing up the kimono
sleeve to show Kakashi something on her wrist.

I drifted closer to look. What I’d initially taken as more cursed-seal markings on her forearm
were clearly not, as despite the rest of her transformation fading these ones had stuck around.
They formed one long line, winding three times around her arm and stopping just where the
stump ended, with an odd open figure of eight at the end.

“Snake summoner,” Kakashi confirmed grimly. “Small snakes would be easy for the strike
team to keep with them, and they’re one of the stronger species. If they didn’t want to be
seen, they wouldn’t be.”

I blinked, glancing automatically at Urushi as I followed that to its conclusion. “The scout
summoned the snake, and the snake brought the strike team with them? That’s how they’ve
been getting around?” And if it was, could we do that with the dogs?

From Urushi’s curious and somewhat doubtful expression, he didn’t think so. Neither did
Pakkun, who’d parked himself between Urushi’s front legs and was resolutely using him as
an umbrella. “Not unless the snakes know something the rest of us don’t,” he said. “We can
bring people to the summon realm if we need to, but not from one point in the human world
to another.”

“Ok, so, how likely is that?” He tilted his head curiously at me, and I elaborated, “That the
snakes figured it out.”
  “They’re snakes. If it’s not a new way to swallow their tails instead of chasing them, they
  don’t care.”

  Well. That didn’t sound dismissive at all, Pakkun. What snake bit you and turned you
  grumpy. I opened my mouth to argue the point, but Crane cut across before I could.

  “Orochimaru’s an inventor,” he said diplomatically. “He’s more interested in the summon
  realm than most. It wouldn’t be impossible for him to have developed something with the
  snakes that they couldn’t have done by themselves.”

  “It’s the most likely explanation,” Kakashi agreed. “Either way, we won’t know for sure until
  the scout can be questioned. We’ll pass our theories on to the relevant people, but our mission
  is retrieval, not interrogation.” His gaze lingered on the byakugan implanted in the scout’s
  other hand, expression tightening; its removal was another thing that would have to wait,
  none of us were skilled enough medic nins to handle eye transplants.

  Not that eye transplants should be a thing. If Hinata didn’t have it, no one should have it, and
  we were all skilled enough with a kunai to destroy it. But. Not my decision.

  Crane nodded smoothly, and I mimicked it on instinct, though I wasn’t sure I quite nailed his
  professionalism. Konoha had a base camp not too far from us, set in the marshes a short way
  back from the border with Rice. With Kidomaru’s and Tayuya’s corpses sealed away and the
  scout kept unconscious by a stasis seal, we took off, pushing hard and fast to reach safety
  before Sound could send someone to intercept us.

  Ten minutes into the run I gave up being cold and shifted my chakra to fire. It helped, but not
  enough, and a few minutes after that I subtly pressed my palms against the tenketsu points in
  my chest and activated the immolation jutsu. I would still much rather be out on a mission
  with Kakashi than back in Konoha without him, but bloody hell. I thought it was meant to be
  summer. Also my socks were wet through and I couldn’t readjust them because I was henged
  into a stupid uniform that didn’t even have socks, so my feet were not only getting frost bite,
  they were getting blisters on top of it just for fun.

  And Urushi was running with Kakashi because ANBU Hound wasn’t meant to be a dog
  summoner. Why was ANBU Hound not meant to be a dog summoner. It was in the fecking
  name. ANBU Hound. Ridiculous.

  The rain lightened from a monsoon downpour to a steady, soul-destroying drizzle that lasted
  until exactly seven minutes before the camp finally came into view. The clouds cleared, the
  moon came out, the stars sparkled merrily in the sky, and I took full advantage of the fact that
  I had a mask on to scowl up at them in outrage for their timing.

  Ridiculous.

   Interlude: Team leader of a divided team

   She picked at dinner. Again. It was rice, grilled pork, more pickled vegetables to accompany
   it than a dinner for two strictly deserved. Tomorrow’s lunch was already made and set aside
   in the fridge; leftovers onigiri, half in neat triangle shapes, half painstakingly - lopsidedly -
   moulded into little white dog faces.

   Her dad hadn’t quite grasped the concept of Tsuki as a summon dog. He thought she was a
   delight, small and fluffy and adorable and absolutely shameless about showing off in front of
   him. Sakura didn’t quite know how to bring up that summons meant clan and that accepting
   Tsuki while rejecting Kakashi had lost her a teammate, so she didn’t. Perhaps if her mum
   were there, but her mum was stuck in the capital on the other side of a war blockade, and her
   dad was doing his best to be supportive of everything she did. It didn’t feel right to disappoint
   him.

   Not that he’d be disappointed. That wasn’t his style. You can’t change a fact by frowning at
   it, he’d tell her. Smile instead, and go where life takes you with an open mind. The world is
   as it is, little flower. It’s up to you to be happy with it or not.

   Sasuke would not have agreed.

   Sakura picked at dinner, smiling for her dad and brushing it off as nothing important, and
   went out after to train. It was a better use of daylight than anything else she had to do.



   “Pakkun wants you,” Tsuki said, ears swinging forwards and curly tail lifting up. “I can get
   him?”

   Sakura didn’t slow from her jog. “Sure.” She dismissed Tsuki in one motion, counted four
   steps, then bit her thumb and smeared it over the scroll to resummon her again, Pakkun
   appearing seamlessly alongside. “Jiraiya’s in another meeting. Try the Hokage tower, he
   should be finished soon.”

   “It can wait,” Pakkun assured her. “I don’t only come back to talk to him.”

   She held her tongue on what she wanted to say in response to that. Pakkun didn’t add
   anything further though, just settled into a steady trot beside her, deceptively dignified for
   how fast his short legs were going to keep up.

   They ran in silence for long enough that it started to feel awkward.
“How are the others?” Sakura finally asked. Tsuki perked up to listen; she hadn’t taken well
to Sasuke leaving. She hadn’t understood why Sakura and Naruto couldn’t just go and join
her, or why they had to stay with the coward-man when Kitten and the big dog-man were
somewhere else. Neither had Naruto - Sasuke was team, she belonged with them in a way
that Jiraiya and Kakashi did not, and though he said it was for Sasuke’s benefit that they
should find her and bring her back, Sakura knew that it was at least in part for his. He and
Sasuke had barely spent a night apart since - since the Wave mission. With everything he’d
faced, growing up alone and hated and even Sakura used to ignore him whenever she could,
she couldn’t exactly blame him for latching on to someone who so obviously cared. She
could think (though not be tactless enough to say) that it made him react emotionally rather
than rationally, but she couldn’t blame him.

Sakura didn’t have that excuse. She was a civilian in a ninja world, sure, it came with its own
problems, but she’d never lived through what Naruto had. Or Sasuke. And she’d been trying
to be more understanding of that - she knew she wasn’t the best at it, but sometimes she
thought it would’ve been easier to work with her teammates’ needs if her teammates would
tell her what their needs actually were. Provide meat alternatives, yes, try to keep them safe
even if the world seemed determined to stop her, sure, be patient with their secrets rather than
demanding they share what they weren’t comfortable with - but. I don’t know what to do,
she’d said. I want to help but I’m not and I’m sorry. What can I do?

And Sasuke had shrugged, and said, Come see the fish?

“Sorry, Pup,” Pakkun said, like he had done for the last three visits that Sakura had asked.
“Still classified.” He licked his nose, then added, “But good. She’s doing good.”

Sakura nodded. “I’m glad,” she said honestly, shaking herself out of her pointless musing.
Sasuke had told her what she needed; not in so many words, perhaps, but actions speak
louder and Sasuke was rarely quiet with those. She’d needed Kakashi. She had Kakashi.
Maybe Sakura still didn’t see why Kakashi was so important - he wasn’t a good sensei, he’d
left too much of the leading to Sakura and too much of the teaching to literally anyone else
for Sakura to have built that kind of trust in him - but it was Sasuke’s decision, not hers, and
like Pakkun said. She was doing well. And if Sakura was going to be a good team leader, a
good friend, then she’d respect that, even if neither Tsuki nor Naruto understood.

“I’m glad,” she repeated, stronger, putting her doubts aside. She wouldn’t get anywhere by
worrying. Sasuke was where she wanted to be, Jiraiya wasn’t ideal but he was teaching
Sakura what she needed to know, and she’d hardly be able to support Naruto by dithering.
The world is as it is, little flower. It wasn’t going to wait for her to have a crisis over it not
being fair.

She changed course so her path would take her up the Hokage monument, settled into a better
stride, and kept running.

The entire situation at the camp, I decided, was designed specifically to annoy me and I
would be well within my rights to set the place on fire.
Well. That may have been a slight exaggeration. Only a slight one though, and it didn’t
change the fact that my feelings were valid and would not be denied - even if they would be
difficult to act on, given how damp and soggy everything was. Because it was shit. All of it. I
mean, fine, the semi-flooded areas that made up northern Fire Country were great for paddy
fields, but consider please the fact that I wasn’t a farmer. I liked the dry forests to the south.
They were dry.

Semi-flooded areas were large bodies of still water. Large bodies of still water, particularly in
the height of summer, had mosquitos.

For entirely unrelated reasons I’d become practiced enough with the immolation jutsu to keep
my skin running at a permanent fever-temperature, with side benefits of flambeing any mini
bloodsuckers that attempted to grab hold. Yes, it was uncomfortable. Yes, it was tiring to
keep my chakra as fire for long stretches at a time. No, I wasn’t taking constructive criticism
on my coping methods, piss off.

Kakashi’s hand was like ice against my forehead, I couldn’t stop myself leaning into it if I
tried.

“You’re warm,” he said, frowning in worry. I waved him off.

“Mosquitos. Don’t worry, I’m fine.”

He didn’t seem convinced. “Don’t ignore fevers. Chakra only burns out most diseases, it
never protects you from all of them. The mosquitos round here can be deadly if you’re not
careful.”

I blinked. “It’s just a stay-warm jutsu,” I said, somewhat taken aback. “It keeps the insects
away.” Then, moving past that to the far more important question of, “Why did they build the
camp in the middle of a swarm of killer insects?” I knew, obviously, that insect-borne
diseases were a thing, but Konoha had the Aburame clan. The diseases were a thing, but a
thing that happened to other people who lived far away where amazing people like Shino
didn’t exist to protect them.

“They didn’t, actually. Samurai did. Do you have a headache?”

“Head - no? What do you mean samurai did, there haven’t been any samurai for -”

“Rash? Nausea, muscle aches?”

I batted him away, wrinkling my nose and sitting pointedly back on my heels so I was out of
reach. “Urushi would’ve smelt it if I was sick,” I told him, gesturing down at the base of the
wall where Urushi was napping in the sun. He, at least, didn’t seem bothered by the insects -
Pakkun said that summons didn’t have the same kind of blood as other animals, there was
nothing for the mosquitos to care about. He didn’t tell me until after I’d spent a full day
carefully carrying Urushi up to the highest parts of the camp so we’d both be out of reach of
the worst offenders, but it had been good practice for us to get used to scaling walls together,
so. I allowed it. “Go back to the samurai, they’re interesting. How are there samurai?”
“The same way there’s anyone else,” Kakashi said, accepting my change of topic dubiously.
“Less now than there used to be. This isn’t a recent camp, though - see the ditch? The wall’s
new, but the ditch marks where the old samurai base was from when Fire Country expanded
north.”

I squinted. I’d assumed the ditch was a natural consequence of using doton jutsu to pull up
the compressed earth and stone mix that the wall and most of the buildings were made of, but
if I looked for evidence of it being older, then. Maybe? It was hard to tell with how wet
everything was. I think I might’ve known, in a general sense, that Fire Country had a military
past that had led to them becoming one of the larger of the Elemental Countries, but samurai
history wasn’t my forte. Konoha certainly didn’t teach it, and the clan had been more
concerned with our own wars than other people’s.

“Ok, so. Why did the samurai build their camp in a swarm of killer insects?”

“Ah.” Kakashi tilted his head thoughtfully. “Maybe there weren’t any back then?”

“There weren’t any.”

He eye-smiled winningly. “Or maybe they didn’t mind. It’s a good place to control the
marshes from, that could’ve been more important.”

“No one doesn’t mind being chewed on. It’s inhumane. The camp’s huge, there must be an
Aburame here somewhere, why has no one fixed this. It’s gross.”

“Saa, you’re being grumpy again. Shall we help out the mess hall or the hospital tent this
time?”

I pulled a face. We’d delivered the scout in the early hours of yesterday morning, been
instructed to stay within the borders of the camp and await further orders, and not heard
anything since. Technically, both Kakashi and I were here on ANBU business and outside the
jurisdiction of either the genin corps or the Jounin commander - I’d run into Shikaku last
night (literally run into, I was mortified and half-convinced he’d done it on purpose because
what, I don’t run into people) which was the only reason I knew he was here, given how little
information anyone gave us. No, I wasn’t sore about that, because I did actually understand
how confidential worked, but also yes I was annoyed because I really wanted to know what
was happening with the scout that, you know, we spent a week hunting down in the rain. But
anyway. Outside of Kakashi’s role in ANBU, no one should be giving him orders. Outside of
my role as Kakashi’s student, no one should be giving me orders. In theory. In reality, we
were at war, the genin corps were stressed as fuck, and we were lending a hand where we
could.

“Mess hall,” I chose, as I had done the past three times Kakashi had decided we needed
something other than training to occupy ourselves. I dropped down next to Urushi and
Pakkun, Kakashi landing beside me with a soundless thump. “Do you reckon they’ll have
found a fruit that grows here yet? Pears have good roots. I bet pears would grow here. I love
that they have fish, but fish aren’t sweet. We should plant pears. Why are you looking at me
like that.”
“I was just thinking that someone should’ve told me earlier how food-motivated you were. It
would’ve made training a lot easier.”

I scowled at him, but Pakkun just huffed and let his tongue loll out. “I did tell you,” he
pointed out, and I shifted my scowl to him. And stuck my own tongue out, because I had one
too, and if he was going to be rude to me I could be rude back to him, so. So there.



The camp was large. I hadn’t been sure at first, but the longer we spent there the more
convinced I was that I was right: it wasn’t just a camp in the north near the border with Rice
and Sound, it was the camp. The big one. I already knew Shikaku was here, and if the scout
was as important as everyone said, I wouldn’t be surprised if Inoichi was the one leading her
interrogation. It made sense, in a Konoha sort of way. Orochimaru had gone to a lot of effort
firstly to get the byakugan and then secondly to keep secret the fact that he was using it;
getting it back and killing the scout before we got any useful information from her would be
high on his priority list. Our options were either to hide that we had her - or at least where we
had her - for as long as possible, or to put her somewhere so well defended he wouldn’t dare
trying to retrieve her.

Guess which one Konoha went for. You know, that sneaky ninja village, full of sneaky ninjas.
Guess.

Though, maybe I was missing some of the subtext. My grasp on ninja politics was filtered
somewhat erratically through my mum’s simplified teachings and what I’d learnt through the
clan histories and memoirs (which even I could admit were biased and old fashioned, but in
my defence the warring states weren’t that long ago and the basic principles of one-
upmanship hadn’t changed much in the interim) - but civilian politics? I. No. There was a
Daimyo. He was meant to be the one in charge, except his wife had more contact with
Konoha than he did and she mainly used us as a cat retrieval service. That was… about all I
knew.

Did it even count as Fire and Rice being at war if Konoha and Sound were? I was guessing
not because the war declaration had come from the Hokage and not the Daimyo and because
no one was officially sending any Konoha nin over the border into Rice, but on the other
hand, really? Sound had disrupted trade across the entire country. If Kakashi was right, then
Konoha had moved into the old Samurai stronghold, you know, no reason, certainly not a
warning to Rice’s Daimyo to fall in line and remember what happened last time Fire attacked
them, how could I possibly think it was anything to do with that?

I mean. If it wasn’t a deliberate warning to Rice, then way to accidentally insult an entire
country. Or maybe civilian politics just worked differently. No self respecting Uchiha clan
head would pass up the opportunity to throw shade like that, but like I said, I didn’t have
much experience with Daimyos. The fact that we weren’t officially sending ninja over the
border didn’t stop a steady stream of stealth missions going out in a suspiciously north-ward
direction each night, so. I could be reading too much into things. Not the genin corps - those
were occupied manning patrols and outposts and trying to fix the infrastructure the remaining
scout-and-strike-team kept destroying - but the corps weren’t the only ninja in the camp.
“Sasuke,” Kakashi said abruptly, appearing in front of me in a swirl of shunshin. “I’m
teaching you.”

I abandoned my attempts to replace the water chakra in my chakra arms with fire chakra so I
could use them while keeping the immolation jutsu running at the same time. We were yet
another day down, and any hope I had for being told what was happening with the scout we’d
caught was dwindling fast. “Yes? You are?” I frowned. “If Jiraiya’s trying -”

“Ah, not quite.” He shook his head, and sank down to a much more comfortable crouch
beside me. “I meant, now. Right now. I’m teaching you. What do you want to learn?”

I paused. Urushi lifted an ear, but didn’t otherwise seem bothered by anything, so I doubted
right now was a code I was meant to know. Pakkun was absent again, and therefore no help.
But if I were a Jounin commander and I had Kakashi sitting around not doing anything in my
camp... “You’re too busy for a mission because you have me?”

He bopped me on the head. “Saa, you don’t always need to worry about why people do
things. You’re too insightful as it is.”

I wrinkled my nose. There was no such thing as too insightful. I liked knowing what was
going on. “You’re not too busy, but the mission’s too dangerous for a genin, and you don’t
want to leave me behind.” By his long-suffering expression, I was either right, or close
enough that it counted. I dropped a hand down to Urushi’s fur, and ducked my head to hide
my smile behind my hair. Not wanting to leave me behind was an excellent reason to refuse a
mission. If anyone asked, Kakashi had been drilling me mercilessly from sunup to midnight,
the training was of vital importance and couldn’t possibly be skipped, and if they didn’t
believe it I’d call them out for doubting the integrity of not one but two clan heads and set
Shiba on them for the insolence.

Unless they were Shikaku. In which case I’d just. Not be there. Foolproof.

In the present though, “Teach me how to add scents? And sounds. I can do the visual part of
genjutsu, but Urushi can smell the difference every time.”

“Scents,” Kakashi repeated, frowning thoughtfully. “You’ll do better encouraging people that
something’s real and letting them fill in the details themselves, but I can show you some. Tell
me if I’m making them too weak for you - I don’t know how bad your nose is.”

I nearly let that slide, because he was Kakashi, then remembered that he’d been brought up
by Pakkun and Pakkun liked to mess with people on purpose. I shouldn’t be encouraging him
to follow suit. “It’s not bad. It’s human. It might even be good, you don’t know. Your nose
doesn’t count, it’s been dogified.” He raised an eyebrow, and I huffed, but held firm. “I’ll tell
you, but it’ll be because you’re underestimating me and making them too strong. My nose is
fine.”



My nose, it turned out, was a lot less fine than Kakashi’s was. Given that Kakashi’s was
literally superhuman that didn’t necessarily mean anything, but I chose not to mention it all
the same. We got my illusions to a stage where your average ninja would be fooled, Urushi
could still tell the difference every time, it was grand. Moving on.



By the third day, it was getting difficult to hide my restlessness. As nice a thought as it was
that Kakashi had turned down any missions because he didn’t want to lead me into danger, by
this stage, I was struggling to believe it. There had to be some reason Shikaku was keeping
him close. I mean, we'd already brought in one strike team, surely we could at least be sent
after the other? Mess hall duty was fine, but it was hardly the best use of someone on
Kakashi’s level. Unfortunately - or potentially fortunately, depending how you looked at it - I
didn’t run into Shikaku again to ask him, but I did see him a few times, mostly by virtue of
spending as much time as possible perched up high to escape the mosquitos. I amused myself
by comparing his body language to Shikamaru and seeing if I could read anything from how
aggressively slouched he was at any given time. No, was the answer, but I did manage to spot
Inoichi once, so. Jounin Commander and Head of T&I's presence in the camp confirmed. Go
me.

Watching them from a distance did jack all to tell me what they’d learnt from the scout. Or
what they’d decided to do with the information. The genin corps were still being sent out -
often with Suna nin - to mend bridges and man outposts (and, presumably for the Suna nin, to
die horrible deaths along the way in case they turned out to be enemies); the assorted chuunin
and jounin in the camp were still heading up towards the border in small groups and coming
back under the cover of darkness; Kakashi was beginning to get twitchy in a way that said he
wasn’t any better at sitting around when everything was so tense than I was, he just had more
experience of it; I’d worked so many shifts in the mess hall I could be on first name terms
with the corps members that staffed it if I wanted to be -

War, I was learning, was a lot of waiting, a lot of being kept in the dark, and only a very little
action or horrific suffering. Even the Hokage had left the front lines to go back to Konoha. If
the insect death trap even counted as a front line given how little had happened here. Pakkun
brought us enough news from Jiraiya to know that there’d been no attacks on the village
itself, and with the new measures in place to shore up the defences no one really thought
there would be.

I felt… cheated. Not cheated. That sounds like I was looking forward to war being awful,
which I wasn’t, but I’d at least expected it to be worse than this. So far it was more
inconvenient than anything else. Yes, people were dying, but. We were ninja. People died a
lot. How was I supposed to convince people that war was terrible and we should avoid it at
all costs if war didn’t follow through and be terrible to back me up?

Maybe I wasn’t. Maybe it wasn’t. Or maybe that was bullshit, and something didn’t have to
be universally, relentlessly gruesome to still qualify as a human rights violation, but then
what was it about war in particular that made it so much worse than anything else? Like I
said, we were ninja. We killed people all the time. It wasn’t great, but I thought war would
be… more. Tangibly different. Like you could draw a line under it and say no, this was a step
too far, the other stuff was bad but this was unreasonable and evil and had to stop. Except I
didn’t think I could.
I didn’t have an answer. I didn’t know how to explain it enough to ask Kakashi either, and
though Urushi whined sympathetically and tried to lick my face to cheer me up, I wasn’t sure
he understood. I wasn’t sure I understood. I’d never been in a war before.

“Equipment,” I told him as we approached the storage building. “Apparently the corps
centralise their supplies and maintenance, they don’t ask everyone to provide their own.” I
pulled a face. We’d been taught back in the academy how to sharpen a kunai and keep it from
rusting, I was sure the corps did at least that for themselves, but a ninja’s life was in their
tools. I’d rather be in control of things myself, thanks, even if that meant I lacked the range
the corps were given access to.

“We’re helping out. Makes a change from the mess hall, at least. Not that I mind the mess
hall. Giant cooking pots are fun, the curry’s just under-spiced. People need to stop being so
wussy, it doesn’t taste of anything if it isn’t at least a little hot. Shunting me off to stack
shuriken is - wait a minute, I know you.”

I blinked. The equipment building was a low, doton-made bunker, with a far greater emphasis
on practicality than ventilation. It wasn’t horrendously lit inside but there also wasn’t an
abundance of electricity this far into the middle of marsh-land, and the small windows and
sharp contrast from the sun outside made it harder to see than I would’ve liked. Still - I
recognised that hair. Wild, messy, at odds with the neat precision of the ninja underneath it;
I’d found Crane.

In the form of Shop-san Suisei.

I squinted.

“Morning, Uchiha-kun,” he greeted politely. “Are you here in search of something?”

I squinted harder, carefully keeping my face muscles still so it was only my eyes that
narrowed. If it was anyone other than Crane, I’d activate my sharingan to check if his hair
was the illusion I suspected it was, but given that it was Crane he’d almost certainly be able
to see through my dark-eyes genjutsu. Without the safety of Kakashi’s mask to hide behind, I
couldn’t risk it.

“Here to help,” I said distractedly, swinging my arm in what I hoped was a natural movement
to try and catch Urushi’s attention. “They said the corps needed some weapons
maintenance?”

It had to be Crane. The voice was off, but not by a lot, and I already knew the masks
disguised that. Besides, voices were easy enough to change if you knew how. A genjutsu
expert specialising in disguises would definitely know how. His height matched, his hands
were the same size, he even held himself a similar way - and seriously, what were the chances
of him not being Crane? How many people fitting his description could the camp be expected
to have? How many people fitting his description who weren’t surprised to see me, even.
Most of the camp assumed I was a random member of the genin corps, either Suisei just
didn’t realise how odd it was that I was here or he already knew I was because he’d
recognised me when I was being Hound.
“It’s no trouble,” he promised. “But if you’re happy to, then I could certainly use the
company.”

Urushi yawned and lay down next to me, giving his tail a lazy wag against my ankle as he did
so. He recognised Suisei as a friend at least, but even without his confirmation I was already
slotting information together. Suisei took random odd jobs covering shifts because he was out
of the village a lot, that was something Naruto’d mentioned before. That fit with ANBU.
Better, that fit with long-term undercover missions, the sort of missions that were perfect for
a genjutsu specialist no one had heard of before - I’d bet anything that his genjutsu skills
were kept out of his official records to stop an enemy making the connection. And his hair,
obviously his hair as Suisei was the illusion. It would let him wear his real hair on his
mission and keep Suisei - and Crane - completely separate from his undercover persona. Can
you imagine being caught in enemy territory with a constantly running henge? You’d be
dead. It made so much more sense to do it this way round.

Not that anyone would catch him. He was too good for that. I’d thought he was perfect before
but I hadn’t understood the extent of it; his illusions were flawless, he could literally dance
between the raindrops he was so fast, he was proven sneaky and cunning in exactly the way a
ninja should be, and he was on the very short list of people who were nice to Naruto and
therefore allowed to continue. Konoha didn’t deserve him. He needed rescuing. We worked
well with him before, Kakashi and I could add him to our team. He was made for us.

He was also reaching for a whetstone and asking over his shoulder if I was familiar at all with
swords, and I may potentially have interrupted him when I blurted, “Do you like ice cream
and will you teach me genjutsu?”

He paused. I paused. Urushi didn’t pause, just dropped his chin to the ground and disavowed
all connection to me.

Genuinely, I swear, I can be subtle when I need to be.

“I’m more partial to sweets, myself,” Suisei finally said. “Or seaweed, though that isn’t quite
the same.” He passed me the whetstone, along with a sheathed short sword that looked
identical to the standard ANBU tanto. “I’m guessing you prefer ice cream?”

“Sweets are good. I like sweets. Not chocolate, it’s boring. Except if you like chocolate then
it’s probably fine, even though it isn’t actually a sweet, but if you want it to be then it can be
and I won’t call it boring anymore - but do you like other sweets? Other sweets are better
unless you don't like them then that’s ok too and um, I should, I’ll just sharpen this. I’ll. Yes.”

Why. When I didn’t want people to like me, they ended up declaring themselves my friends.
When I actually did want to make a good first impression on someone, I produced this. Why.
Why. The world was unjust and cruel, and I was going to take my tanto and my whetstone
and sit against the wall as I checked it over, and then everyone would forget this ever
happened and things could be good again. I hadn’t missed that Suisei had dodged the
genjutsu question but I also wasn’t going to risk pressing it at the moment because who knew
what string of nonsense words I’d come out with if I tried.
Thankfully, Suisei seemed more gently amused than anything else, and was happy to leave
me to it while he busied himself with other tasks. He hadn’t given me anything to oil the
sword with so I assumed it was fine on that front, but the biggest danger to metal tools -
particularly in a hot, wet environment like the one we were in - was water damage. I used my
fingertips to check the scabbard for cracks or anywhere that needed re-waxing, and only
moved onto the blade when I was sure everything else was fine.

When I pulled it out though, I hesitated. Swords weren’t a clan weapon or taught in the
academy, and Kakashi had never shown an inclination to pass those particular skills on, but I
was at least vaguely familiar with what a tanto should look like. Or, what Itachi’s tanto
looked like, and as his was ANBU issue I assumed it was pretty standard. This one looked...
off? Maybe. No it definitely did, it just took me a second to work out why.

“You’re more used to the shinogi?” Suisei guessed when he saw my confusion. I blinked up
at him, and he elaborated, “The ridge down the length of the blade.”

“No, I know what it is.” I hadn’t known what it was called, but I knew what it was. He was
right; where Itachi’s had a clear divide between a thicker side and a thinner, cutting edge, the
blade of this tanto was one flat piece, more like a kitchen knife than what I thought of as a
sword. Still deadly, I was sure, and still strong enough to do what it was designed to - but not
as strong as it could be if it had been made with more support. “I was just trying to work out
why you’d leave it off.”

“For cost, Uchiha-kun. These ones are faster to make, and the smithing process is easier to
learn.”

My confusion turned to an annoyed frustration. “That’s stupid. People die if their weapons
break. Genin corps are people, that means they die. Cutting corners because they’re not full
ninja is shit.”

Suisei was quiet, enough that my brain caught up to my mouth and I remembered - he wasn’t
Kakashi, or even Sakura or Naruto. Your average Konoha citizen might not be quite as
blindly obedient as I’d used to assume they were, but badmouthing the system so carelessly
was still not the best idea I’d ever had. I glanced up at him, keeping my head angled down
and my shoulders deliberately relaxed as I waited for his response.

All he said was, “Your beliefs are admirable, Uchiha-kun.” I wrinkled my nose; they weren’t
admirable beliefs, they were basic facts. There was a difference. He flashed me a smile when
he noticed my offence, soft and almost sad but gone too fast for me to properly read it. “It’s a
good thing,” he promised me, which was completely missing the point. “I hope you’re able to
keep them. May I suggest though that you don’t call the genin corps ‘not full ninja’ where
they can hear you?”

“Sorry,” I said, fighting the sudden urge to glance around the room to check no one had been
in earshot. They hadn’t been - other than the three of us, the storage room was empty - so I
turned back to the sword in my hands. “Do you want me to just sharpen it, or…?”

“There’s always more when you’ve finished with that one, but if you notice anything that
needs doing then let me know. And I’m sorry too; I can’t teach you any genjutsu today, but
maybe another time.” He tilted his head apologetically, and offered, “When we’re back in
Konoha, perhaps, if your sensei approves.”

I chewed my lip, trying to decipher if there was any ulterior motive, but if there was I
couldn’t see one. I was being too cynical, I decided. Suisei was nice. A little bit melancholy
behind the politeness, but nice. Naruto liked him, Kakashi called him loyal, and my instincts
said to trust him.

“When we’re back in Konoha,” I agreed. “I’ll bring sweets. But not chocolate, I lied about
that being good. Unless you really like it, but fruit sweets are still better. They’ve got colours.
And flavour. Chocolate’s fine too. I can bring chocolate, unless it’s not your favourite, then I
won’t because we deserve better in life than that.”

Fucking hell, brain. Stop.

“I like both,” Suisei assured me, and I smiled back at him rather than risk opening my mouth
again.



Sound attacked at sunset. The egrets had flown over on their daily migration an hour or so
before, the sky was a burnt-orange fading to a starry black, and the clouds were pink-outlined
silhouettes against it. I was in the middle of the camp, perched on the tall centre-pole of one
of the octagonal accommodation tents, waiting for the mosquitos to calm down so it would be
safe to return to ground level for the night. My immolation jutsu was running hot, and I was
down to a loose crop top and a baggy pair of pants in an attempt not to overheat.

They were borrowed from the corps. The clothes, not Sound. Following your sensei to war
with only the clothes on your back sounds great in theory, but without the pressing urgency of
a tracking mission to keep you distracted the reality of permanently lived-in clothes was a lot
harder to ignore. I still wore my own clothes, but I also washed them as frequently as
possible, and instead of washing myself at the same time and wearing damp clothes until both
they and I dried together, I’d just… not done that.

The camp was huge. Kakashi was there. Shikamaru’s dad was there. I spent most of my time
training or helping out with menial chores. Maybe saying I felt safe wasn’t right but I hadn’t
seen the harm in borrowing some clean clothes for the evening while I waited for mine to dry.

And then the sun went down, and Sound attacked the camp.

They came so fast.

One ninja, travelling low. Left hand held in front of his face, byakugan exposed on the back
of it. The other scout. He wasn’t supposed to be here - he was supposed to be way off to the
east, summoning his strike team to mess with our supply trains from the coast and harass our
fishing villages. Scouts travelled on foot; it shouldn’t have been possible for him to have got
here so fast. Except - behind him, curving round to approach the camp from the other side; a
girl. Red hair. No byakugan (where would she have got it from? Hinata only had two eyes) or
if she had it she wasn’t using it in her hand like the other scouts had. She didn’t seem to need
it, evading the patrols just as deftly as her partner did. The only reason I saw her - him, either
of them - was because I had my sharingan open to monitor the insect levels.

I shifted to high alert, leaning forwards to drop down and raise the alarm. The movement
should have been too subtle for either of them to notice but the girl turned towards me all the
same, honing in on my position -

“Karin,” I breathed, wide-eyed. She grinned at me, cocky and confident, and held a finger to
her lips. I flicked my gaze down to her bare forearm as she did so; it was tattooed with the
same snake-summoning seal that the scouts used to summon their strike teams. And if the
strike teams could be summoned, then, logically, so could the scouts; the male scout had been
way off by the coast. Karin hadn’t been. She’d been using her chakra sense to get close
enough to the camp to call him, and now they were nearly at the gates and Konoha was only
starting to realise they were there, and I’d been so thrown by seeing Karin that I hadn’t
reacted in time and other people in the camp had already spotted them.

As soon as the alarm call went up, they abandoned stealth. Karin’s chain shot out to keep the
first responders at a distance while she ran through the seals of the summoning jutsu, and
when she slammed her hand into the boggy marsh, six ninja appeared, armed to the teeth and
already diving forwards to fight. The other scout did the same from his side of the camp; he
summoned Jirobo, Sakun and Ukon, and Kimimaro. Karin barely gave herself a moment’s
pause before moving again, six more ninja spilling out to join the fray - then again, again,
again until there were another twelve, eighteen, twenty four Sound and Suna nin. The genin
corps were pushing out to meet them but they were genin corps and the Suna genin already in
the camp were turning on them as well and they'd never been genin to begin with, Suna had
always been stacking the exam with chunin and then people were dying, I couldn’t tell you
what happened I don’t know what happened I heard people shouting and Jirobo grew four
times his size and was crushing people and a flash of silver to my left marked Kabuto with
his hands glowing blue as he cut people open with his scalpels and just ran past them while
they bled and the war had gone from inconvenient to chaotic I was sorry I’d ever doubted it -

“Sasuke,” Kakashi repeated, voice steady despite the tension in it. His fingers were on my
chin, pulling insistently until I looked at him. “Sharingan off. Now.”

“But -”

“Now, Sasuke.” He held my gaze until I complied, too shaken to argue. “It stays off, unless
you need it to survive. These aren’t memories you want to keep.”

“They’re fighting,” I said weakly. “We should -”

“Wear this,” he interrupted, all but putting Hound’s ANBU mask on my face for me. “Get
clear, and stay hidden. If it looks like someone’s found you, run - your speed is your greatest
asset.”

Over his shoulder, one of the ninja I’d worked with in the mess hall started convulsing,
collapsing in on herself as she died. Her killer stepped out from behind her, a nameless Sound
nin, I had no way of telling who. His right side was covered in armour, his left side in bits of
  people, and Crane appeared beside him in the next second and dropped him with a single
  kunai slice before shunshining on to kill someone else.

  “Run,” I repeated, my voice as flat as I could make it. Calm - no. Flat was the best I could do.
  “Run, yes, I can run. Can Urushi -”

  “Urushi will go with you,” Kakashi said, shoulders dropping a fraction in relief. Had he
  expected me to be stubborn about it? He’d made me promise not to fight. I didn’t want to
  fight. Bullheaded bravery was for the very strong and the very dead, I’d always chosen to
  survive. “He can lead you back here when it’s safe, or to another rendezvous point if it isn’t.”

  I nodded, already searching for the best thing to kawarimi with to get out of the camp. Not
  the furthest; without my sharingan, I was limited in distance, so I couldn’t afford to pick the
  wrong direction. Sand and Sound had started just outside the camp but the walls on two sides
