Some, based on my past experience, would lead to the formless grey void where sounds
didn’t exist.

I’d rather avoid that option, if I could. If Pakkun hadn’t pulled me out with the others, I
honestly wasn’t sure I’d’ve been able to leave.

I paused, chewing my lip as I assessed the threads. Or - I didn’t have a lip to chew, I was an
amorphous mass of water that was in danger of dissolving into nothing if I didn’t pay
attention to where I stopped and the river began, but my brain remembered what having lips
was like and what it felt like to chew on them. It was close enough, and thinking of myself as
a physical being with a body made it easier to stay separate from the chakra around me.

But; Pakkun. The dog contract. Bridges across the river. I hadn’t signed it so I couldn’t use it,
but I had given Urushi enough blood - however unintentionally - to form a similar
connection, and that was my best bet for getting out.

I hoped.

“Urushi,” I tried, throwing the name out to the river. “Um, he’s a dog. He wears a bandana
and a vest thing, his fur’s grey. With, he’s got white bits, and his tail’s fluffy. So’s the top of
his head. He likes melon?”

Nothing. Was I misremembering? No, it had definitely responded to my connection with
Urushi before. More to the point, I didn’t have any other ideas, so this one really needed to
work.

I swallowed, and kept talking. “He’s loyal. He’s not that heavy, but he wriggles when you try
and carry him. He can’t climb. When… When I panic, he knows how to stop me, and he
listens when I need to talk. He, um. He makes things better.” Still nothing. I tried to run my
fingers through my hair, but that was an action that didn’t quite translate to water-physics. “I
don’t know what you want me to say,” I admitted. “I just want to go back to him.”

And - there. A handful of threads, curling off to the side; they twisted together, growing
brighter and straightening out. One end was anchored to me, the other disappeared off further
than I could see. If I relaxed my guard I could feel the river’s current tugging at me, pulling
me along to follow it.

I blinked. “Well, ok then. Thank you.”
I reached after it and the river fell away, the lights winking out and the threads snapping
around me. It deposited me in a heap, one hand flung forward for balance as I adjusted to the
unfairly weird sensation of being squished into a body again, full of wet and cold and the
itchiness of dirt and blood drying against my skin.

Urushi’s startled growl stuttered into a whine. His first step forward was cautious, head low
and nostrils flaring as he sniffed, then his tail went up and he pressed closer, paws in my lap
as he climbed on me and tongue licking frantically at my chin.

“I know,” I promised him, burying my hands in the long fur over his neck and subtly
checking him over for injuries. “I know, I’m sorry, I’m back. All good. I’m sorry. I’m back.
Not leaving again.”

He abandoned my chin in favour of everywhere else he could find, ears going back as he
identified the blood on my clothes as mine.

“No - healed now. See? Karin fixed it. Don’t blame Gaara, I don’t think he knows how sleep
works. He tried.”

Even as I reassured him, I activated my sharingan and checked around us to see where we
were. Not too far from the camp was the answer - I could see it clearly, but in this darkness I
doubted they could see me. Not unless they also had a vision-enhancing dojutsu, at least.

Wait. Hyuuga were a thing, that wasn’t something I could rely on.

But no one reacted to my appearance, and other than an assortment of suspiciously corpse-
shaped objects that I really didn’t want to inspect too closely, I didn’t see anything in our
immediate vicinity either. No Gaara, no Kabuto, no Karin; just remnants of sand, which I
guessed Urushi had been doggedly following in an attempt to track down where I’d gone.

The battlefield was almost eerily quiet.

How… how long had I been in the river for?

“What happened?” I asked, one shade above a murmur. “They can’t have killed all the Sound
and Sand nin.” Could they? Stars were harder to tell time from than the sun was, but I didn’t
think it’d been that long. Maybe they could have done? Konoha had been winning before
Gaara arrived, but I hadn’t exactly been paying attention after that. Or if Gaara was the final
attack, then he could have been the distraction for the others to retreat. Orochimaru tended to
inspire a ‘to the death’ sort of loyalty in his followers, god only knew how, but Kabuto at
least seemed squirrelly enough to survive. “Did Karin get out? Gaara?”

He’d started to tilt his head at Karin’s name, but changed it to an unhappy growl for Gaara. I
grimaced at him sympathetically. “I know. But he’s good. We like Gaara, he’s allowed to
make mistakes. I don’t think he’ll do it again now he knows, if that helps.”

Urushi sneezed.
“You know, given the way Pakkun sneezes I’m fairly sure that’s an insult. Don’t insult Gaara.
Honestly.”

He lifted an ear, licked his nose, and, very deliberately, sneezed again.

“Urushi.”



Gaara had not got out. Karin had, as far as Urushi knew, and unfairly so had Kabuto, but
Gaara was being held under guard in the camp. I was torn - however misguided, he had been
trying to help me escape, the least I could do was return the favour and break him out as well
- but realistically, there was nothing I could do. The camp was in a state of high alert
following the battle, too professional to let exhaustion drag them down, and even if our
numbers were significantly lower than they had been that morning, there were still enough
people to make a jailbreak attempt almost suicidally risky.

Our numbers. Konoha’s numbers. Was I part of Konoha, or not. If I broke Gaara out, that
would be a pretty decisive way to choose sides. If I didn’t break Gaara out - then what? I
couldn’t just leave him. Convince people he was a friend and get him let out on good
behaviour? Trust that he was being held for political leverage and that nothing too bad would
happen to him? I didn’t have a plan. If they were going to kill him in the next hour they
would’ve done it already, that would have to be good enough.

For now, though, Gaara wasn’t my first priority. Kakashi was. Urushi and I stayed on the
fringes of the camp, circling it cautiously while we searched for him. He wasn’t immediately
obvious, but that was fine; he wouldn’t have expected me to be looking for him so soon -
except, the longer I looked without finding him, the less fine his absence became.

He wasn’t in the building that had been set aside as a hospital. Lots of people were, and
others were putting doton jutsu to use trying to reconstruct the walls and the half of the
ceiling that had been flattened, but Kakashi wasn’t among them. At least, not in a way that
was visible from a distance, and not that Urushi could tell either.

But did I have to choose sides? Free Gaara, or stay in the camp? Leave with Karin, or go
back to Urushi? I mean, that one had been something of a snap decision, but still. Run to
Itachi or stay with Kakashi? The fact that I was here now instead of wherever the snake had
been trying to take me - did that mean I’d already chosen?

Urushi walked in a tight circle around me until he found a dry patch of ground and sat on it. I
watched him without seeing him, trying to work out if I was betraying the clan by not
immediately leaping at the chance to escape. Hound’s mask was in my hands, tilted so it was
looking at me. I didn’t think I’d ever seen Kakashi wear it, but then, I hadn’t seen Itachi wear
his either. It was weird I’d ended up quasi-inheriting both.

“Konoha’s… complicated,” I said, putting my thoughts into words in the hope they’d make
more sense. “Karin’s wrong, it’s not that simple. She’s family, but Itachi’s also family. My
mum was family. I like Kakashi, and Suisei, but they’re both loyal to the Hokage. I like
Naruto and Sakura, but they chose Jiraiya. Konoha killed the clan because the clan was going
to rebel, but the clan was going to rebel because Konoha was killing the clan. Danzo’s never
going to be right.”

Urushi kept his head towards me, ears cocked as he listened. The light from the camp
reflected off his eyes, and if I turned my sharingan off, all I could see was a faint orange
outline of his left side, and a fainter outline of the moon reflecting off the rest of him.

If he was going to tell Kakashi my secrets, he already would’ve. Besides, it was Urushi. He
was allowed to know.

“But… Danzo and the Hokage aren’t all of Konoha. I don’t think? I don’t know. Konoha was
meant to be Uchiha and Senju but it ended up just Senju and Senju are the enemy. Except
Sakura doesn’t think she’s Senju. She’s pretty adamant she’s not any clan. There’s no reason
the Hokage has to stay in the Senju line. I mean, Minato was kind of student-teacher
connected to Tobirama, but I don’t think his policies were the same? So, if Naruto actually
did become Hokage, and Sakura was on his council, then. Konoha could be good. Maybe.”

I drew my knees up closer to my chest and buried my chin in them, hiding the mask against
my shins. If I could just undo the realisation that, for Kakashi, I was willing to stay in
Konoha - but I couldn’t. It’d always been the plan to run. I’d kept it at such a distance for so
long, this mythical future time when I could escape and leave them all behind, except now it
had arrived and I couldn’t procrastinate my decision anymore. Karin, and now the need to
either rescue Gaara or leave him, were forcing my hand.

I didn’t want to leave Kakashi. I didn’t want to leave Naruto and Sakura. I didn’t want to
abandon Itachi. I didn’t want Karin to come to Konoha. I didn’t want Gaara to stay captured.
Politically important or not, no jinchuuriki being held by another village was ever in a good
place. But I didn’t know how to have all of them without giving at least one of them up along
the way.

The world would be so much easier if I wasn’t attached to people.

“We need to find Kakashi,” I decided. “Waiting isn’t helping. And then, I don’t know. Ask
him about Gaara. Or do something useful. Repurpose the grand fireball as a sterilisation jutsu
for the med-nins, or something.” Heat sterilised things, right? Heat was useful. I stood up,
frowning down at the mask as I tried to remember if medics used boiling water for anything.
“Maybe we should go back to the mess tent. Food makes life better, everyone will want
food.”

Urushi’s ears twitched, and he turned suddenly to look over his shoulder. I squinted in the
same direction, sharingan scanning for any sign of what he’d heard. Not for the first time I
wished I had better hearing, but short of stealing a handy bijuu to enhance it for me -

There. Over the marshes, just on the edge of my vision. A flash of white lightning, easily
mistakable as a distant storm unless you recognised the flicker-pattern. It lasted too long to be
natural. It moved over the surface of the ground, not down towards it out of the sky. It wasn’t
lightning. Chidori.
  I pressed the mask back on my face for want of anywhere better to put it. I was still in baggy,
  casual clothes, but Karin had restored my chakra to full and I had enough shuriken left to be a
  problem - and if I didn’t then with enough water, my chakra arm was easily solid enough to
  mimic a weapon. We were surrounded by water. And if Kakashi wasn’t, wherever he was, I’d
  make it work without. I knelt beside Urushi, stretched my chakra as far towards where the
  chidori had been as I could reach, and wrapped my arms around his chest.

  “Let’s go,” I said grimly, and switched.

   The chidori went dark before we reached it. Urushi followed Kakashi’s scent trail for the rest
   of the way, striking a careful balance between speed and accuracy - we knew the general
   direction, and neither of us wanted to waste time tracing every step Kakashi had taken. It led
   us to a small hill crowned with a thicket of trees, dense enough that we couldn’t see through
   it and an obvious spot to stage an ambush from.

   Kakashi would have known that though. He would’ve skirted round it if he could, or at the
   very least have been on his guard when he went through. Urushi and I were certainly
   cautious, despite the urgency I felt; we crept round the outside under a henge until Urushi had
   narrowed down where in the trees Kakashi was, then went in silently with all our senses alert.
   I took to the branches and he stuck to the roots, curving round from opposite directions so
   between us we’d be better placed to catch someone who tried to run.

   There was a clearing in the centre. From the broken stumps and scorched earth, there hadn’t
   always been a clearing in the centre. Kakashi was crouched to one side, his posture slack in a
   way that didn’t quite look natural. Not in the way it sometimes did when he was being Hound
   either, just… wrong. The lack of obvious injuries should have been a relief, except they made
   me worry what had happened that I couldn’t see, and the overall effect was unsettling.

   I pulled my chakra further in, until even Karin wouldn’t have been able to sense me, and
   edged round the tree to see the other person in the clearing. He was tall, though not quite as
   tall as Kakashi, built for speed over strength, wearing ANBU clothes. I was behind him and
   couldn’t see his face, and the way the shadows fell hid most of his hair as well, but his mask
   was in his hand and I recognised the narrow line of the beak painted on it.

   “Suisei?” I mouthed soundlessly. There was no way he was an enemy. Surely? But why else
   would he be here? Why else would Kakashi be here, if he hadn’t been chasing someone?

   I bit my lip, trying to work out the best route round to Kakashi while staying out of Suisei’s
   reach. If he had turned traitor, he probably had Kakashi in a genjutsu, though what genjutsu
   could overwhelm Kakashi’s sharingan I didn’t know. My best bet would be to set up a
   kawarimi in advance, then run in, grab Kakashi, and switch out before anyone could react.
   Breaking an illusion on someone else wasn’t exactly my strong suit, but if the disruption
   didn’t give Kakashi a chance to do it himself, I’d work something out.

   I’d barely started to move though when Suisei blinked, dropping out of his tense pose and
   letting his arms fall to his side, a kunai appearing out of nowhere between his fingers. I froze.
   Kakashi pitched forward, catching himself on his hands, shoulders heaving as he gasped for
   breath.

   “I’m sorry, Kakashi-san,” Suisei said in a flat, low monotone that was markedly different
   from his usual politeness. It should have sounded dismissive, even mocking or sarcastic
given how obviously not sorry he sounded, but it didn’t. It sounded familiar. “I don’t have
time for you today. There are more important things I have to do.”

He threw the kunai. It rocketed towards Kakashi; I wasted a precious half-second waiting for
Kakashi to dodge it, block it, anything, genjutsu was bad but it wasn’t that bad Kakashi get
up -

I slammed my kawarimi into the kunai and switched, appearing between Kakashi and Suisei
with my sharingan spinning and my chakra arm defensively raised. I lashed out with it,
instinctively shielding my eyes from Suisei’s own sharingan as I did so, and backed up a
hurried step to reach for Kakashi and -

And -

My chakra stopped, hovering scant inches from Suisei’s face.

Shielding my eyes. From. From his sharingan.

His voice had sounded familiar.

“Aniki?”

I blinked. He was older than I remembered him, his features harsher and his angles sharper,
but - I knew that face. That was Itachi’s face. His face, his sharingan, his voice - his long hair
and his hands and his everything. His - Crane. Crane! Itachi was Crane, no wonder he’d been
so good at - and he was kind, like I knew he was, and he’d promised to teach me genjutsu,
and he worked well with me and Kakashi and, and, and for one glorious, euphoric moment I
had everything I wanted in the palm of my hand and the world was good. Beyond good. It
was great.

My shoulders relaxed. All the stress I’d ever felt drained out. I hurriedly pushed my own
mask to the side so I could beam up at my brother, and I even forgave him for the way his
expression was so closed off and cold. He didn’t know I loved him. He didn’t know that
everything had gone right, but that was ok. He didn’t know yet. Now that he was here all the
secrets I’d been keeping were finally finished - no more lying to protect him, no more hiding
to protect me; no more pretending and no more fear and no more paranoia around the people I
loved. I was safe. I was safe.

“Aniki,” I said again, taking a step towards him.

I walked into Kakashi’s arm.

“Kakashi, what -”

“Run,” he demanded, short and clipped. I blinked at him in incomprehension. He was barely
standing, sweat in his hairline and even his normal eye bloodshot and red. “You gave me your
word, Sasuke,” he said when I didn’t move. “This isn’t the time for heroics. I can -”

“I doubt it, Kakashi-san,” Itachi cut in. “Whatever your plan is, I won’t let you do that.”
“No one has to do anything,” I complained, shaking Kakashi off. I could see Urushi, keeping
low to the ground as he slunk behind Itachi and waited for an opening. He wouldn’t find one
- Itachi would already have noticed him and calculated how to deal with any attack - but I
signaled for him to stand down all the same. “He’s my brother. I know you think he’s an
enemy, but he’s -”

“Sasuke,” Itachi interrupted mildly, and, when I paused and looked at him: “Tsukuyomi.”

Everything stopped.

The sky bled red. Shadows deepened, the moon brightened; in the harsh contrast, everything
was flat and unrealistic. The trees around us stayed, but they looked like a two dimensional
facade with nothing behind them, painted black and lit with a crimson glow. Kakashi
vanished. Urushi vanished. The Itachi that stood before me seemed taller, somehow, or
maybe I was shorter. Seven years old again, trapped in a nightmare after my brother killed the
clan.

I shook the feeling off, slowing my racing heartbeat through sheer force of will. I wasn’t that
successful but I was successful enough that I could grit my teeth and ignore it, standing up to
face my brother and refusing to let him see that I was afraid.

Because he was my brother. What the fuck did I have to be afraid of. He loved me.

“Aniki,” I started again.

“Sasuke,” he returned, a deliberate, almost mocking bite to his tone. I tensed. I didn’t
remember him as a mocking kind of guy. “You are a failure of an Uchiha.”

“I - no, I’m not, I’m -”

“You’re weak,” he said. The forest started warping around us. It was two dimensional to
begin with; getting rid of it was as easy a washing off a layer of ink. I caught a glimpse of the
endless reality stretching beyond, infinite versions of the conversation between me and Itachi
acted out simultaneously in every direction.

Not infinite. Three days in one second. It was a lot of moments, but not an infinite number.

Only the copies of me in my immediate vicinity were standing.

“I’m not,” I protested. Walls sprang up, cutting us off from the rest of the Tsukuyomi. A solid
one to my right, a wall with a door in it to my left. Shogi screen in front of me. Tatami mats
beneath my feet. “I’m not. The people we fight are insane -”

“You do not bother to fight.”

“I - what, no, I do - I fought the scout, you told me I was good at fighting the scout -”

His face twitched; with my sharingan I was meant to be able to read people’s expressions, but
I couldn’t interpret his.
There were tatami mats beneath my feet.

“You fight people who are inconsequential, but when it matters, your only priority is to run.
You yield when you should win. You’d rather hide behind your allies than face your enemies
yourself. You’re worthless.”

Tatami mats beneath my feet.

I grit my teeth. “I’m fixing me,” I insisted. “I’m a, a work in progress, and I’m sorry I’m not
there yet but I’m trying, it takes time -”

Tatami mats beneath my feet.

“You don’t have time, Sasuke. Six years ago I told you to avenge the clan - and you’ve done
nothing.”

They were sticky against my knees. When did I fall to my knees. They were sticky, slightly
slippery. The red soaked through to stain the floor. No amount of scrubbing would ever get it
off.

But I didn’t do nothing, I wanted to protest. I kept your secrets. I was protecting you. I tried to
warn off the kazekage to save your village for you. I was going to help you on your mission.

My mouth didn’t work.

You were going to leave him for Kakashi, my thoughts whispered in the back of my head.

“Perhaps you need a reminder.”

Two figures appeared, kneeling opposite me. My father, who I used to dislike, until I saw
how hard he was working to try to save the clan. His face was stern. Unyielding.
Disappointed. I willed my eyes to skip past him, but they didn’t, and with my sharingan open
the image of his disapproving expression was seared unerringly into my brain.

“You have forgotten your clan,” Itachi accused, and my dad was dead. The sword sliced
through his back, emerging from his chest in a clean cut, a killing cut, angled to slide
between the bones and spear through the heart for a quick and inescapable death.

I flinched.

Itachi turned to the other figure. I didn’t look. I refused to look. I had too many memories of
her to risk them being overwritten, but the sharingan activated in high stress situations and I
couldn’t turn it off.

“You have forgotten your enemy,” he said. He put a hand on her shoulder. I felt the ghost of it
on my own.

“Sasuke.”
I looked at the tatami. The pool of red. The way it spread, until it perfectly matched the
outlines I saw every time I went into the main room in my house.

“Sasuke.”

I flicked my eyes up to his. Only to his, nowhere else. I didn’t want - I couldn’t - she was my
mum.

“You must be stronger,” he insisted, pleaded, ordered, I couldn’t read him anymore or maybe
I never could. His sharingan were spinning. There was blood on his face. It looked like it had
spattered from when he killed my dad, but he was too much of a professional to let that
happen. The last time I’d seen his sharingan he told me I wasn’t worth killing, and now he
was telling me I wasn’t worth anything at all.

“I’m trying,” I begged him. His face hardened, the familiar lines of it turned alien and cold.
With no room for mercy, he said:

“Try harder.”

The sword tore through my mother’s lungs and drowned her in her own blood.

Interlude: Kakashi, who can’t abandon Sasuke because she refuses to abandon him

“How do you make it reflective?” Sasuke asked. Kakashi tilted his head, not sure what she
meant, and she frowned and gestured at the genjutsu wound she was practicing with on her
leg. “The yuck bits. They’re wet, they should reflect the light properly. How does it work?”

He hummed his understanding. “You don’t,” was the simple answer. “The best you can do is
imagine where the reflections would go and mimic that, but genjutsus aren’t solid enough for
light to interact with.”

The simple answer didn’t seem to be the one she was after. “Crane got the raindrops in his
hair to work, and they were genjutsu. You can’t just imagine that, so. I mean, I can’t, he
probably can. How would you do it?”

He… wasn’t sure, actually. His genjutsus tended to rely more on suggestions than perfectly
constructed illusions, and Sasuke was already pushing the limits of what he could teach her.
He had a few he’d copied with his sharingan stored up to pass on, but he’d need to expand his
repertoire soon or he’d run out. The more pressing question though was, “Crane?”

“Every individual strand,” she confirmed enviously. “Hang on. I need to test something,
where’s the nearest puddle gone.”

“Pick a direction,” Pakkun offered, yawning, and ignored the reflexive scowl Sasuke sent his
way.

Kakashi kept his own expression carefully hidden. Not all sharingan were created equal, he
knew, and it was certainly not impossible that Sasuke’s could notice an illusion his could not.
His was a lot more battle focussed than hers. Even so, the thought that Crane was good
enough with his henges that Kakashi hadn’t even registered them was…

Well. It was worth knowing.



Crane was a hard man to find. Unlike Kakashi, he didn’t have a reason to be restricted to the
camp or to short-range missions outside it. He was at least being kept close - so was Kakashi,
and Shikaku was being cagey but it was hardly a secret at this point that something big was
being planned that would need the excessive firepower two elite ANBU could bring - but he

was suspicious, but frustrating all the same.

But when Kakashi left Sasuke with Urushi for the afternoon, Crane just so happened to be
assigned duty in the weapon depot, exactly where he needed to be to run into her.
Conveniently.

Kakashi did his best not to leave Sasuke alone for too long after that.



“Teething problems,” Pakkun reported. “Sakura specialises in direct damage techniques,
Jiraiya prefers diversity and non-combat arrays.”

“She’s a combat ninja, though,” Kakashi said. At least, he’d thought she was. That was what
he’d been training her for, but if Jiraiya thought otherwise then he didn’t want to get in the

Pakkun licked his nose. “Like I said. Teething problems. She’s allowing it because her
confidence’s taken a nosedive, but if she doesn’t say something soon she’s going to find

sense to risk them unnecessarily.”

… He admitted he didn’t know what he was doing, but he really didn’t think he’d got it that
far wrong. “She’d hate it. It’d be a waste of her skills. There’s no reason for seals to be

“If only there was someone who understood Sakura enough to teach her what she wanted to
know,” Pakkun said dryly. “What a thing that would be. A team she was comfortable with
that believed in doing the best for her and not for the village as a whole. How nice.”

“Enough, Pakkun. She’s not comfortable with me.”

“Because you gave up -”

“Enough. How’s Naruto?”
He huffed, but as disapproving as Pakkun was, he accepted the subject change. Ish. “Angry
that you stole Sasuke. Still. Distrusting of Jiraiya. Still. Angry at Sakura for not being angry
that you stole Sasuke. Angry at -”

“Jiraiya’s been teaching him rasengan. He’s also worked out how to turn an entire platoon of

“Rasengan,” Kakashi repeated, glossing over Pakkun’s sarcastic last statement. He could see

Pakkun raised an eyebrow at him, huffed, and dispelled.



“Sasuke,” Kakashi said for the third time, physically grabbing her chin and forcing her to

“Now, Sasuke.” He thought at first she might be stubborn. In truth, she was probably more

He needn’t have worried. She was shaken, but she listened to him, and after that first moment

it, and that was all Kakashi could ask from her just then.

That, and to survive. It was an unfair burden to put on anyone, to demand they come back
from a mission alive. In his experience, it rarely helped. He hesitated, the words crowding
forward and demanding to be said, but in the end he just put his hand on Sasuke’s head,
nodded, and left her to it. He trusted her speed and her common sense, and he wouldn’t help
anyone by showing doubt.

It didn’t stop him keeping an eye on her, just until she and Urushi left and he could be sure
she’d got away.

It didn’t stop his heart stuttering over its beats when he saw the sand rise up next to her as the
Ichibi’s container announced his presence.
It didn’t stop the panic when he remembered Pakkun’s explanation of what had happened in
the exam, when he recalled the memory of how narrowly Gaara had focussed on Sasuke in
the preliminaries. She called him a friend, but Kakashi had seen people before who were too
broken for friendship - people who held too close, who let jealousy turn them bitter, who only
knew how to own someone by destroying them so they’d never walk away.

Sasuke switched. She took Urushi with her. The towering tanuki demon turned on the camp
in a seemingly blind rage that didn’t hide the way the sand kept chasing her behind its back.

Kakashi wasn’t the only one who noticed; Crane was there, a silent streak of black and white
zeroing in on the way Sasuke dodged and evaded with alarming focus. Speak of people too
broken - between Gaara and the man Kakashi suspected Crane to be, it was difficult to say
who he wanted near her less. He had no proof, not beyond half-remembered familiarity and a
series of coincidences that didn’t make sense, but if he was right -

“On me,” he said, shunshining up to Crane’s left. “Our priority is the jinchuuriki.”

“Captain,” Crane acquiesced with a sharp nod. Take Gaara down, and Sasuke’s safe from
him; keep Crane busy while doing it, and Sasuke’s safe from him too. It was the best
compromise Kakashi could make. On the edge of the marsh, Sasuke escaped the sand’s
reach; she was difficult to see in the dark, and though another Sound nin split off to follow,
Kakashi had to have faith that she’d make it out ok.

He’d never been ANBU Crane’s captain.

They worked together seamlessly. Even so, it wasn’t easy - Suna’s jinchuuriki was notorious
for having poor control over his bijuu, and as good as they were they were just two ninja,
neither of whom were seal masters. Killing or harming Gaara enough that the Ichibi got loose
was the last thing they wanted, and containing him without pushing him that far was a slow
and tedious process.

Too slow.

Too slow.

Sasuke’s scream wasn’t loud enough for the weight it carried with it. It should’ve echoed. It
should’ve - Kakashi’d seen people die before, he knew how small and insignificant a single
life could be, but it should’ve been something. Not strangled, not muffled first by the sand,
then by the choking gurgle of a throatful of blood. Not trailing off, frantic and gasping, and as
Kakashi watched her fall all he could think was that it shouldn’t sound like that. It shouldn’t
sound like something she couldn’t survive.

She was limp. Crushed. She landed in a heap and the sand was already rising up to swallow
her.

He didn’t remember doing the hand seals for chidori. He didn’t remember moving, but he
remembered the impact, lightning driving into the sand and sending jagged shards of glass
flying out where he hit. He remembered Crane slamming into the tanuki from the other side,
fire spilling out in an explosion that burnt black before he got himself under control and
toned it down to red. There was only one jutsu in the world that could summon black flames
like that, and for a moment Kakashi hated that he was well trained enough to be able to
analyse so dispassionately while Sasuke was -

He shut the emotions down. They weren’t useful. They didn’t help him. Hound completed
missions without them, and he turned on Gaara with a single-minded destructive force.
Friend or enemy, it didn’t matter; Crane’s attacks provided opportunities, and Hound was
strategic enough to take them. The other ninja on the field - unimportant. Some of them were
forming defensive barriers against the sand’s continuous advance, some of them were still
fighting the invading Sand and Sound nin - they weren’t relevant. He ignored them.

He and Crane broke through the sand, but not in time to stop Sound stealing Sasuke. They
defeated the tanuki, beating the sand back by relentlessly destroying it wherever it tried to
form, and the jinchuuriki behind it was easy to take down once they had. Again, they worked
in sync. Old training. The same training. Whatever had cracked Crane’s facade earlier, there
was no trace of it in the way he fought. With the enemy contained, Hound turned to tracking;
Crane circled the perimeter to ensure no one could sabotage the trail, the way he had done
when he was younger, the way Hound had taught him to do. They worked well together.

There was no trail to sabotage.

No trail - no way to know where Sasuke had been taken, other than a general ‘to Sound’.
She’d vanished as surely as any of the strike teams had after the scouts dismissed them, and if
it was summon-based there wouldn’t be any leads to find. The best thing to do was to gather
further intel on the location of Orochimaru’s bases and plan a retrieval from there, but that
wasn’t something Hound could do just then. He focussed instead on the rest of the battlefield,
zeroing in on the Sound nin that had stopped Sasuke escaping. Distantly, he recognised him
as the fake-genin from the chunin exams, but the information brought very little useful data
with it - medic, intelligent, important enough that Orochimaru had made a point of breaking
him out - and he discarded it. Even medics died to chidori, and he completed the hand seals
with precise efficiency, lining up his strike while he waited for Crane to complete the other
half of the pincer movement.

Crane did not.

Crane paused, regarding Hound just long enough to be noticed, then took a step back and
fled. It was a clear signal that he wanted to be followed, and at first, Hound dismissed it -
Kabuto was the enemy, even without Crane Hound could use a jutsu to hold him or fuck it,
charge forward and try his luck because Kabuto was the reason Sasuke might be - but Kabuto
wasn’t the important one here. He abandoned the chidori, ignoring Kabuto’s considering look
as he did so, and turned to follow Crane. If he were being Kakashi, perhaps he would have
waited long enough to summon one of the dogs and have them pass the knowledge of Crane’s
identity on to someone else, but Hound wasn’t used to working with backup. Crane was an
enemy, and there were advantages in springing even the most obvious of traps. He slid
silently into the shadows, dropped low to the ground, and chased.

They ended up in the trees. Surprisingly neutral ground for a confrontation, and Hound was
cautious as he approached.
“Kakashi-san,” Crane said, standing with his hands held loosely at his sides. “Please. I only
want to talk.”

Hound didn’t reply. It wasn’t his job to talk to missing nin.

“Please,” Crane repeated. He was wearing his mask, but he removed it, hands still carefully
visible so Hound could see the lack of seals. It wasn’t the guarantee of safety it would be
from a lesser ninja, and Hound took care to avoid catching his eyes, but it was a gesture of
peace all the same. For a second Suisei stared back at him - Hound couldn’t see through the
henge, but against Crane’s sharingan he wouldn’t expect to - then the illusion fell.

He looks like Shisui, Kakashi thought. Then, He looks defeated.

He pushed the thought aside. Itachi only looked like Shisui because of the hair he’d chosen
for his disguise; once he’d dropped that, there was only the passing familial resemblance that
all Uchiha shared. As for looking defeated - faces lied. Whatever game Itachi was playing,
Hound was hardly going to drop his guard because of it.

(Faces also told the truth. Wasn’t that why Kakashi wore a mask?)

“Please,” Itachi said for the third time.

Hound waited. He wasn’t entirely sure why.

(Itachi had been Sasuke’s age, when Kakashi had failed him so badly he hadn’t noticed him
going mad. Uchihas don’t deal well with trauma. They care too much. It tears them apart.
He’d done his best to do right by Sasuke, but it didn’t make up for the way Itachi had joined
ANBU wanting peace and left it dripping blood.)

“There’s a tablet,” Itachi said next. “Under the shrine. It needs to be destroyed.”

It was enough of a non-sequitur that Hound paused, confused. “Why?”

“You’re the closest to an Uchiha Konoha has. The tablet…” Itachi’s face didn’t twist into a
grimace, but it looked like it wanted to. “There are people it should never reach.”

“Sasuke -”

“Trusted you.” The defeat came back, edged with a jagged kind of despair. “You let her be
kind.”

There were a lot of reasons, Hound was finding, to be confused about this conversation.
Itachi had no right to look like that. My brother killed me, Sasuke had said, waist deep in a
river she was terrified of and flinging the truth out like a weapon. He killed my whole clan, I
wasn’t special. The only difference was he held me in a genjutsu so it didn’t stick.

Itachi had no right, and Kakashi’s anger flared, pushing aside his calm control.

“Trusts,” he corrected sharply. Until he saw her body, there was no space in the universe for
the alternative. “I don’t make a habit of abandoning my teammates just because they’re hurt.”
“He crushed her,” Itachi said. “If she wasn’t dead then she’d have activated her seal to keep
them from getting her eyes. She -”

“What seal?”

Itachi paused. Between one moment and the next, his face shifted, the broken desperation
replaced with suspicion, realisation, and sudden, frigid blankness. “She wasn’t ANBU.”

Kakashi’s own expression shuttered. Active ANBU seals came with a self-destruct, activated
either voluntarily or on the ANBU member’s death. Revealing to Itachi that Sasuke didn’t
have the seal wasn’t ideal - but it had been necessary. The Uchiha had been so paranoid about
bloodline theft after Obito, it honestly wouldn’t have surprised him if they’d copied the
Hyuuga and Sasuke had somehow forgotten to let him know. Still; Itachi was a lot less
confusing and a lot more hostile now than he had been before he knew.

“Neither were you, Crane.” If Itachi even was Crane. Kakashi hadn’t been lying when he’d
called Crane one of the Hokage’s most loyal, but it was hard to know which was more
outlandish - that Itachi had killed Suisei and replaced him, or that Suisei had been Itachi all
along. Either way, the fragmented facts were struggling to add up to the truth as Kakashi
understood it. He tilted his head, part leading, part to distract from the way he shifted his
weight ever so slightly forward and formed a hand seal behind his back. “Unless there’s
something I’m missing…?”

Itachi’s eyes narrowed. “I apologise, Kakashi-san,” he said, icily polite. “You’ve become an
inconvenience.”

Lightning crackled. Mangekyou spun. The trees burnt around them.

“Tsukuyomi.”

                                              ___

I didn’t stagger when it ended. I wanted to, and the effort of keeping myself stable was an
almost unbearable strain on my muscles, but I didn’t. The step I took back was measured.
The way my foot moved too heavily, scuffing embarrassingly loud against the leaf litter - that
was unfortunate. I’d work on it. It wasn’t a mistake I’d usually have made, but excuses didn’t
mean much and the world wouldn’t go easy on me just because I asked.

Kakashi moved past me. It was the same movement he’d started before Itachi’d - before. One
second. It’d only lasted a second. I let him, taking another step back to stay out his way and
trying harder to keep this one silent. Then another, and a fourth, until my back hit a tree and I
slid down it to crouch on my heels and watch.

My brain was too full.

That was the worst of it, really. Three days in one second; I wasn’t hurt, my chakra wasn’t
even drained, but I’d been awake for too long and had too many memories rattling round my
head. They wouldn’t even merge together, no matter how similar they were. Each one was
preserved in crystal clear sharingan accuracy, and left me - not tired, but not exactly awake.
Just. That numb sort of clarity, when time is stretchy and reality feels gritty between your
thoughts.

Kakashi’s muscles were shaking. He wasn’t doing well. Whatever Itachi had done to him in
his version of the monochrome world, it hadn’t been as kind as what he’d done to me.

I blinked. Why would it be kind. Itachi didn’t love Kakashi.

I blinked again. Why would it be kind. Itachi hadn’t even been kind to me.

I blinked, again, or for the first time, and Kakashi was down. I flicked my sharingan on to
check for a pulse, then absently chided myself when I realised it was already active.

He was breathing. It was fine. Urushi was on the other side of the clearing, trying to make
eye contact with me to work out what I wanted him to do.

I stayed against my tree.

Itachi turned to me, face perfectly blank but a frown hiding behind it. “You aren’t going to
attack me?”

“Do you want me to?”

Whether he did or not, it wasn’t the answer he was looking for. I flicked my eyes away on
instinct. I didn’t know what he’d do if he thought I hadn’t learnt what I was supposed to, but I
didn’t want to go through the lesson again. It was unfaithful of me, but. I didn’t. “Remember
the clan,” I recited dutifully. “Be strong, not weak. Remember our enemy. I can attack you if
you’d like, but I’m pretty sure you’d beat me.”

“I would.” I couldn’t read anything in his voice and I didn’t have anything to say, so I didn’t.
Just waited, until he turned away, giving me a last instruction before he left. “Face me again
when you have the same eyes as I do.”

“I’ll add it to the list,” I promised. Urushi was getting antsy. If I left him any longer he’d try
something by himself - it was only that neither Kakashi nor I were in any actual danger that
had kept him from attacking already.

Well. Kakashi was unconscious, so any actual danger other than that. And if you didn’t know
that Itachi was good, I could see how the situation looked bad, but. Urushi would understand.

When I looked away from Kakashi and back to Itachi again, he was gone.

I gave myself a minute, waiting to see if my thoughts would start picking up again after the
breather. They didn’t, but that was fine; the next steps were fairly simple, as far as rescue
missions went, and there’d be time later to sort the memories into something more sensible.
For now though I pushed myself reluctantly away from the tree and used my chakra arm to
manhandle Kakashi into a reasonable attempt at a piggy back.

Urushi crowded too close round my feet.
“I don’t want to step on you,” I said, using my knee to move him aside. My hands were
occupied - Kakashi was a fair bit larger than me, it wasn’t the easiest job to keep him
balanced. “I’m fine. Fuss later, go back to the camp now. Kakashi needs a blanket.”

He didn’t seem convinced, but he did give me enough space to be able to walk and I
considered that close enough to a win. It was slow going, heading back. I didn’t run, and I
kept my head down with my sharingan focussed on the ground, all my concentration poured
into moving forward and making sure I didn’t trip. In fairness, I probably could have
survived without it - it was still dark but the moon was bright and I could easily see by it if I
had to. I just. Didn’t get round to turning it off.

We avoided the patrols on the way in. I didn’t want to talk to them. They’d probably want to
talk to me, even more so when they realised I had Kakashi on my back, but unfortunately for
them I was sneaky and good at genjutsu, and they were easy enough to go around.

Also, Itachi would be disappointed if I failed again.

But; we made it back to the camp. I considered the tent we’d claimed as ours, then moved
past it and kept walking. Kakashi was hurt. Hurt people went to hospitals. It made sense.

The way the med-nin startled when I dropped my genjutsu and deposited Kakashi in front of
him did not.

“It’s sharingan related,” I said helpfully, already turning to go.

“Sharingan - people are dying, I don’t have time to deal with Hatake Flipping Kakashi and
his chakra exhaustion again. He can -”

I frowned at him over my shoulder. “I didn’t say it was his sharingan.”

He went pale, eyes fixed on mine. I held his gaze just long enough to be sure he’d treat
Kakashi seriously, then reapplied my genjutsu and flickered out. Urushi was waiting outside,
and I ran a hand over his head so the illusion covered him as well.

Remember your enemy. This was a Konoha camp. I didn’t want to be seen. I didn’t want to
leave Kakashi with them, but they weren’t his enemy and I didn’t know much beyond basic
first aid. Antidotes, maybe. I’d be a pretty shit ninja if I didn’t know the antidotes to my own
poisons. I didn’t want to leave him, but I wanted to risk him being hurt even less, and the
med-nins were the only way I knew to heal him.

Someone left the hospital at a furtive hustle. Genin corps. Not furtive, wary. They were
headed to the building I’d seen Shikaku and Inoichi hanging around.

“Pretty shit ninja anyway,” I continued, voice low and muffled through the genjutsu. “When
you actually think about it.”

Urushi shifted next to me. He didn’t whine - it’d be too high pitched, those sounds were
harder to filter out and I’d practiced enough with him that he knew what my limits were - but
he did lean his weight against me in a way that said he disagreed.
“I’m not looking for sympathy. And I’m not being blind, I know I’m strong. Can be strong.” I
was still right when I’d said the people I was fighting were insane. But Itachi was also right.
“I’m weak because I act weak.”

I turned it over in my mind. Was that it? It sounded plausible.

“I… react. Things happen, and I try to stop them. I don’t take control of any situation, just
always panic and defend against everything everyone else does. Wait for other people to save
me.” Yeah, a mulish, distant part of me protested, because how the fuck am I meant to save
myself? I’m a genin.

I pushed it away. Remember the clan. Don’t be weak. Remember your enemy. None of that
had space for being a genin.

“I’m Uchiha. Defence isn’t my style. Blocking just wears you down and draws out a
stalemate, you’ll only win if you go for the attack.” It was what my taijutsu revolved around,
wasn’t it? Assassin’s taijutsu. Hit once, hit hard, don’t be there when they retaliate. Why had
I waited so long to go to Itachi anyway? Stopping to plant a garden was a shit way to run
away.

I paused, side-stepping round a corner to avoid someone going the opposite direction. They
looked stressed, I doubted they’d appreciate walking into someone they couldn’t see.

“Not run away,” I told Urushi. “We got that wrong. Escape is what weak people do, he sent
us back because we have to be strong. Wait here, let me know if someone’s coming.”

He took a step after me, then hung back at my signal and settled reluctantly to keep watch. I
waited long enough to check that he was hidden, then swung myself up to the ceiling of the
building we were next to and started creeping in. It hadn’t been hard to find; there weren’t
many places in the camp capable of holding a jinchuuriki, and while the illusion over it may
have kept other people away it was basically an invitation for me to snoop around.

Well. I had more on my mind than snooping.

The cell was small. Not in itself anything special - no seals, nothing to stop me reaching
through - but the chain inside was chakra suppressing and sunk deep enough into the floor
that only a doton jutsu could have put it there. The other end split into two metal cuffs,
wrapping round Gaara’s hands and holding his fingers still as added precaution. His gourd
was missing. He was awake, seemingly unhurt, and trying to hide how scared he was.

There were two ninja guarding the cell from the outside.

I refused to let myself hesitate. The ninja were Konoha. Remember who your enemy is.
Don’t be so fucking weak.

The shuriken hit the first of them in the throat, layered under another genjutsu so they never
saw it coming. I switched with it as soon as I saw blood, landing heel-first on the wound and
kicking down to finalise the kill. In my hands, I held a makeshift garrotte, a length of wire
with the ends wrapped around two kunai for handles so I wouldn’t damage my fingers. It
went round the second ninja’s neck; cross it over, pull it apart, and if it didn’t slice through an
artery then the strangulation would be enough to finish her either way.

It took less than a minute. If that. I’d gone from someone who’d killed a pig on a school trip
to someone who’d assassinated two ninjas from her own village, and it hadn’t even been
difficult. The hardest part was catching the bodies so they wouldn’t make too much noise as
they fell.

Not my village, I corrected myself, oddly distant, and cancelled my genjutsu to focus on the
chain instead.

“You came back,” Gaara said - asked, maybe. I wasn’t paying attention. This close, I could
see the seals on the chain, but they were woven together too tightly for me to decipher. They
also repelled chakra, and my chakra arm slid harmlessly over them when I tried to force them
apart. The seals were just on the surface though, so if I could find a way to damage the metal
enough I should be able to disrupt them. Fire, perhaps? If I ignited the air around the chain,
not the chain itself, and relied on the heat to warp it out of shape?

I chose a pebble on the other side of the bars and kawarimid with it while I was thinking. It
brought me close enough to Gaara that my elbow brushed against his bare arm. He stepped

Iron. Iron had… I couldn’t remember its melting point. High. It’d need a lot of fire. But it
became malleable at a much lower temperature, so if I got the chain part way there and hit it
hard enough, then -

Outside the building, Urushi whined. Short, and patterned to mimic one of the many frogs
that lived in the marshes, but clear nonetheless: a warning.

I revised the plan. Gaara’s hands were too tightly held, and if I couldn’t break the chain in the

My first attempt scraped a shallow layer off the surface. Gaara shifted restlessly behind me; I
ignored him, dug my chakra as deep in around the chain as I could, and tried again.

(Perhaps you need a reminder.)

Urushi repeated his warning call, and this time I could hear the people coming. They seemed
agitated about something, but I was too distracted to work out what. All my attention was
focussed on the patch of ground the final chain link was sunk into, forcing my chakra to

Gaara stepped closer, not touching but too close, and I shook him off in frustration. I had to

I switched, landing in the jagged hole in the floor in an inelegant tangle of knees and elbows,

“Holy shit, it’s the Uchiha -”

They dropped into a battle stance, fingers flying through the seals to an earth jutsu of some

He stumbled as we landed. Kawarimi was rough on passengers, but I didn’t have time to be

“No,” I told him, aiming a kunai straight up in the air and letting it fly. “Gaara’s good. We

He didn’t seem convinced. Nor did Gaara, and he kept trying to twist out of where I was

First switch; we hung suspended in the air for a too-short second, then rapidly began

Second switch; we ploughed into a clump of reeds, ripping up the shallow roots from the

would have been able to see which way we’d gone. Even so, we weren’t far enough, and the

“No,” Gaara said, scrambling back away from me.

I frowned and reached for him again, frowning harder when he flinched. “We’re escaping,” I
told him frustratedly. Adrenalin was a wonderful thing, but that many kawarimis in a row

“You hurt me.”

I barely resisted rolling my eyes. No I hadn’t. We were wasting time. I scanned him for
injuries all the same, noting and ignoring the way he was leaning defensively away from me
as I did so. He was shivering, hunched and frightened, arms desperately clutching the stone

I bit my lip so hard I tasted blood.

“What the fuck,” I mumbled. What was I doing. That wasn’t me. Was I rescuing him or. Or
what.

He set his jaw belligerently and scowled. “You did.”

“No, I - I mean, yes. Sorry. I’m sorry.” I shook my head, weirdly disorientated. The numb
clarity of a moment ago lingered at the edge of my mind, and for a second I swayed back

But I’d made Gaara flinch. I’d made - maybe he wasn’t badly hurt and it wasn’t a big deal,
but he wasn’t meant to be scared of me. Besides, hadn’t that been what set him off in the
original timeline? He’d got hurt, and hadn’t known how to handle it? And even if it wasn’t,

I took a breath. Then another, because if I was what-the-fucking over things, then now was as
good as any a time to realise that I’d just killed two whole entire people and - nope, no, not a
good time, stop brain holy shit. Breathe. Just.

Breathe.

“Sorry,” I said again, opening my eyes. “I wasn’t thinking. I should have noticed you weren’t
ok.”

He eyed me warily. Normal social norms of accepting apologies weren’t in his skillset, but
truthfully, I appreciated the honesty.

“Why didn’t you?”

I bit my lip as I tried to work out how to answer that, then winced as I hit the same patch as

“Not still hurt. Karin healed me, I’m all good. I promise.” And wasn’t that ironic, that Gaara

annoyed at him when he pointed it out. Maybe not quite the same level of hurt, but. Still.
Which of us had been raised to believe they were a monster again? Be stronger means be
better. Not be a fucking dick. Get it right.

“Then you’re afraid,” he concluded. I shook my head.

“Not every bad thing people do is because they’re hurt or scared,” I said. “Sometimes they’re
just wrong.” But; scared or not, we were still mid-way through an escape. I ran a hand
through my hair, fingers brushing over the flower-pins for reassurance as I tried to work out
what to do. “We need to go. They’ll send people looking for us, you for your - um, your
mother, me for my eyes. And because I’m pretty sure I’m now labelled as a traitor.” Like
brother, like sister. I’m sure our parents would be proud. “They didn’t see which way we
went, but they could have trackers. We aren’t safe here.”

God, would Kakashi be one of those trackers? When they healed him? What the hell would I
do if he was?

“Mother isn’t with me,” Gaara finally said. There was very little inflection in his voice, but
he managed to sound small and lost all the same. “Konoha took them away. I don’t know
where they are.”

“Not with - oh.” I very briefly considered then discarded the idea that Shukaku had actually
been extracted. Gaara wouldn’t have still been in the cell if that had been the case. “Still with
you,” I promised. “You just can’t hear them because of the chains.” I hesitated; caution said
that the fire jutsu to get him free would be too noticeable, even as far out from the camp as
we were. Practicality said the extra firepower of Gaara having his sand back would be
invaluable if we were chased. And speed. He’d go a lot faster with chakra to help him, but the
lack of stealth still felt too risky to me.

I dropped my gaze down to Urushi for moral support. His ears went up as he looked back at
me, but I couldn’t tell from his expression how much he was following of what was going on.

If I’d listed what caution and practicality demanded, then I should also include decency.
Decency said it was Gaara’s decision as much - if not more than - mine. He was the one
wearing the chakra suppressors, he should be the one to decide when they came off.

But what if he made the wrong choice. I didn’t have Pakkun waiting in the wings to step in
and dispense wisdom when people misunderstood. No Pakkun, no Kakashi, not even Sakura
to be the team leader. No one to watch my back, which meant I had to watch it, which meant
I was on edge to begin with and I really really wanted to do things the way I was comfortable
with. I wanted stealth. I was pretty sure Gaara would want his chakra back, and life would go
much smoother if I overlooked that and didn’t let him know it was an option.

Urushi tilted his head, waiting for me to decide what to do.

“I can get the chains off,” I said reluctantly. Gaara held his hands out immediately, and I
stifled a wince. “It’s risky. We’re - someone might see the fire. We’d be safer if we hid and
took them off later.”

“If someone sees the fire, Mother will kill them,” he said flatly.
  Right. Yes. More dead people. Maybe if I did the fireball underwater I could melt the chain
  with a jet of pressurised steam and no one would notice the flames and come running to their
  untimely but very sandy doom.

  I shook my head, dislodging the thought. Fire jutsu and water didn’t mix. Get it together,
  Uchiha. “Chains off,” I repeated. We were a long way out. Even if we were seen, we’d have a
  decent headstart on anyone coming after us, and between us Urushi and I could do enough to
  hide the trail. “I’ll try to keep the heat on the bits furthest from your hands, but let me know if
  it’s burning you.”

  Gaara nodded impatiently. I cast a last glance back at the camp and started cycling my chakra
  in preparation for the jutsu.

  Maybe I was being too cautious. We were a long way out. Or maybe the camp and being in it
  with Kakashi just felt very far away.

  I put it aside. Remember the clan, Sasuke. Next time I saw Itachi, I had to have something to
  show.

   Gaara’s chains came off with an explosion of sand and sandy chakra that sent both Urushi
   and me scrambling back to avoid it.

   “It’s fine,” I told Urushi, one hand on his back to calm him while the other pressed against
   my chest to calm me. Killing intent or not, his chakra was heavy. I don’t know what I’d been
   expecting when I aimed a grand fireball at the chain and blew until my lungs gave out, but
   the sudden spike in air pressure as the suppressants failed - not to mention the way the sand
   fucking tore the cuffs off him - yeah. My heart was racing. A bit.

   “It’s fine,” I said again, firmer, tugging on Urushi’s fur to get his attention. “Naruto’s fire is
   fine, Gaara’s sand is fine. Stop growling at it. We like Gaara, don’t be rude.” Urushi flicked
   an ear backwards, but otherwise ignored me. “Urushi. Desist. He’s a friend.”

   A friend who was currently bent over, hands cradling his head while his entire body seemed
   to ripple with sand. It was just reforming his armour. It was - hell, that looked weird. It was
   fine. I deliberately moved to block Urushi’s line of sight and crouched down to give him an
   unimpressed look.

   “He made a bad first impression,” I allowed. “But it’s good now. He was trying to help. He’s
   going to be sticking around - if he wants - and he’s scary, but not to us, and life will be better
   for everyone if you give him another chance. Ok? No growling.”

   Urushi licked his nose. The growl stopped. The hackles, however, stayed raised, and he in no
   way relaxed from his tense position. “Stubborn,” I accused him.

   He licked his nose again.

   I used the excuse of rolling my eyes at him to subtly check on Gaara. He’d stopped holding
   his head, which was good, and his sand armour had settled down, which was even better. “All
   good?” I asked, standing up and turning to face him in the same movement. “Your mum and
   your chakra are back where they’re meant to be, the chains didn’t do anything permanent?”

   “All good,” Gaara confirmed slowly, tilting his head as he stared at Urushi. I nodded and
   went to move on, but he continued, “Your dog doesn’t like me.”

   Urushi sneezed. I really needed to find out what the sneezing meant.

   “Last time he saw you you attacked us and sand-coffined me,” I explained. “It’s fine, don’t
   worry about it. How fast can you run?”

   He considered. “Not as fast as at home. I don’t like the water, and I don’t have enough sand
   to carry us.” I pulled a face at that. His gourd - it was probably somewhere back at the camp.
Or strewn liberally over the battlefield, and though he’d been able to form his sand armour
again, that seemed to be his limit.

“I can kawarimi us again to make up the -”

“I’m sorry,” he interrupted. I blinked, frowning at him curiously. “I didn’t know that I should
have noticed him.”

“Um.” I shared a blank look with Urushi. “No? You’d never met him.”

That didn’t seem to be the answer he was looking for, and he pressed, “I saw him. He was in
the way. But I didn’t notice him. And I hurt you, because I thought I wouldn’t but I was
wrong. I’m sorry.”

“You - wait.” I squinted. It was the oddest apology I’d ever received, and the strange wording
made it sound almost insincere, but Gaara was waiting very intently for my response. “It’s
ok,” I offered uncertainly. “I forgive you?” More importantly though, “Can we escape now?
Someone might have spotted the fire and the sand and the big chakra thing. We should move
in a not-here-ish sort of direction. Preferably at speed.”

He nodded, his posture relaxing in satisfaction, and I put it aside. Urushi wasn’t actively
antagonising him, he didn’t want to upset Urushi, everything else would sort itself out later.
You know, when we weren’t in grave danger of being arrested by Konoha for murdering
people and running away.

And after a nap. Dear god I wanted a nap.



We ran. Left, right, doubling back and changing direction. Between us, Urushi and I had
enough tracking knowledge that we could avoid leaving a trail, and enough familiarity with
the area from chasing the scout through it that we could avoid most of Konoha’s outposts and
patrol routes. I kept a list of them, running it through my mind and ticking off landmarks as
we passed them. Also on the list was everything else I now had to plan for - food, sand,
weapons, preferably somewhere I could get a whole new outfit, a damn direction to go in
other than just ‘away’ - how the fuck did missing nin survive? We were two kids and a dog in
the big wide world, and all we had to our name were two remaining protein packets; a
somewhat meagre collection of kunai, shuriken, and wire; and a borrowed ANBU mask that
I’d forgotten to give back to Kakashi.

What were we meant to do.

“I don’t know,” Gaara said, as though that helped in any way. “I’ll follow you.”

“That’s very sweet and all but there’s a reason that I made Sakura be the team leader and not
me.”

“What is it?”
I faltered. I was pretty sure, actually, that the answer at the time had been that I couldn’t be
asked. Investing effort in people I didn’t want to care about sounded exactly like the sort of
thing I tried to avoid. Also that I had negative skill in managing people, but given who I was
talking to, I wasn’t sure that was the best answer I could go with. “Not important. Karin can
be the leader, we should find Karin and make her decide things.”

Urushi wagged his tail. Not that he played favorites, oh no, he just happened to like Karin.
Probably because he associated her with ice cream instead of death, or some other
insignificant detail like that.

“I want to know what the reason is,” Gaara pointed out. “That makes it important.”

I shot him a pinched look. “I’m impulsive and I get stressed when I realise I don’t have a
plan. Karin? Yes or yes?”

He blinked, but gave no other sign that he’d heard my answer and moved onto my question
instead. “She was with us in Sound. She might still be there.”

“In Sound? How the fuck did Orochimaru smuggle you all into Sound? I left her in Konoha. I
left you in Konoha, I thought you’d be staying with Sand people somewhere. Fucking -
Sound, right, fine. Do you still know the way?”

He raised his arm and pointed wordlessly behind us. Of course he did. Why on earth
wouldn’t he, the border with Rice was behind us, obviously that was the direction to go for
Sound. Being a missing nin was off to a grand start.

I chewed my lip. The border with Rice was too dangerous to cross, but Iron was just north of
us. They also had a border with Rice, and Iron had a reputation for being aggressively neutral
when it came to anything shinobi. “Sound,” I repeated, visualising the route on my mental
map. Following the rivers would probably be the easiest way not to get lost, and with any
luck the silty marshes would be replaced by sandy river beds at some point. Gaara was able
to get some sand out of the soil, but it would be good to properly refill his supplies.

Speaking of, “There’s a village. Kakashi and I went through it before - I don’t think they had
a lot of ninja supplies, but they might have something.” I narrowed my eyes, trying to work
out how much of a delay it would add. Not much. Worth investigating, at least. Would it be
too risky? Maybe. But useful. Investigating under genjutsu? Or - I bet no one would look
twice at a stray dog hanging round a food stall. Yes. That could work. “Ok.” I took a breath,
and resettled myself. Ok. I knew what I was doing, we could figure out the next steps once
we got closer to Karin. Actually going into Sound to retrieve her was going to be an issue,
but we could cross that bridge when we came to it. “Ready to sprint again?”

Gaara’s expression soured unhappily, but he obligingly sped back up. I was doing my best to
mimic the way Kakashi had pushed me, alternating between running flat out and slowing to a
more manageable jog for a rest, but it wasn’t the easiest thing to judge. I think I did ok. No
one pulled a muscle and I didn’t work Gaara so hard he collapsed out of exhaustion, so. Win.

I, on the other hand, did collapse out of exhaustion, frustratingly soon after we’d decided on
the plan. My muscles weren’t tired - flat out for Gaara was fast, don’t get me wrong, I’d just
got used to faster - but sleep deprivation was a form of torture, and though it wasn’t Itachi’s
intention with his Tsukuyomi, I was wrung out and struggling all the same. My attention kept
drifting. I’d pick up the pace without realising it, and keep accelerating, and forget to go
around the lakes instead of over it because all that mattered was I had to keep moving and
detours slowed me down -

Urushi could say he didn’t trust Gaara all he liked, but he was the only reason we didn’t leave
him behind. The fifth time Urushi ‘accidentally’ knocked into me and snapped me out of it, I
called a halt. It was a bit after dawn, we’d run - I hadn’t kept track. A long way. Maybe
halfway to the village, though we weren’t taking the direct route so it was difficult to say for
sure. Either way, we’d thrown in enough kawarimis and stretches of running along or through
the water to throw off anyone tracking us by scent, and we were far enough from the camp
that the chances of anyone following us were low.

Not impossible. We’d tracked the scout over longer distances and through worse conditions -
and I never thought I’d be actively missing the rain, but here we were. Even so, I was fast
approaching my limit, and resting was a risk we had to take.

“Keep watch for me,” I told Gaara, bunking down in one of the trees and covering myself
with a camouflage henge for good measure. “I won’t be asleep for long, but if I don’t sleep
now I’ll crash and never wake up again.”

He looked at me in alarm. “That’s not how sleep works.”

I scrunched up my nose in thought, then gave it up as too complicated. “Eh,” I settled for.
“Maybe. Lack of sleep is bad, but you’re still alive, so. Not unavoidably fatal.” Although,
that was a thought. Could Gaara have slept while he was wearing the chakra chains? I didn’t
know how his insomnia worked. I considered asking him, then decided against. Nap first,
what-if scenarios later. And if Urushi wasn’t the happiest that I was making myself
vulnerable and relying on Gaara to keep me safe, well, he hadn’t been the one living through
three days in one second. I was done. We’d escaped, I was tapping out, I said an absent
“Wake me if someone tries to kill us,” to the other two, and that was it.

I meant for it to be a catnap.

Brains use sleep to sort the memories of the day. It’s where your dreams come from, I think. I
read it somewhere. I don’t know if it’s true. Learning to fall asleep on demand was one of the
best things the academy ever taught us, but they were never that concerned with what
happened while you were out. You needed to reset yourself back to peak condition, to set an
internal timer to wake up whenever you wanted, and to stay alert enough to react to an enemy
attacking you - but dreams? Nah. What would they teach us about them? There was nothing
useful to learn.

Whether I did dream or not - I don’t know. I didn’t remember it, if I did; I remembered
curling into the tree, being grumpy at it for daring to have branches and being grumpy at
Konoha for making me too paranoid about leaving traces to snap the branches off and make
myself comfortable. Urushi sat at the base of the trunk, Gaara stationed himself a few feet
away. His head was tilted as though listening to someone, and he seemed to be frowning at a
nearby frog. I wasn’t paying much attention, just noting it in a vague aware-of-surroundings
kind of way as I drifted off.

Then - my chest was tight. My heart raced, but unevenly, flopping against my ribs and
making me light-headed and nauseous. It didn’t feel like my heart. It didn’t feel like my
chest, and I was gripping the branches hard enough to hurt like I was terrified I would float
away if I didn’t. My breath was coming too fast and too short, uneven, each one running into
the next until I almost choked - my lips were tingling, why were my lips - dizzy, dizzy dizzy
going to fall, where was, what was, tree? I couldn’t see. What - all I could see were the tiny
cracks in the bark, I think it was bark but I couldn’t pull back enough to make it out and it
was overlaid with red and I had to, I’d lost track of Itachi where was he behind me I -

Urushi barked. I slammed my eyes shut on instinct, flinching so hard away from the sound I
almost dislodged myself, and it was only when he trailed off into a steady, plaintive whine
that I managed to identify him as him and calm down.

“I’m ok,” I told him. “It’s ok. I’m fine. We’re good.”

My heart was still trying to break out of my ribcage. Rude. What the fuck kind of wake up
call was that, I couldn’t even remember what had made me so panicked in the first place.

“It’s fine. It’s - nothing happened. All fine.”

Even so, it took a minute before I was able to relax enough to drop out the tree and run my
hand over his head. It was grounding - the dizziness was gone, I could breathe again, and
when I opened my eyes the world was made of objects and not just unrecognisable patches of
shape and colour. “See?” I said, spreading my fingers out for Urushi to lick to keep him away
from my chin. “I told you I was good. Nothing to worry about.”

“You weren’t good,” Gaara disagreed. I blinked; I hadn’t forgotten he was there, but I’d been
more focussed on Urushi than on him. “You were scared again.” He sounded a mix of
frustrated and put out, which made no sense, until he elaborated: “I was keeping watch. There
was nothing to be scared of.”

I stared at him blankly. He tilted his head, and insisted, “I’d’ve killed it if there was.”

“Um. Thank you?” I resisted the urge to shake my head to clear it, and moved swiftly on
before Gaara could start asking questions. Questions were great, I was in full theoretical
support of curiosity, but just then I didn’t want to talk about it. “Do we have anything to eat?”

He held out - no. What the fuck. I’d been mistaken before; he hadn’t been considering a frog,
it was a toad. The sort that secreted poison from its skin. The sort you didn’t mess with.

“Gaara, that’s not food.”

“Mother says it is.” He frowned at it, and blatantly lied, “I’m not hungry though.”

What, did tanuki eat toads now? I thought Shukaku lived in the desert. “It’s not food for
people,” I said diplomatically. “Or dogs.” I stretched as I stood up; judging by the sun I’d
been able to get an hour or so of sleep, and even if it had ended abruptly I still felt a lot more
awake now than I had done before. “It might be food for fish, I don’t know. I know they eat
frogs, if they’re big enough, but toads are different. We can try using it for bait and see if it
works.” And when it inevitably didn’t work, and the toad unfortunately escaped, we’d have
to resort to shuriken fishing like normal people used. Alas. What a shame.

“It’s not bait,” Gaara insisted loyally. “It’s food. You just need to know how to eat it.”

“I’m getting fish. You can join me if you want, but no one can run anywhere on an empty
stomach. Let’s go.”
