Interlude: That one building in the camp that’s serving as headquarters for the war

“Well,” Shikaku said, not so much sitting in his chair as attempting to osmose back into it.
“Shit.”

Inoichi hummed, only looking up from the notes in front of him for as long as it took to slide
a thermos down the table. Mealtimes were a thing that happened to people who weren’t
jounin commanders, but Shikaku still needed to eat.

“Any shit in particular, or just a general-purpose one?”

“Aburame came back. No luck; Uchiha’s been burning off kikaichu for days now and none of
them managed to stick, and the jinchuuriki killed the ones that were on him after he got his
sand back.” He grimaced; he had two Inuzuka in the camp, except Hatake used dogs too. If
Uchiha paid any attention at all, he’d know how to evade them. In an ideal world Shikaku’d
have a better selection of trackers to choose from, but he was in a recently invaded war camp.
Ideal worlds were in short supply.

“Soup,” Inoichi pressed, aiming a pair of chopsticks to roll to a stop next to it. “Do we have a
direction, at least?”

“Sound. Uchiha’s leading them through Iron. I have some patrols in the area, but if he
continues as he is I can’t guarantee they’ll intercept him.” He curled his fingers round the
chopsticks, but made no move to open the thermos or use them. “Iron don’t like missing nin
at the best of times, the chances of Orochimaru coming through that way were too low for
more than a skeleton defence.”

“Her,” Inoichi said.

“What?”

“Intercept her. Sasuke’s a girl.” He raised an eyebrow, and added teasingly, “Don’t tell me
Shikamaru didn’t mention it. I have it on good authority from Ino that they’re best rival-
friends forever.”

“Please don’t remind me that we’re dealing with someone the same age as my son. It’s not
the realisation I need in my life.” Shikaku grimaced; same age or not, Uchiha had already
proved herself a threat. The fact that she was a friend of Shikamaru’s made it worse - though
best rival-friends was pushing it, he was pretty sure the two of them had genuinely disliked
each other in the academy. Jiraiya had sent a warning that she’d be accompanying Hatake to
the camp and had mentioned his worries that Orochimaru was recruiting her, but honestly?
Neither Shikaku nor Inoichi had thought it that high a risk. Not from what they’d picked up
from their children, not from the admittedly brief impression he’d got of her in the camp, not
from Hatake’s bitingly terse answers when Inoichi asked him either. She wasn’t ambitious
enough to be tempted away by power, nor isolated enough to have no ties to Konoha, nor
even bitter or angry enough to deliberately break the ones she did have. Bitter about what, it
wouldn’t matter - people who wanted to turn traitor tended to look for excuses and find them,
in Shikaku’s experience, and the vast majority of them boiled down to a childish sense of
arrogant entitlement. As young as she was, Uchiha just didn’t fit the profile, however hard
Orochimaru tried to persuade her.

Except that she’d betrayed them anyway. Without Hatake’s report, they couldn’t say for sure,
but the working theory was that she’d traded her loyalty for his life. It would explain why she
took the effort to bring him back before leaving, and if Shikaku could frame the battle as a
distraction while Orochimaru achieved his true goal of gaining the sharingan, he wouldn’t
have to worry so much about what else it might have been trying to hide.

He didn’t bother to consider that the purpose of the attack was to win the war. Orochimaru’s
absence from the battlefield was a glaring omission that all but announced the outcome didn’t
matter, and add onto that the fact that he’d sent the second of his two scout-and-strike teams
in as well? On the surface, Sound had lost. Both byakugan were back in Konoha’s
possession, Sound’s numbers had been so depleted they’d be hard pressed to launch a second
assault, and if the Ichibi had been a trump card then it was one that had been played far too
early. Excessive property damage just didn’t have the same impact when it was happening to
a temporary war camp.

But if not to win the war, then… what had Orochimaru gained, other than the sharingan? A
collection of dead Konoha nin, smaller than it could have been, still more than Shikaku
would have liked? An estimation of how many of the village’s active forces were
concentrated in the marshes, and how many therefore were left to defend the rest of the
country or the village itself? Orochimaru’s motives were hard to decipher at the best of times.

“Give me some better news,” he said, turning his thoughts away. Saving her sensei or not,
Uchiha had killed two Konoha nin on her way out and taken with her their best chance at
peace negotiations with Sand. Shikaku was acting as her jounin commander, not the father of
one of her friends; his priority was to end the war as decisively and with as few casualties as
possible, and he couldn’t afford to be distracted from it.

“... It looks like Crane defected,” Inoichi said, without even the decency to be apologetic
about it. This was not the good news Shikaku requested. “We found evidence of a fight not
far from the camp, and we can place both Crane and Kakashi there, but not Orochimaru or
any other third party from Sound. It’s consistent with what we’ve been able to gather from
the surviving Sound nin - wherever Orochimaru is, it isn’t here, and we don’t know what he’s
working on.”
Shikaku abandoned the chopsticks. Soup just wasn’t going to happen, not if he had to
untangle this mess on top of everything else. “Crane,” he repeated. “Fabulous. I hate it. Tell
me what we know.”

                                              ___

We spent the rest of the day moving, sticking with the river enough that I knew roughly
where we were without staying so close we became predictable. The village was still the
goal, though with the benefit of sleep to de-fog my brain, I realised what I’d completely
overlooked the day before: neither of us had any money. We were literally the worst prepared
missing nin you’d ever come across. It would’ve been laughable, if I wasn’t the one living
through it.

I refused to miss my kitchen. Or my washing machine. I’d been fine living outdoors for
Kakashi, I could be fine doing it for Itachi. I was fine. And even if I wasn’t, there was no
point crying about it, because which part of remembering the clan or being strong was crying
meant to help with? It didn’t, so. Leave me alone.

Some time around noon, Urushi’s ears went back. He didn’t move his head, too experienced
to let a pursuer know they’d been spotted, but he did drift closer to me with his tail up in
warning and his senses trained very carefully behind us.

“We’re being followed,” I told Gaara, keeping my voice low. I couldn’t see them yet, but I
could read Urushi’s signals; it was one person, not making any particular effort to be quiet,
and closing in.

“Yes,” Gaara agreed. He didn’t sound particularly surprised. Why was he not surprised. Did
everyone have better hearing than me, damnit.

“Outrun them, or ambush?”

“We’ve done a lot of running,” he pointed out. I grimaced; we could push up to a sprint, but
if our pursuer wasn’t trying to be quiet then that could easily mean they were trying to scare
us forward into a trap. It might also mean they were spoiling for a fight and confident enough
to be clumsy about it. Stupid people existed. Admittedly, we were a pair of thirteen year olds
running by ourselves - was Gaara thirteen? He was taller than me but not by much, maybe he
was only twelve - and neither of us looked particularly dangerous on the surface, but still.
Don’t judge a book by its cover, dumbass. Shukaku wasn’t twelve.

I scanned the trees for a decent hiding place. “Can you send clones forward pretending to be
us?”

He shook his head. “I don’t have enough sand to be everyone. We can just crush them
instead, then it won’t matter if they think we’ve kept running or not.”

I paused, burying my instinct to scowl at him for his reliance on death as a universal solution.
It was a different style to what I was used to, is all. And I was hardly one to talk, given the
recent increase in my body count, but - it was different. Lots of things were different. There
wasn’t time to be precious about it. “Yeah, ok. Up, we can drop down on them out of this
tree. Urushi, get behind and cut off their escape.” It wasn’t quite a Hashirama tree, but it was
tall enough - and sturdy enough - to lift us into the canopy. Anyone used to fighting Konoha
nin would know we liked attacking from above, but I was counting on the leaves for my
camouflage henge. That, and the reason Konoha nin liked attacking from above was that no
one raised outside a forest ever remembered to look up.

We crouched on the branches, waiting. From this angle I could see Urushi in the
undergrowth, ears forward and body taut in a ready position as he waited for the enemy to
pass him. Ten seconds. Fifteen. They got close enough that I could hear them, the snapping
twigs and rustling leaves giving them away as someone unused to moving through trees.
Twenty seconds, almost there -

Urushi relaxed suddenly, laying down and letting his tongue loll out in a clear friend signal.
My heart leapt, then sank just as fast; Kakashi wouldn’t have made so much noise. I couldn’t
think who else though Urushi would be happy to see.

“Wait,” I mouthed to Gaara, barely breathing the word. “Maybe ally. Don’t engage.”

One of us really needed to learn the other’s hand signals. Talking through your plans was just
asking for an enemy to overhear.

Then -

“I know you’re up there, idiots!”

“Karin?”

She aimed a sour look in the branches’ general direction. “Oh, were you waiting for someone
else? Sorry to disappoint. At least the damn dog’s happy to see me.”

I dropped to the floor. Urushi was already there, tail wagging as he said hello, and though I
flicked my sharingan on to check for genjutsu his word was all I needed to trust that it was
actually her. “Urushi,” I told her. “Not damn dog. He’s called Urushi. How are you here?”

“Gee, I don’t know, could it be that Murder-boy flared his chakra loud enough to call me
from literally the other side of the marshes? I can’t believe you both pissed off and didn’t
wait for me to answer your fucking summons, how quick did you expect me to get there?”

“We didn’t call you,” Gaara said, coming up behind me. “I had chains. Sasuke took them off
for me.”

She scowled. “I’m a chakra sensor. You know I’m a chakra sensor. If you were trying not to
call me you did a shit job of it.”

“We thought you were in Sound,” I said honestly. “We’d’ve called you if we knew you were
there, but it was just a side effect of Gaara getting his chakra back.”

“Why the fuck would I be - you told me not to go to Sound, and he got himself kidnapped.
And then the snakes said they lost you, I didn’t know where anyone was, I tried to come back
to get at least one of you but you’d already gone and then I think you’re showing me how to
find you but you’re actually just - seriously? I hate you. You suck.”

I couldn’t help but laugh, the surprise of seeing her fading and being replaced by relief. Even
the insults were familiar and therefore comforting, and I rocked forward on the balls of my
feet, grinning in the face of her anger. “I suck,” I agreed. “And give mixed messages and am
complicated, all of that. I’m glad you’re here. How did you track us? Was it just Gaara’s
chakra - wait, did anyone follow you? Can you sense if anyone else is coming?”

She crossed her arms and glared at me. I hesitated; it didn’t seem like her usual sort of glare.
It seemed, actually, like the sort of glare you’d wear to cover up how hurt you were.

“Sense them yourself,” she said. “I’ll leave you to it.”

“What? Wait, Karin -”

“I can take a damn hint, Uchiha. You didn’t want me to rescue you from Konoha. You didn’t
want me to follow you. You don’t get to use me now I’m here because I’m convenient.” She
shifted her glare to Gaara, opened her mouth, then changed her mind and shook her head. “I
hope the two of you are happy together,” she said scathingly, and turned on her heel to go.

“Karin.” She ignored me, so I jogged after her, reaching out to grab her sleeve. She jerked her
arm forward, snatching it out of my grip. “Karin, wait. I’m sorry, that’s not - we thought you
were in Sound so we were coming to get you. It’s not that we didn’t want you to follow us,
it’s that we didn’t know you were there.”

She stopped, but scoffed and didn’t turn back to us. “Yeah, right. You were coming to get me
in Sound, that’s why you’re pissing about in the opposite direction. Makes perfect sense.”

“The Fire-Rice border has too many people,” Gaara said from behind me. “We might fail to
get through. Sasuke’s scared of failing.”

“Hey,” I objected. “Breaking through enemy lines from an unexpected direction is good
strategy. Don’t knock it.” To Karin, I said, “He’s right though. We were going to go up
through Iron, it was the best way we could think of to get past the border and find you.”

She eyed me warily, but at least she was facing me now. I tried to project as much sincerity
into my expression as I could. “Because you needed a chakra sensor?”

Would a shrug be too casual, and therefore insulting? Or would a shrug project how little I
cared about her abilities because she was more important as a person? Fuckit. I shrugged.
“It’s useful, but that’s not the reason. We have Urushi, and apparently Gaara’s got super
senses.” I wrinkled my nose. Jury was still out on whether Gaara had super senses or I had
shit ones, but I was assuming that Shukaku helped him. “And before you bring up your
healing again, ew. It’s never not going to be disgusting.”

“Oh, sure, because your eyes aren’t freaky as -”
“So,” I continued, raising my voice to speak over her. “So, stop thinking we want whatever
collection of abilities you have. We don’t. Although, how the fuck did you get three kekkei
genkai, that’s completely ridiculous and I can’t believe no one’s trained you to take advantage
of them, what the hell. Grass are morons.” Unless Grass were in fact playing the long game
and sabotaging her combat to keep her from the front lines? She was invaluable as a medic, if
you were the sort of asshole to use her as a magic-medicine dispenser. Plus, Uzumaki were an
overpowered but rare bloodline; if she died in battle Grass would lose not just her but any
future Uzumaki she might have given them. Good thing Grass had already lost her and any
kids she may or may not choose to ever have, but still. “Dicks. We should visit them when
your taijutsu’s fixed and show them how wrong they were. Do you only have one chain, or
can you make more? If you had more you could use them like legs and just hold yourself out
of their reach while you throw things at them.”

She huffed, crossing her arms and giving me a pinched expression. “My taijutsu’s fine.”

“It’s really not. Are you happy now, or do I need to convince you more?” I squinted, but
truthfully, she didn’t look that happy. Which. Ok. Convincing, I could do that. “We want you
to join us because you’re a person who happens to have cool skills, not because you’re a cool
skill with a person tagging along? Um. Your life experiences resonate with ours, let’s be
friends?”

I winced. Resonate. What kind of crappy nonsense-speak manual did I crib that from, wow.

“I thought I was family and that was the important part,” she said. I waved her off.

“Yeah, but you already knew that. You…” I cast around for another reason. One that wasn’t
quite so selfishly pathetic as I want you to stay because I don’t like being alone. It had been
short-sighted to get so attached to people in Konoha because I was always going to leave
them, but it didn’t change that I’d got used to having people around. Karin was a person. One
Itachi wasn’t going to make me leave. Therefore, I wanted her around. Simple. “You came
back for us,” I settled for. “You look out for us, we look out for you. It’s how it works.”

Was it? I hoped so. I was running out of arguments, one of them had better have worked.

“You keep saying we,” Karin said, tipping her head to gesture at Gaara and Urushi. “You
seem pretty confident that the others will agree.”

I blinked. “Urushi likes you,” I said, glancing down to check with him. He lifted his ears and
wagged his tail, so that was one out of two, but she was right that I hadn’t actually checked
with Gaara. I angled my shoulders towards him, stepping back so that the four of us formed
more of a circle all facing each other. “Gaara, is it ok if Karin joins us?”

“You forfeited against her in the exam,” he said. “I assumed she was on the list of people I
wasn’t allowed to kill.”

That threw me for a second. For all it had only been a couple of months ago, the exam felt
very far away. Still, it was a good base line, and I nodded my agreement. “Yes. On the list.
Definitely on the list.” And, ignoring the somewhat incredulous look Karin aimed at both of
us, “But besides that. Are you happy if she comes with?”
  He paused, frowning slightly in what I guessed was confusion, though I wasn’t sure what I’d
  said that had been confusing. “... I don’t mind,” he said eventually, his tone almost uncertain
  enough that it sounded like a question.

  It was close enough. I decided to take it as an answer instead.

  “See,” I said, turning back to Karin. “Unanimous. Come be a missing nin with us, it’ll be
  great.”

  She wavered. I fought the urge to scowl; I got that I hadn’t been the most consistent of people
  - not that I thought it was my fault, I’d had a lot on my plate to deal with - but it shouldn’t be
  this hard for her to believe we wanted her. It wouldn’t be this hard if people hadn’t taught her
  she was unwantable, and the fuckers responsible better hope I never found out who they
  were. Assholes. She was a whole entire person and they’d given her trust issues because it
  was convenient for them. Who did that. Assholes.

  “Fine,” she relented, her body language shifting back to being combative instead of
  defensive. “I’ll be a missing nin with you. Which was my idea in the first place, do you know
  how rude it is to live someone’s dreams without them? You’re the worst. Both of you are the
  worst. You aren’t because you’re a dog, but just so you know, your mistress is the worst.”

  My shoulders slumped in relief. “Oh thank fuck. You have no idea how glad I am not to be
  breaking into Sound to find you.” I also wrinkled my nose, and added, “Urushi’s a summon.
  He doesn’t have a mistress,” because it was important people knew not to treat him like an
  animal.

  “How were you going to do it?” She nodded her head behind us in Rice’s general direction
  and clarified, “The whole rescue plan. Sound’s inside a mountain, it’s kind of well defended.”

  “Um. You know.” I made a vague hand-wavy movement that I hoped she’d interpret as
  something competent. “Improvise.”

  “I hate you so much, Uchiha.”

Chapter Notes

   There was no more need to go to Sound now that Karin had joined us, but it made sense to
   keep heading for the village all the same. Apart from anything else it gave us something to
   aim towards while we tried to work out what we were doing, and would be a helpful
   waypoint on the road to Iron if we did decide to go there. It was a possible option. On the one
   hand, they were close to Rice and didn’t like shinobi; on the other, our age should help us fly
   under the radar, and at least Konoha and Sound would be discouraged from following us.

   In the more immediate sense, we needed supplies. I wasn’t holding out hope for the village to
   have weapons and bedrolls, but food was an issue - surviving wild for more than a few days
   at a time was a recipe for stomach cramps and exhaustion. Technically, we’d been taught at
   the academy how to sustain ourselves from a wide range of environments found in and
   around Fire Country. Practically, no. Foraging took too long, if it went south it went south
   badly, and it wasn’t worth the risk. We stuck to the limited range of things we knew for
   certain were good and made up the bulk of what we ate with fish and, that particular evening,
   eels; the rain made it difficult to see through the surface of the water, but eels hid in the
   muddy shallows and their holes were easy enough to find.

   “Better than toad?” I teased Gaara when he took a very small, very suspicious bite to taste it.

   He chewed methodically, swallowed, and said, “You didn’t let me eat the toad. I can catch
   you another one and you can compare them, if you like.”

   I blinked. I also tried to catch Karin’s eye to see if she could tell if he was joking or not, but
   she’d apparently decided she didn’t want to know and was pretending to ignore us.

   He was probably joking. Maybe. One hell of a deadpan, but he wouldn’t actually have eaten
   the toad. Ninety percent certain. “That’s ok,” I offered, with more confidence than I was
   convinced I felt. “There aren’t any around here, it’s not worth going looking.”

   He nodded. “If I see one I’ll let you know.”

   “Please don’t,” I said, and moved the conversation on before he could answer. “Are we ok to
   keep going? At least until we find shelter, the ground’s too wet to sleep.” The ground and
   everything else; tonight’s weather was that sort of patchy, intermittent drizzle that made
   everything miserable and never rained enough to burn itself out and move on. Gaara had a
   white sash-shawl that could double as either a blanket or a very narrow and not very
   waterproof tent canvas, but other than that we had the clothes we were wearing and very little
   else to camp under.

   “By shelter,” Karin asked, “we mean…?”
“Dry?” A handy cave would be too much to ask, but, “There were more trees further out from
the lakes. Not enough for a solid leaf layer, but we can at least avoid puddles.”

“By shelter we mean dry,” she confirmed, just barely withholding her grimace. “Sure. Why
not. We’ll follow you.”

“Welcome to the high life,” I said dryly, and threw my eel bones in the water for the fish.



We did actually manage a decent lean-to for the night. I didn’t know if we were lucky or if
the frequent storms meant fallen branches were just common in the area, but the small forest
we reached had enough of them for us to build an angled roof to keep the steadily worsening
rain out while we slept. Nothing that would survive longer than a night, and nothing that we
couldn’t deconstruct and remove all evidence of in the morning, but it was a relief to retreat
underneath it and gently steam dry from the immolation jutsu.

Urushi lay down decisively next to me, stretching out to steal as much heat as he possibly
could. It was a novel experience; usually I was the cold one using other people for warmth,
and if I could’ve kept the jutsu going for him, I would - but when I jerked awake a couple of
hours later it was in a cold sweat with no trace of fire left to lull me back to sleep.

“I’m fine,” I promised him. In an immediate sense, I wasn’t, but I reached out blindly and ran
my hand over his fur while I waited for my breathing to fix itself and my vision to zoom back
out to something workable, and it helped. “It’s just - it’s a bad dream. I don’t even remember
it. It’s fine. I should - do we have water?” My throat was dry, enough that the words I was
whispering were coming out hoarse and barely audible. “I should drink something. I’ll be
back in a sec.”

He followed me out, his shoulder pressed so close against my knee he almost made it difficult
to walk, and his head tipped back to watch me instead of looking where he was going.

“Stop that. I said I was fine. I’m thirsty, is all.” The rain had reduced to a fine mist, making
the wet grass stick to my feet as soon as I left the bare earth beneath the trees. I ignored it,
wrapping my arms around myself and sitting down on my heels at the edge of the nearest
water. It was silty and opaque, and for a full minute I focussed on a narrow stream of it,
drawing it out with my chakra and leaving the dark residue behind.

I wasn’t actually thirsty. I drank it anyway, then shook my hands out and ran my wet fingers
through my hair. They caught on my headband and for a moment I sat there, fingers on my
forehead and eyes staring blankly into nothing.

“I don’t get missing nin.”

Urushi cocked his ears curiously at me. I undid the headband and held it in my hand, the
metal plate across my palm and the black fabric hanging limply either side.

“Why would you go to all the effort of leaving a village, then still wear its symbol like you’re
proud of it? Crossing it out just lets everyone know you’re illegal. What’s the point of that?”
Should I keep it? There might be times when it would be useful to impersonate a konoha nin.
If I threw it in the lake, someone could find it and know which way we’d gone. A dramatic
gesture was a stupid way to get caught. But realistically, the lake was deep and the bottom
was so muddy that anything dropped in it would be buried as soon as it landed. Even if you
knew the headband was there you'd struggle to find it, and there was very little unique about
it to identify it for certain as mine.

“Your choice,” I said eventually, holding it out to Urushi. “You have one too, I don’t want us
not to match. You keep yours, I keep mine, or we get rid of them both. What do you think?”

He blinked, his eyes faintly reflective in the dark, then dipped his head towards my hand. For
a moment I thought he was going to take the headband, but he didn’t; he used his back paw to
hook into the bandana he wore round his neck and pulled his head up until it slipped off over
it, then dropped it, and the metal Konoha plate sewn onto it, in a heap on top of mine.

I swallowed. “You sure? They don’t like people asking for replacements.” I shook my head; I
wasn’t going to ask for a replacement. “You’re sure,” I checked again, and when he wagged
his tail, I stood up and threw them in a smooth arc before I had the chance to second guess.

They landed with a single splash, tangled together and sinking to the bottom as one piece. I
stared at the spot until the ripples had faded away, then turned wordlessly to go back to our
makeshift camp, Urushi padding along beside me.

Interlude: Furthest corner of the hospital building in the war camp

Kakashi woke up with a headache, the lingering burn of overusing his chakra coils, and a
toad on his chin.

“Rise and shine, eh sir? Up up and at ’em. Took you long enough. I have a message for you
sir, a message I do, and I’m told to be giving it to you if you’re alive and to be letting Jiraiya-
sama know if you’re not, and no one says anything about if you’re snoring, do they? Mighty
inconsiderate but what do I know, just does as I’m asked all polite-like and nevermind the
fuss.”

It took more concentration than Kakashi liked to parse the rapid-fire dialect, and he hid a
frown of annoyance as he pushed himself to a sitting position. The toad hopped down to a
more stable position on his knee, and in the back of his mind, Kakashi ran through the usual
status checks of waking up somewhere he didn’t remember going to sleep. No injuries,
enemies not present, nothing about the toad or the room around him immediately identifiable
as fake. Chakra levels low but thankfully not dangerously so, and by the feel of his clothes
and the taste in his mouth he’d been out at least a day but not much more than that. Which
was in itself unusual; other than chakra exhaustion, there weren’t many injuries that kept
someone unconscious for longer than a few minutes at a time without -

Itachi. Sasuke. The looped genjutsu, three days of brutal attack with no opportunity to fight
back.
He jerked upright in alarm.

“Message, sir,” the toad prompted. “Only I got a job to do, don’t I, and the longer I spend
here the less I spend there, and if you ask me you’ve made me wait enough. Not that anyone
does ask me, mind. But if they did, I’d say it’s no trouble sir, because that’s the sort of
gentletoad I am but on the inside see I’d be thinking that I got a job to do and all this hold up
is causing an hole in our eyes and ears on the ground, and what will we do then if we misses
summin’ important-like because I was here with you?”

Kakashi was not a fan of small talk at the best of times. This was not the best of times. He
was clearly back in the camp, so if he was lucky that meant they’d been rescued - but Sasuke
had still been exposed to Itachi’s mangekyou and he didn’t know what she’d seen.

“Report,” he said, more to get rid of the toad than out of any desire to listen to what Jiraiya
had to say.

“Right sir, as you says sir, Gamanuma checking in.” She resettled herself, squatting back on
her haunches to draw herself up to her full height, and began. “In the morning, sir, at oh-sun-
is-up-hundred, I was at my station, watching for enemy action, when I senses a disturbance in
the marsh. So I investigates it, and I find this ’uman, with this other ’uman, except the other
’uman is a cannibalistic maniac, and also this dog what isn’t a dog but is, in fact, a summon.
And the dog don’t know I’m there mind, he thinks I’m just a toad because of my cunning
disguise of being a toad, and the ’uman is asleep, but the second ’uman what’s cannibalistic
and all, he nearly kills me and I barely gets out with my life.”

“Gamanuma,” Kakashi interrupted. “The message.”

“All in good time, sir, I was setting the scene for you so as you’d understand. So the first
‘uman wakes up, and I makes my daring escape, but before I go I think to myself: that’s one
of Jiraiya’s kids, that is, the short one with the wonky arm, ’cept the arm’s not wonky no
more, but when he got kids he showed us what kids he’d got, right, or showed one of us but

recognise them, and that there was one of ’em, and it ain’t right that one of Jiraiya’s kids be
keeping company with a cannibalist if you know what I mean, so I makes sure Jiraiya knows
in case he’s lost a kid and needs to know where they are.”

Jiraiya’s kids. Kakashi grit his teeth but let it pass; it wasn’t worth getting into with a
summon.

“Where are they?” Sasuke, Urushi - who was the third? Itachi? Sasuke wouldn’t have left
with him.

“Thataway,” Gamanuma supplied, kicking one leg out to the side. If Kakashi knew which
direction he was facing to begin with, it might have been more helpful.

If Kakashi knew he was right when he said Sasuke wouldn’t have left with Itachi, that

Than she had been of Kakashi when she’d first met him, and Kakashi didn’t know what it

Gamanuma cleared her throat and waved at him. “Are you ready for the message now, sir?”

The door to Kakashi’s room, if the vaguely partitioned area of the hospital building could be

“Don’t let me stop you,” he said with a vague attempt at a greeting wave and a nod at

“Joining Orochimaru, roger that,” Gamanuma repeated. “Two people dead, Ichibi confirmed,

Kakashi fought the urge to shake his head, in denial or just to make everything pause while

the leap from Itachi to Orochimaru.

“She wouldn’t,” was the answer. “Orochimaru wasn’t involved, and she’d never go with him
even if he was.” That much at least he was sure of; her fear of Orochimaru was very real and
very justified, she wouldn't cast it aside that easily - it was more likely that she was after
Karin on some mad rescue mission than that she was going to turn herself over to Sound.
“Uchiha Itachi was acting as ANBU Crane, for the duration of this mission and possibly

confronted after the battle.” As far as reports went it wasn’t the most formal, but it would do.
“How long ago did she leave?”

“You’ve been out approximately thirty six hours,” Shikaku said. If he was surprised to hear
that Crane was Itachi he didn’t show it, but his expression was grim. “She returned with you
to the camp shortly after the battle and left again immediately. We tracked her long enough to
know she’s cutting through Iron, but don’t currently have a position for her.” He turned to

“No sir,” she said, then added defensively, “She were with a cannibalist, weren’t she? Eyes
and ears I am, not teeth and claws. Can’t do nobody no good if I’m eaten, can I?”
Smaller toads were better suited to stealth than pursuit; it was frustrating, but not unexpected.
“At the speed she was going we’d expect her to reach the border any time in the next few
days,” Shikaku continued, frowning as he thought. “But if she left for her brother -”

“Not willingly. He murdered her entire clan, there’s no way -”

“Kakashi,” he interrupted. “I can’t change the facts. If I don’t know the facts, I need you to
tell me, but I also need you to appreciate that she’s currently down as a missing nin and
suspected Sound turncoat with a bodycount under her belt.”

The laws for retrieving missing nin were flexible. The more valuable the ninja, and the more
allies they had arguing their case, the more likely they were to be reabsorbed back into the
village if they could prove their loyalty. It would be a stain on their record, but minor
misdemeanors could be - for certain people - overlooked.

Killing a fellow Konoha nin was not a minor misdemeanor. It was also blatantly out of
character for Sasuke, but Shikaku wasn’t one to jump to conclusions: if it was what he said
Sasuke did, then Kakashi had to accept she did.

Was it out of character. It had to be out of character. Within her abilities, yes, he’d been the
one to train her in them in the first place, but could Kakashi have missed…? No. Not this
much. She saw Gaara as a friend (a friend who’d crushed her, how in the fuck had she
survived and was it depressing or was it a sign of her loyalty that she probably still called him
a friend despite that) - but the murders? Running straight to Sound straight after?

“Not willingly,” he said again, slower. “Itachi’s genjutsu are unparalleled. He held her in one
when she was a child that she was still feeling the effects of as a genin, and I was unable to
prevent him holding her in another after the battle. The time dilation aspect of the genjutsu
gave him three days unrestricted access to her, and before it, I can confidently say that she
would not have betrayed Konoha like this.”

There was a silent pause. Gamanuma shifted restlessly on Kakashi’s knee, looking between
the two of them as though unsure if she were meant to be memorising this or not.

“A sleeper agent is not an improvement,” Shikaku finally said. “All you’re doing is casting
doubt on her actions for the past six years, and reopening the question of why Itachi left her
alive out of everyone else he killed. Are you sure this is what you want me to record?”

“What I’m doing is saying she’s a victim. She’s an asset to the village and worth too much to
write off for actions that were not her own. Whatever purpose Itachi had for forcing her to
leave, we’ll only be playing into it if we let her. And,” he said, choosing his words carefully,
“if Itachi is controlling her, then I’m the most likely one able to break her out of it.”

Shikaku’s eyes flicked there-and-back to Kakashi’s covered sharingan, but his expression
didn’t waver. Eventually, he straightened, pushing off from the wall as he came to a decision.
“All active duty jounin are remaining in the camp until we know Orochimaru’s next move.”
For a second, Kakashi’s thoughts spun; he’d disobeyed orders before for the sake of his
teammates but never so overtly. Even if he could prove Sasuke’s innocence when he got her
back (and among those spinning thoughts was the possibility that had to be considered,
because what if he couldn’t what then) he could still go down as a missing nin himself for
going after her -

“But,” Shikaku continued, “As far as I’m aware, you aren’t here as an active duty jounin.”

Kakashi stopped. Hound sat straighter, waiting for orders.

“Sasuke is aiming for Sound, approaching via Iron. We have minimal border presence and
will most likely be unable to stop her there. It’s in Konoha’s best interest that Orochimaru
does not gain access to the sharingan, and we have confirmed eyewitness reports that Sasuke
has activated hers. Understood?”

“Sir,” Hound confirmed with a sharp nod.

“Solo mission. No backup provided. And Kakashi -” he stood, collecting Gamanuma despite
her protests and moving away “- know when to pull out if you’re wrong.”

He closed the screen that was acting as a door behind him. Hound gave himself a minute to
stretch and test his limbs after being unconscious, then planned a route, prepared for his
mission, and left.

We reached the village late in the afternoon. Gaara and I were still skint, but it turned out
Karin had money. Not enough for what we needed, but she also had a completely blasé
attitude to thievery that she argued made up for the lack.

“We’re missing nin. Who cares if we short some random village a few yen?”

“I care,” I said hotly. “I’m the heir to one of the oldest clans in Fire Country, I’m not a petty
crook. Also, it’s not a few yen. I want clothes that actually fit.” The baggy outfit I’d
borrowed while my own clothes were drying wasn’t horrific, but of the various things I
regretted, not grabbing my gear on the way out the camp was one of the top ones. At least,
one of the top ones of the uncomplicated things I felt entirely justified in regretting, which
made it a much easier thing to complain about than the others. “If we’re missing nin, we
should do it properly. They can’t all steal stuff, they take missions. And collect bounties and
shit.”

“Bounties and shit,” Karin repeated incredulously. “You have no idea what you’re doing.”

I scowled at her. “I know exactly what I’m doing,” I corrected. “Currently I’m scouting a
village under genjutsu and deciding not to be a dick when things are already rough for them.
You know, that war thing that’s happening, making life difficult for people and being
inconvenient.”

Gaara resettled his weight on the roof next to me, glancing between us with a slight frown.
We’d colonised one of the taller buildings, high enough up that we wouldn’t be overheard
and with a clear view over the market place. With a clear view over the majority of the
village, actually, it wasn’t very big. Urushi was sat between Karin and me, perched right on
the top ridge so he wouldn’t slide down the tiles. He’d abandoned not only his bandana but
also his navy vest, and with his fur naturally scruffy to begin with and made scruffier by the
traces of mud clinging to his legs, he made for a very convincing stray.

“The village hasn’t been attacked,” Gaara pointed out. “The war is between ninja, civilians
aren’t affected.”

I made a noise of disagreement. “National trade routes are down. Everyone’s affected. Also,
this is the closest farming settlement to the camp and they’ve been working overtime to feed
it.” The food had to come from somewhere, we hadn’t all been eating protein packets and
fresh caught game in the mess hall. The wetlands were used to producing enough rice for
most of Fire, true, but the added demand for everything from seasoning to soap would
definitely put a strain on local supplies.

I hummed, looking over the village with fresh eyes. The added demand hadn’t just put a
strain on supplies, it’d visibly affected the village - just from where I sat I could see easily
half a dozen basic maintenance jobs that had been put off because the workers were busy in
the fields. Cracks that needed patching, wood piled haphazardly because it hadn’t yet been
cut and would rot if it wasn’t moved to better storage soon, loose flagstones rocking as
people walked over them…

“Missing nin take missions,” I said. “D-ranks are missions. What if we just did d-ranks to pay
for our stuff?”

“What’s a d-rank?”

I squinted at Gaara. Surely he was joking. How could he - ok, no, I could actually see how d-
ranks had passed him by. When I glanced over to Karin though, she looked as nonplussed as
him, and that I refused to believe. “D-ranks,” I said again. “Manual labour to practice
ninjaing. You know, like painting fences and herding pigs.”

“Wait,” Karin said. “You mean Konoha treats those as missions? You guys get paid to run
errands?”

“Yes? What does Grass do?”

Her face shuttered. “Not that,” she said, deliberately flippant. I squinted, but she shrugged it
off. “I was in the hospital most of the time, I didn’t really get involved. But hey, you want to
paint fences to make you feel better about stealing, you paint fences.”

… I let it slide. She didn’t want to talk about it, so I wouldn’t talk about it. If at some point
we happened to swing by Grass and ‘not talk about it’ in a cathartic, setting places on fire
kind of way, that would also be fine.

“It’s not stealing,” I said, focussing on the other half of what she said. “It’s an exchange of
goods for services, it’s basic economy. Can either of you do a solid henge? Naruto can, but I
don’t know if that’s Uzumaki chakra or - um, something else.”
No, was the answer. I debated internally; an illusion henge was great at a distance, but would
fall apart the moment we tried to pick something up from a stall and had to use our real hands
to do it. If we pretended to be little old ladies, we could get away with being so obviously
short… But, how the hell would little old ladies have travelled so far to get here?
Impersonating other members of the genin corps was a possibility, some of them were about
our age, but I didn’t know what agreements were already in place between the camp and the
village and I didn’t want to out myself by making a mistake.

“You’re at least marginally sneaky,” I told Karin, ignoring the face she pulled at that. “You
and Urushi grab stuff from the market without being seen. Gaara and I will take the d-ranks,
also without being seen.” It was a logical split; his sand would speed the process up, I was
apparently the most experienced at property maintenance - which wasn’t something I’d ever
thought I’d be, but if the glove fits - and Karin, at the very least, didn’t have Shukaku in her
ear trying to convince her that toads were food. She’d get sensible things that we could
actually eat. “But if anyone senses another ninja anywhere, we scram. Surviving first, paying
off debts later. Plan?”

“Plan,” Gaara agreed. Urushi wagged his tail, Karin gave an only slightly mocking salute,
and we split up.



I missed d-ranks. It sounds stupid, particularly given how sick I’d been of them when we
were stuck in Konoha, but. D-ranks were nice. The cracked walls seemed one of the more
pressing issues - if too much water got into the damaged area, it could cause the whole thing
to go bad - and the steady repetitiveness of drying the bamboo base with low-level fire jutsu
then mixing fresh mud for Gaara to fix in place was… peaceful. Nice. They might not be the
best walls the village had ever seen, but they were better than they had been before.

There was a little market garden behind that house. The sort of mix of herbs and salad
vegetables that were more for flavour than nutritional value, the sort that someone hadn’t had
the time to look after with everything else that was going on. It needed a bit of weeding, a bit
of cutting back to stop the herbs getting straggly. The peas needed retying to keep them on
their canes. And - the gate was sagging on its hinges. I rehung it, but it was sagging because
one of the bolts had rusted through, and it took me a while to find a replacement. The bulb in
the shed had blown, and in searching for a new one I passed a water trough and accidentally
cleaned the drain leading out from it.

Maybe I didn’t miss d-ranks. Maybe I just missed houses, and narrating what I was doing to
Gaara like I used to do to the fish. Not that - Gaara wasn’t fish, he was people, and this
wasn’t my house that I was neatening up while its owners were at work. I should probably
stop. It was probably verging into creepy territory. I’d checked all the shelves in the shed, but
the shed didn’t have light bulbs, and when I was seriously considering jimmying the lock on
the back door to look for spares inside, I acknowledged I’d maybe gone as far as I reasonably
could.

“We should go,” I told Gaara reluctantly. “It’s getting dark, and we can’t spend too long here
anyway. We’re still technically on the run.”
Karin and Urushi were waiting outside, both hidden from the civilians’ view but easy enough
for us to find. Idly, I wondered if Karin would be any good at genjutsu. Even if she didn’t
want to specialise in it, basic ones would be useful for situations like this. Could Gaara learn,
or would he have too much chakra for the fine details? Would Karin have too much chakra?
It wouldn’t make it impossible, just fiddly, but in a way I didn’t know how to help with
because it wasn’t a problem I’d ever had. What would they learn instead? Whatever they
wanted to, it was their choice and I wasn’t trying to take that away from them - but they both
left their villages to follow me. I’d be lying if I said I didn’t feel at least a little responsible
for them. But then, what would I learn? I needed to get stronger for Itachi, I couldn’t stagnate
as a genin forever. Muddling through by myself was fine in some ways, but all of us would
benefit from a teacher.

I wanted Kakashi.

We doubled back the way we’d come, following our own trail until we found a better place to
split off from it. If someone did connect the mysterious string of thefts and unasked-for d-
ranks in the village with us, then retracing our steps was a better way to disguise our route
than leaving in a different direction to the way we’d come.

I wanted my house. I wanted to go back to Konoha. I wanted Naruto. Itachi’s instructions
were an unmoving barrier that I couldn’t afford to disobey, but I didn’t know how to follow
them either. How was I meant to be strong? I’d been trying. And I told him, he’d been Suisei
so he’d seen, and all he said was ‘try harder’. I didn’t know what I was meant to do. Break
Gaara out, fine, reunite with Karin and keep her away from villages that wanted to use her,
fine, abandon Konoha and never forgive them for what they’d done -

And then what? Fix rusty hinges and clear blocked drains? Remembering the clan was all
very well, but it didn’t come with a checklist.

“Uchiha?” Karin broke in. “We going to stop at any point? Some of us want to sleep some
time, you know.”

Sleeping meant dreaming meant waking up with a panic attack even if I couldn’t remember
why. “Later,” I dismissed. Couldn’t remember why - don’t be stupid. I didn’t have to
remember why. Any idiot could make an educated guess. “We’re too close to the village still.
We need to find somewhere safe.”

Besides, it was a clear night. There was too much rain over the marshes for us not to take
advantage of the easy weather while we had it, and I edged my speed up unthinkingly to put
more distance between us and the dangers behind.

Any idiot could - was it any wonder I was having nightmares. Night terrors. God, that made
me sound like a little kid again, and I wasn’t, I fucking - but could you blame me? Where the
fuck did Itachi get off, trapping me in that moment of all moments - seriously? Seriously? I
hadn’t been able to enter the damn room for six years, and now he just decides out of
nowhere that I need to spend three days in it reliving the worst memory of my life? What the
actual fuck, Itachi. What’s wrong with you.
Urushi knocked into my shins. Not enough to overbalance me, so I lengthened my stride and
ignored him.

Also. Also. Remember the clan - did he think I just. Forgot? What, was I going around calling
myself Konoha no Sasuke like I didn’t have a family anymore? Was it Urushi, did Itachi
think I’d signed the dog contract and abandoned the cats? That wasn’t my fault. I was saving
Urushi’s life, because, you know, he’d got hurt saving mine because some people showed
they cared by actually being there for me what a fucking wild concept that was. But no.
Almighty Aniki didn’t love people by protecting them, don’t be ridiculous. He loved people
by invading their brains and telling them they were a failure and not an Uchiha and, and
worthless and - and replacing every single fucking memory of my dad I’d ever had with the
sharingan-perfect image of him being disappointed in me and then just up and dying, how
was that - who did that -

“Uchiha, slow down!”

“I am an Uchiha,” I snarled, whirling on Karin and forcing her to come to an abrupt, skidding
halt. “I’ve always been an Uchiha, I’m not - do I look like Konoha? I care more than he does,
it’s just I kind of thought I’d do a better job of remembering the clan if I was alive to
remember it, but fuck me right? I’m only his brother, it’s not like I matter or anything.”

“Um.” She stared back at me with wide eyes, red but not the right shade of red and half-
hidden behind her glasses. “I know you’re an Uchiha? You were kind of insistent about it.
That’s why I call you Uchiha.” She glanced at Gaara, but he just looked blankly back, too
preoccupied with catching his breath to offer her much support. “Are, um. Is everything ok?”

I hauled myself back to the present. “Sorry. I - ignore me. I’m just.” I shook my head. “I’m
fine. Ignore it.”

“Yeah, that’s bullshit.” I grit my teeth, waiting for her to force the issue. She was right; I
wasn’t fine, but did she ever stop to consider that it helped to pretend - “But if you say so,”
she continued, shrugging awkwardly. “I mean, alive sounds good to me, you keep, uh, doing
that.”

I faltered. That wasn’t… what I’d expected her to do?

She looked at Gaara again. He still wasn’t saying much, so she tried Urushi, who cocked his
head and wagged his tail encouragingly. I followed her gaze, and we ended up both waiting
for the other to say something, neither of us with any idea what that was going to be.

“Thanks,” I said eventually. “I’ll keep doing that.”

“Great.” She nodded, then a second time, more decisively. “Great. Except, can you do it at a
normal human speed? I think I hurt something trying to keep up. Gaara’s basically choking.”

“Mother wouldn’t let me choke,” Gaara disagreed. “But I don’t like running.”

“We’re missing nin,” I protested automatically. “Running is what we do. I didn’t mean to go
that fast, that’s fair, but - running. Saves lives. It’s good.”
He didn’t appear convinced. “If we were in the desert I could stand on my sand and we
wouldn’t have to run anywhere.”

Were we really going to skip right over my outburst and turn this into a discussion about
conditioning training? It… looked like we were, actually. “See,” I said, still somewhat
uncertain, “That’s exactly why you don’t like running now. You rely on your sand too much,
it’s dangerous for when you don’t have it.”

His face dropped into a mulish expression. “I like my sand.”

“I,” Karin cut in, “Like to feel my feet. No one’s in sensing distance, we’re taking a break.
Sit.” She dropped to the ground. I stared at her, then at the perfectly good copse of trees a
little way ahead of us. Why would she sit on the ground. “Uchiha,” she said warningly. “Sit.”

Urushi sat. I shot him a betrayed look, but also folded my legs obediently beneath me. Gaara
joined us, and suddenly we were four people in the middle of the long grass, nowhere near a
tree. Why. At this height, it tickled uncomfortably against my back and arms, and I had to
bend and flatten sections of it so it wasn’t trying to go up my nose. We were leaving a trail,
and if Karin wanted a picnic in a field, the least she could have done was bring a blanket to
sit on.

“Onigiri,” she announced, throwing one at each of us. Including Urushi, who caught his and
swallowed it in the same movement. “I didn’t get a lot, because rice is bulky, so enjoy it
while it lasts. And… radishes, jerky, and this thing is wrapped in paper, and a whole jar of
pickled something. Cucumber? Oh, and clothes. I got you clothes.”

I blinked. As far as trail rations went, it was an eclectic selection. “No thank you to jerky,” I
said, passing it back. “I don’t eat meat. Did you actually get clothes? I was joking when I
asked for them. Mostly.”

“Put the damn clothes on, I want to see if they fit you. If they don’t, too bad, you’ll have to
do more chores to earn another set.”

I held my hands up in defeat. “Dinner first.” And, looking at the odd array of components, I
couldn’t help but add, “You went to so much effort to choose things that went together, it’d
be rude not to enjoy it properly.”

“This is strawberry milk bread,” Gaara said, holding up the mystery paper parcel. “It doesn’t
go with pickled cucumber. Or radish.”

“And?” Karin asked. “Have you tried it with pickled cucumber? Shut up and eat, Murder-
boy.”



The clothes Karin had bought were civilian - unsurprisingly - but fairly practical despite that,
dark leggings and a top that was loose enough to be easy to move in without being so loose
that it’d get in the way. It was also clearly feminine, made out of a summery blue fabric, and
patterned with flowers down one side.
“Is it ok?” she asked hesitantly, her bravado slipping. “I thought - I mean, I just assumed, but
you said brother earlier so. I’m sorry? They didn’t only have pretty ones, but you wear -” she
started to gesture at her hair, then changed her mind and said instead “- kid sizes, there wasn’t
a lot of choice.”

It took me a second. I squinted at her, trying to work out what was wrong. She’d got me girl
clothes, so she was clearly fine with me being a girl, so why - brother. I called myself brother.
She thought I was a girl, not a girl in a guy’s body but fully, 100% a girl, and then I referred
to myself as a guy, and now she was worried she’d got it wrong.

And... people had called me a girl before. Of course they did; I spoke like a girl, I acted like a
girl, I called myself a girl - but, somehow, it still felt like they knew I wasn't. Not in the same
way other girls were. Which was - it was splitting hairs. It was picking at tiny details, it didn't
mean anything that they only called me a girl because they'd been told to. I mean, not exactly,
but - no, I did mean exactly. Sakura called me a girl because I said I was one. So did Naruto,
and everyone, and as much as I appreciated it, I couldn’t trust it. I could be the manliest he-
man to ever live and Sakura and Naruto would still call me a girl if I asked them to. But not
Karin. Karin didn’t know. She thought I was a girl, and she'd apparently thought that from the
start, because - because I looked like one. And. And gender was stupid so it shouldn’t matter,
but at the same time, it really really did.

“It’s ok,” I told her, trying to smile reassuringly and ending up wobblier than I meant to. I
took a breath and shook the feeling away. “It’s good. Pretty’s fine. Are you accusing me of
being unladylike? I could tea ceremony the shit out of you if I tried, don’t test me.”

She huffed, rolling her eyes at me in a way that did nothing to hide her relief. “A tea
ceremony? Geez, what century are you from?”

“This one, you uncultured swine. I can’t help it if my mum taught me manners.” Then - I’m
not sure why I did, but I kept talking. “I thought I was a boy. When my brother was around, I
was his Otouto. I didn’t realise I was a girl until later.” I shrugged, carefully casual. As far as
secrets went, it was a minor one. Old habits though. I’d never talked about Itachi with anyone
before. “I guess I forgot to update it to sister, is all.”

Urushi rolled over, stretching out in the grass in a way that put him in convenient reach for
petting, and I buried my hand in the ruff around his neck on instinct. See dog, pet dog. It was
the way the world worked.

“This is the brother that killed you?” Gaara clarified.

Karin baulked. “The brother that - I’m sorry, what?”

“A little bit,” I said. “He killed me a little bit. Not much. Tiny. Barely anything, it doesn’t
count.”

“In what universe does it not count?” She blinked, leaning away from me. “Wait, is that why
you don’t have any chakra to sense? You’re a ghost? I did not sign up to go travelling with
ghosts. What the fuck, Uchiha.”
“It doesn’t count because he did it in a genjutsu. Genjutsu aren’t real, no one dies in
genjutsu.”

Try harder, Itachi said, and stabbed my mother through the chest.

I flinched.

If the others saw, they didn’t comment on it. “No disrespect,” Karin said, “But your brother
sounds like a dick. No wonder you were pissed at him earlier. Does he have anything to do
with you finally deciding to see sense and leave Konoha with us?”

I shook my head, then nodded it, then shook again in frustration. He was a dick. He was also
my brother, and I loved him, and he was the whole reason I’d planned to run away in the first
place - but that was to be with him, not to roam around lost and aimless by myself. But I
didn’t know how to explain that, not without spilling too many other secrets, and I couldn’t -

I stopped. Why couldn’t I. What were Karin and Gaara going to do with my secrets? Nothing.
They weren’t going to blow Itachi’s cover in Akatsuki. Nor were they going to run to Danzo
and tell him everything, so why was I still keeping secrets? Urushi already knew, at least in
part. I hated secrets.

“Konoha used him to kill my family,” I said, haltingly, keeping my eyes focussed on Urushi’s
ear and the way it turned inside out as I stroked it. “Not just my parents, my whole clan. We
were going to rebel, and the village didn’t want us to.” The others were silent. I still didn’t
look at them, but it was easier to keep talking once I’d started. “It would cause too much
uproar if someone else killed us, so they made him do it and take the blame as a missing nin.
And. And, I can’t prove they stole the eyes from my family’s corpses, but I know they have
sharingan and I don’t know where else they’d’ve got them from. They think I don’t know so
they made this big thing of me being the last loyal Uchiha, but I’m not. I hate them. My
brother’s the last loyal Uchiha, not me, and he wants me to -” I floundered. To what.
Remember the clan, be strong, remember my enemy, but what was that meant to mean. “I
don’t know. I don’t know what he wants me to do, I only know I failed and he was mad at
me.” Attack him? Take revenge against him? He wasn’t my enemy, Konoha was my enemy,
but if he was loyal to Konoha why the fuck would he send me against them?

I frowned.

Why… why was Itachi loyal to Konoha?

Konoha made him kill the clan. He had no choice.

Yes he did. He could have joined us. Forgive me for remembering where my loyalties lay, but
if the entire clan is united against a threat then you don’t jump ship and betray them without
stopping to ask them why. Had Itachi even seen the work our dad was doing to try and hold
everything together? We weren’t exactly a mob in the street with pitchforks. We were
desperate. We were trapped in a village that wanted us dead, and as soon as Itachi got the
order to kill us he should’ve wondered if maybe, just fucking maybe, the clan had a valid
reason for being afraid.
  My sharingan was active. It’d zoomed in, filling my vision with a perfect clarity image of
  Urushi’s whiskers and the mix of white and grey hairs around his muzzle, but for the first
  time that didn’t stop me seeing anything else. I looked up to the others, registering every
  piece of visual information they had to offer in the time it took me to sweep my eyes over
  them. Gaara’s sand armour pulsed with a heartbeat, faster and shallower than his own. The
  shorter bits of hair on the side of Karin’s head stuck up because they’d been snapped off, not
  cut, most likely from her tugging on them. Useless information. Distracting information, but I
  wasn’t going to be distracted. In my periphery, Urushi rolled onto his front, and though it
  looked coincidental I saw the muscles flex in his back legs to make sure he ended up pressed
  against my knee.

  “My brother chose the Hokage,” I said. “He’s forgotten the clan. He’s forgotten his enemy.” I
  took a breath; everything about me was steady, but loud, the breath echoing around my head
  and my pulse drumming in my ear. I felt like baring my teeth, like I could be vicious and be
  justified in it, like if I had to live through my heroes being killed in front of me then my
  hypocrit of a brother could do the same. “Perhaps,” I said, almost surprised at how icily the
  word came out. “Perhaps he needs a reminder.”
