   The plan was simple. If Itachi was going to listen to me, he already would’ve, but he thought
   he was right and that in turn made him righteous in a way that blinded him to anything I had
   to say. I mean, why would he bother? He was the one who’d shaped me, wasn’t he, he knew
   who I was and that I believed what he told me to believe - what was the point of listening
   when he’d written the script I was reading from? Deviations were mistakes to be corrected,
   not valid opinions worth giving any credit to. If we fought, he’d find a way to override me
   again; if I somehow got strong enough to beat him, he’d take it as proof that his way was the
   best.

   So: I couldn’t confront him. I couldn’t talk to him. I couldn’t argue with him. I couldn’t give
   him what he wanted either - well, no, I could, but I wasn’t going to - but what he wanted and
   what he’d asked for were two very different things. It wasn’t my fault he hadn’t specified
   who, exactly, our enemies were. If he cared about who he set me up to assassinate, then
   maybe he should’ve stopped to find out who I considered worth assassinating first. Maybe it
   would encourage him to have a fucking conversation with me next time instead of being a
   dramatic little shit and dropping pithy one-liners before shunshining away, what kind of
   freaky sideways thinking would that be.

   Actions speak louder than words. If he wasn’t going to let me tell him who I was, I’d show
   him. I’d tried the slow route, it hadn’t worked, so the Hokage had to go. It was logic.

   … It was also insane. If there was ever a time to stop and question my life choices, this was
   probably it, but I was free falling and desperate in a world where parachutes didn’t exist. The
   Sandaime was the God of Shinobi, ruthlessly terrifying, Tobirama’s student to the end.
   Konoha was at war, barricaded behind every defence it knew how to raise, and everyone
from foreign kages to Danzo had been trying and failing to kill the Hokage for years. I was a
genin who thought she’d have better luck.

No I wasn’t. I was a missing nin, representative of the Clan Uchiha, and Konoha owed me
my pound of flesh. Itachi owed me more than he’d left me with, and if I had to kill his
current master to get his attention, then fine. Fine. Remember the clan. Be strong. Remember
your enemy. I wasn’t going to be a disappointment again. Hell, there was a non-zero
possibility that I’d fuck up and not be anything again, but what’s the point of lashing out
when you’re angry if it doesn’t make you a little bit reckless along the way.

“You don’t have to come,” I told the others reluctantly. “This is my mess to live with, not
yours. You shouldn’t put yourselves in danger because of it.”

Karin scowled. “Do we have to not come?”

I blinked. Odd phrasing, but, “Your choice? That’s kind of the point of my asking you.”

“Well fuck you very much for assuming I’d ditch,” she huffed, rolling her eyes. “Maybe if I
heal you enough you’ll finally admit it’s useful.” And, when I didn’t react to that fast enough,
she crossed her arms and clarified: “I’m coming. Deal with it.”

“No, I mean, great, I want you to come.” I shook my head, and moved on to the other half of
what she’d said. “You’re healing’s not not useful. It’s just icky. There’s a difference.”

“Baby.”

“It’s blood. Blood isn’t for eating.”

“I bet you have to take medicine soaked in a sugar cube. It’s not meant to taste nice, it’s
meant to save people’s lives.”

“I - no. I’m not going to rise to this. I refuse.” And, when she adopted an over-the-top smug
look of victory, I followed up my refusal by sticking my tongue out at her. Because it was the
mature thing to do. As was asking if she wanted to come in the first place, because friends
didn’t drag friends into stupid plans without at least some kind of warning and I wasn’t
convinced she’d known me long enough for the general one to apply. If she’d said no, I’d’ve
respected it, but selfishly? I didn’t want her to say no. Or Gaara. I’d abandoned Naruto, left
Kakashi, hadn’t been able to stop Itachi walking away -

“Gaara?” I said, forcibly dropping that train of thought. Itachi had walked away, but that was
his fault, not mine. His and the Hokage’s. I wasn’t the one who made my brother loyal to
someone who wasn’t me. I was the one who was going to fix the situation, and any feelings
of guilt or blame went firmly on the self pity pile to be set on fire. They didn’t help, they
didn’t stay. Easy.

Gaara looked at me blankly. “I’m coming,” he said. Then, in the same flat tone, but with a
faint shadow of a combative smirk, “Deal with it.”

“Oh my god. Karin, you’re an awful influence.”
She grinned, entirely unrepentant. Even Urushi joined in, letting his tongue loll out in a dog
equivalent of laughter, and completely ignoring the outraged look I sent his way. I pointedly
turned away from them both, and reminded my facial muscles that they weren’t meant to be
smiling, Karin was unmanageable as it was and she didn’t need the encouragement.

Even if I was happy they both wanted to stay.

It took us the better part of five days to get back to Konoha. After the first two, I felt
confident enough to say that no one from the camp was following us - if they’d been a
professional tracking team, they’d’ve caught us by now, and if it was anyone else then
between Urushi and me we’d done enough to lose them. That didn’t mean we let our guard
down, and we also took care to avoid patrols and outposts, but we weren’t pushing ourselves
to the limit either. Konoha was distracted by the war. A runaway genin and an escaped
prisoner clearly didn’t matter that much in comparison.

On the sleeping front, things were better now that I had a plan. The nightmares didn’t go, not
entirely, but they felt more like actual nightmares now, and less like the panic attacks I’d
woken up to before. I didn’t sleep through every night but I was good at running on catnaps,
and so long as I kept forcing myself to take the uninterrupted hours where I could get them,
I’d have enough to keep me going.

“I’m fine,” I told Gaara on one of the less lucky nights, rolling away from the tree roots and
pushing myself up in a forced-casual stretch that almost hid how fast my heart was racing.
“Don’t worry about it.”

“You said people needed sleep,” he pointed out. “You’re a person. You need sleep.”

“Yeah, well, so are you, and you do just fine without.” I shook my head, searching through
our supplies for any spare clothing and coming up with the borrowed top from the genin
corps. It wasn’t quite a jacket, but it would have to do; my own jacket was back with the rest
of my stuff in the camp. “Seriously, don’t worry. I know my limits, I’m not going to do
anything stupid.”

If he nodded, I didn’t see it. It was dark - my instincts said to sleep during the day and run at
night, but in reality that was more likely to get us spotted than not. Patrols during the day
tended to rely too much on their vision, and were far more likely to assume something
moving through the trees was a bird or other animal. At night, every sound seemed
heightened, and any moving shadow could be an enemy. People were naturally more wary,
and it made it harder to sneak past them. For now, we were travelling in daylight, and holing
up somewhere safe to wait out the night until we could move again.

‘Somewhere safe’ rarely translated to a large camp, and Gaara wasn’t far away. There was
enough light - just - to see his general silhouette, but we were back in the heavily forested
parts of Fire Country and the moonlight was mostly blocked by the thick canopy of leaves
above us. I could’ve turned my sharingan on to read his expression, but it didn’t seem worth
it just then. Sometimes I liked the plausible deniability of not seeing people’s reactions to
things I said.

“What happens after?” he asked. “When you’ve killed the Hokage.”
“Honestly? I don’t know.” I didn’t have to see him to hear his exasperation at that, and I shot
a brief grin in his general direction. What did he expect, really. It was me. I never knew.

The grin faded. “I don’t know,” I repeated. “I don’t have any plans. Konoha won’t take me
back if I actually kill him. Even if I didn’t manage to -” I cut myself off. I didn’t want to
think about what would happen if I tried and failed. There was no way it was ever going to
turn out well. “My brother works for an organisation that hunts down tailed beasts and kills
their jinchuurikis, I can hardly go back to him. I don’t even know if I want to.” And with no
Konoha and no Itachi, what did I have left? Kakashi was part of Konoha. My clan? The clan
was part of Konoha, I didn’t exactly have a holiday house with a second set of history
carefully archived inside it. There were the cats, but I lost them when I rescued Urushi and I
refused to regret my decision. The only Uzumaki I knew of were in Akatsuki or Konoha
again, and that left Gaara’s family - but Suna were currently allied with Sound.

Who else did I know? Haku? Somehow I doubted Zabuza would be happy to have us tagging
along.

“Why?”

I blinked, turning to face Gaara fully. The outline of him, at least. “Why?” I repeated.
“Because I love him so much I think I’d try to kill him if I saw him again? Except I wouldn’t,
because I don’t want him to die and because that’s what he wants me to do, but I don’t trust
myself not to do something else stupid to get back at him instead.” Blow his cover, maybe.
Go for his eyes, so he’d never be able to use them against me again. I fought the urge to
hunch my shoulders, or bring my knees up to my chest. I refused. “He hurt me, Gaara. If I
didn’t love him, it wouldn’t matter like it does. Maybe because I love him it shouldn’t matter,
but that’s not how it works. He hurt me, and now I’m hurting him, and I don’t know what
happens after that but just at the moment, I don’t really care.”

He was quiet for a bit after that. I deliberately untensed, leaning back against the tree and
trying to will the night to be warmer. Urushi was sprawled too far away to be a hot water
bottle, for once dozing heavily enough that I didn’t want to disturb him. Summons didn’t
need to sleep, but they weren’t meant to need to eat either, and he’d been doing both since we
left Kakashi behind. If it helped him adapt to life without the summon realm, I wasn’t going
to stop him.

“That wasn’t what I meant,” Gaara finally said. “Is that the answer? For love? You said you
were working on it.”

I pulled a face. “No. It’s not the answer. There isn’t an answer. Everyone keeps working on it
until the day they die, and no one understands it. They just pretend they do because it makes
them feel better.” Love was stupid. Love was meant to be great and meant to be amazing, but
it made everything complicated. Think how much easier life would be if I didn’t care about
the clan, or my brother, or the way I’d left so many people behind. “What did you mean then,
if you weren’t asking why I didn’t want to see him again?”

He had to notice the subject change, but mercifully, he went along with it. “I meant, why does
your brother’s organisation hunting tailed beasts mean you can’t go to them?”
“Oh.” My shoulders relaxed, and I shrugged at him. “You’re a jinchuuriki. They’d kill you to
get your mum. Not an option.”

“Even though that’s where your brother is?”

“Well. Yeah.” I tilted my head, frowning at him. “You’re important too. Killing you means
you die, I’m not going to let that happen.”

There was a pause. He nodded, I think, or maybe I was just getting better at reading Gaara-
silences. Either way I left him to it and resettled myself again, using one of the tall roots to
act as a makeshift pillow. Morning couldn’t be too far off, and with it, the insects swarming
on the surface of the river. I could go fishing. If I used my chakra to scoop water up and let it
trickle down like rain, would the fish come and investigate it like my koi did? Maybe. I
considered it, then wrinkled my nose and decided against. It felt like too much of a betrayal
to invite someone to play and then eat them for it.

“Karin’s wrong,” Gaara said, breaking the silence. I raised an eyebrow, looking over at him
without lifting my head. “You don’t make sense all the time, but you don’t never make sense.
You know some things.”

I snorted. “Glad to hear it. Do you want me to take watch, or are you ok if I nap again? I
won’t actually sleep. Just eyes closed for a bit.”

“Mother and I can keep watch,” he promised, and I let my hair fall over my face and drifted.

                                               ___

Interlude: Northern marshes of Fire Country

Hound ran with Uhei. He was the fastest of the dogs, though not the best tracker, but they
were too many days behind for Sasuke to have left much of a trail. They passed through the
marshes. They slowed as they went through trees - Sasuke was clever, but she was also
predictable, and she disliked being wet. She’d’ve gone for them as soon as it rained, and if
she left traces, Hound wanted to know, both to assure himself he was going the right way and
to prevent anyone else from following her tracks.

In a small wood roughly two day’s travel from the camp, he found them. Branches carefully
scattered in a way that looked natural at first but that was too deliberately haphazard to have
fallen that way by chance. A patch of earth under a low angled branch that was pressed flat
and had markedly fewer rocks and pebbles than the areas either side. Off to the side, a stretch
of soil that was an oddly dense, claggy texture, littered with tiny holes and still smelling
faintly of chakra. It wasn’t any technique Hound recognised, but it was the first clear
evidence he had of Gaara’s presence - the rain had washed any other traces away.

The village he and Sasuke had passed through on the way to the camp was less than a day’s
journey ahead. Like he thought; she was predictable. At least in this, and he buried the
frustration that accompanied it. He’d never taught her how not to be, he could hardly blame
her for the mistake.
For now, it worked in his favour. He reached the village early enough that he had to wait for
the market to open; the delay was unwelcome and grating, but he needed information before
he went on. Uhei was silent next to him. He considered, briefly, summoning Pakkun while he
waited - and yet. The pug was vocal when he wanted to be, and he’d never approved of the
way Kakashi retreated to let Hound deal with things he didn’t know how to handle. Pakkun
would demand he be Kakashi. Kakashi would want to know why Sasuke defected and pick
apart the things that only made sense on the surface until everything was unsure and
uncertain and he didn’t know what to do. Hound didn’t want, just then, to be Kakashi.

The market opened. He didn’t bother with a disguise, relying instead on his uniform and his
headband to get the information he needed. After barely half an hour, he had it: several days
ago a stray dog had passed between the stalls. Every time a seller took the time to shoo him
away they turned back to find someone had helped themselves to their wares. He only
questioned the food sellers at first, but one of them referred him to a vocal old man
complaining about an entire missing outfit from his clothing stall. The size, the man recalled,
was small. A child, and not a very tall one. The quality was outstanding, the workmanship
some of his best, the cost - but Hound had already turned to go.

Theft was not Sasuke’s style. Kakashi would want to know what changed her mind. He’d ask
further, keep going until he could place Gaara as well as Urushi, wonder if perhaps he’d
misunderstood. Hound didn’t. He had the confirmation he needed. Sasuke had passed through
the village, and if she kept going in the same direction, it’d take her to the border with Iron
and from there to Rice and to Sound. Her caution would make her take a winding route, away
from patrols and pausing at night to rest. If Hound took the direct path, he could arrive at
Sound before her, or head her off before she reached it. It would mean abandoning any
chance of tracing her steps through Iron, but the time gain was too beneficial to ignore.

He calculated a shortcut, aimed for Sound, and started running again.

                                              ___

“So,” Karin said, somewhat wide-eyed. “Konoha, huh?”

“Yes,” I answered, looking between her and the village in confusion. We were in the branches
of one of the Hashirama trees, high enough up that we could look over the wall and into the
village on the other side, but also far enough away that we wouldn’t be spotted. Urushi was
up with us - the trees were so large, and Konoha nin so rarely travelled along the ground,
there wasn’t any point leaving him to watch the roots. “You’ve… been there before?”

“No shit,” she confirmed dryly. “It didn’t have that last time though.”

I squinted in the direction she was gesturing. As far as I could make out, that direction was
‘all of it’, and it didn’t help. “We repaired some of the older parts of the wall?” I guessed.
“Um. The gates are closed? I think someone repainted the hospital roof.”

“Oh, they painted the roof, why didn’t I notice that - no not the roof, the giant dome. The
whole village is in a fishbowl.”
“Don’t put fish in bowls,” I said absently, flicking on my sharingan. I couldn’t see chakra as
clearly as Karin could sense it, but I could at least identify what she was talking about: the
barrier seal. A single, unbroken shield of chakra protecting the village from any attack from
the ground or sky. “Shit. They must’ve activated the defences after Sound attacked the camp,
I didn’t realise they’d done that.”

“Is it a problem?” Gaara asked.

I chewed my lip. “... Maybe.” I didn’t know how the barrier worked, or how to bypass it. It
wasn’t the sort of thing they taught genin, surprisingly enough. “There are paths through it
that Konoha shinobi can take, but they monitor chakra signatures. If anyone goes through
who isn’t registered it sets off an alarm, and the only path I know to get in is through the front
gate. Unless you can sense another one?”

Karin grimaced. “Not from here. Maybe if I was closer, but whoever built it had sensors in
mind. I can tell that there’s more than one chakra signature guarding the gate and less than…
seven. Less than seven, unless they’re all from the same family in which case there’s however
many people can fit in a gatehouse. It’s almost impossible to read anything through though,
everything’s fuzzy.”

“Fuzzy. Great.” I tugged on my hair in frustration, automatically finding my mother’s pins
and pressing against them hard enough to leave flower-shaped indents in my fingertips. We
were so damn close. How could I not have thought of a way to break in before? I’d thought
of everything else. That was a lie, I’d thought of a few key phases and trusted that I’d be able
to fill everything else in as I went, but I’d at least done some planning. The timing, for
example; we were a couple of hours before dawn, in the dead zone where even those who
stayed up late would have gone to bed but those who started early would still be sleeping.
Night patrols were still going, of course, and ninja were light sleepers, but most of Konoha
was active during the day. The last thing I wanted to do was run into Gai or Lee doing
burpees to celebrate the sun coming up.

“Can we force our way through?” Gaara offered. “If Mother creates a distraction, and you
sneak in?”

“No distraction,” I said immediately. “Last time you faced an army of Konoha nin you got
captured, it’s not worth the risk.” Still, though; could I sneak in? I’d been registered as an
active duty genin up until a week ago, how likely was it that they’d updated the record?
“Karin,” I said, changing tack. “When you say you can’t sense me, do you mean hard to tell
can’t sense me, or genuinely nothing?”

“Now? Hard to tell. When you’re being a creepy void of a person because you’re actually a
ghost and forgot to tell us? Genuinely nothing. It’s weird. And creepy.”

“Ok.” I nodded, tilting my head as I considered it. The gate was closed, and unless Konoha
was completely stupid, there’d be Hyuuga watching it. Genjutsu wouldn’t help. I couldn’t
scale the walls, there weren’t any paths through the barrier there, but when Kakashi and I had
left we’d gone out an ANBU side exit. “Ok,” I repeated. “I think I have a way in. It’s going to
have to be just me though, you two will set off the alarm.”
“I don’t like this way in,” Gaara said immediately. I frowned at him, already sliding my pins
out of my fringe and twisting the top half of my hair up into the familiar twin buns. “If you
get caught we’ll have to rescue you, and fake your death again so they don’t come after you,
and I don’t want to do that.”

“Honestly, I’d rather you didn’t either. The thought is appreciated but it’s not the most fun
I’ve ever had.”

“It wouldn’t work anyway,” Karin cut in. “They’re not going to fall for the same trick twice.”
She turned to me, her mouth turned down unhappily. “There’s really no way for us to come in
with you?”

Was there? People had invaded Konoha in the past. Orochimaru had been waltzing around
Konoha just fine, and maybe the barrier seal hadn’t been active then, but the monitoring jutsu
should have been. “Do you have a chunin exam up your sleeve?” I asked helplessly. “That’s
the only time I know they don’t watch for foreign chakra signatures. There might be a way
past, but it’s not going to be one we can find.” I looked to Urushi for confirmation, just on the
off chance that he knew, but from the way his tail was down he didn’t. Kakashi would never
have needed one, why would he.

Karin glanced between us, then nodded decisively and started making hand seals. “Ok, then.
Here.” She bit her thumb, swiped it over the tattoo on her forearm, and formed the final seal
with her other hand. A puff of smoke later, and a snake appeared in her hands - the same one
she’d given me before.

I took an instinctive step back.

“Oh, there is no way you’re scared of snakes.”

“I’m not scared,” I retorted. “I’m just not sure what you’re hoping to achieve. Are they meant
to be venomous?”

The snake helpfully reared up and bared its fangs. They weren’t particularly threatening, as
far as fangs went, and I still wasn’t scared, but I may have tilted my shoulders so my bare
arms weren’t directly in the line of fire.

“She’s a pipe snake,” Karin said. “She’s not going to hurt you, stop moving away. And no,
she’s not meant to be anything. If she’s with you and I summon her, she can bring you back.”
She rocked back on her heels, and added, cautiously proud: “Jails can’t hold summons. I’m
your escape plan. I mean, so long as you actually hold on this time. She said she lost you
before because you wriggled. Don’t wriggle.”

I blinked. The snake nodded, which was either an agreement to what Karin said, or an
attempt to blink back. Did snakes have eyelids? I was pretty sure they didn’t. “Um.” I was
pretty sure also that there was no good reason to avoid taking the snake with me. Pakkun
might not have been fond, but Urushi certainly didn’t seem to mind, so I couldn’t use him as
an excuse. “Ok. I’ll um. I won’t wriggle. Wait - won’t she be picked up by the barrier?”

Urushi and the snake both shook their heads. Why was Urushi turning against me like this.
“Summon chakra feels completely different,” Karin explained. She held her hands out and I
forced myself to stay still as the snake wound her way forward to my arm. “You’ll be fine. If
you need saving, flare your chakra. Really flare it Uchiha, I know it’s hard for you but I have
faith.” She hesitated; in theory, it was a good system, but it would be easy for her to miss my
signal through the barrier. “If things start exploding I’ll also summon you, and I guess if
you’re not back by dawn?”

“What is this, a curfew?” The snake was settling herself under my collar. Of course she was.
Why wouldn’t I want a snake around my neck like a shiny banded choker. It was a logical
choice if she was trying both to stay hidden and stay safe in case I had to fight someone, but
it was also pants and I didn’t like it. “An hour after dawn,” I argued. That was not long after
six, when people (normal people, at least) would start their morning training routines; if I
wasn’t out by then then something would have gone wrong. “And while I’m gone, you have
to stay at a safe distance. Not the mountain, people climb it for fun.”

“Deal,” Karin said.

“If things start exploding, we can make a distraction,” Gaara added, clearly reluctant to let go
of his original plan. I nodded my assent - if things started exploding, many somethings would
have gone wrong, I didn’t really mind what happened in that case - and crouched down to
pick up Urushi for the descent out the tree.

“We need a better way of carrying you,” I told him. “You’re perfect in every way, but my
arms aren’t long enough for this.”

He craned his head back to lick my ear in agreement. At least, I assumed agreement; maybe
he liked pretending he was a little dog and being carried in my arms, who knew.



The ANBU exit Kakashi and I had used before was near where the river entered Konoha,
towards the Uchiha side of the village. Closed, it formed a hidden door, the edges so neatly
blended into the wall around it that it was impossible to identify unless you already knew it
was there. Open, it was a short tunnel, with a collection of seemingly innocuous flagstones
sunk into the earth to make a floor. Step on the wrong stones - or forget to step on the right
ones - and bad things would happen. Kakashi hadn’t exactly explained what, but given that
doton jutsu were involved, I didn’t like to guess.

There were several problems with this plan. The first was that I knew the door was there, but
not its exact location. I’d gone from the inside out, and though I could recognise the right
stretch of forest, I hadn’t been looking back to pick the right stretch of wall. That, it turned
out, was easily solvable; ANBU might be specialists, but no one could be perfect all the time
and they left easily enough evidence to show us the way. The second and third problems
though were trickier: Kakashi had opened the door, not me, and I didn’t know how to do it.
Even if we did get it open, I didn’t know if the pattern of stones we’d stepped on before
would work for someone going the opposite way.

I went to run a hand through my hair and stopped, remembering the buns in time. “It’s
definitely here,” I told Urushi, standing in front of an otherwise featureless patch of wall.
“The tracks just stop. I can see it, you can smell it - unless they’re fake? No. They’re too
varied to be fake. And hiding the edges of the door doesn’t hide the door itself, the plants
wouldn’t grow like that unless something was disrupting them.”

Doton jutsu was excellent at many things, but mimicking natural patterns of moss and lichen,
not so much.

“Except, could it actually be a trap? But like. A really really subtle one that’s only meant to
catch trackers?” I squinted. It wasn’t impossible, I guessed, and I wasn’t the most
experienced of trackers - but Urushi was. I didn’t think we’d got it wrong.

Kakashi’s mask was in my weapon pouch. I didn’t know enough about seals to know if the
door would only reveal itself to someone wearing the mask or not. It sounded far fetched, but
so did summoning a death god, and seals could manage that. I took it out and hesitated, my
hand holding it close to my face but not pressing it on. Kakashi was loyal to Konoha. He was
also loyal to me, I knew that, he’d done everything he could to protect me - and against
anyone except Itachi ‘everything he could’ would have been everything I needed - but. It
didn’t feel right to involve him in this.

“We should check if we missed something,” I told Urushi, lowering my hand and turning
away from the unopenable segment of wall. I didn’t let go of the mask though. Even if it
wasn’t right to involve Kakashi, if I needed to, I would. “This is the only way in I know of,
there’s got to be something we can use.” I tilted my head, going slightly cross eyed as I tried
to look down and see the snake, but she was stubbornly well hidden under my collar. “You’re
allowed to speak up if you spot anything as well,” I said. “If you want to. Or not, if you’d
rather I left you alone. I can leave you alone.”

Nope. No answer. If I couldn’t feel the slight pressure of her weight, I wouldn’t know she
was there.

“Well. Ok then. After you, Urushi.”

We stuck close to the wall, following it round as far as we could before the forest changed too
much from what I remembered. It wasn’t that far, and we drifted a bit further away from the
wall on the way back, but there were no signs of any other ways through it. Moss and lichen
doing the moss and lichen things, no moving parts to upset them here.

What there was was a beech tree with a series of vertical and curving lines among the natural
horizontal ones in its bark.

I stopped. A couple of paces ahead of me, Urushi stopped too, looking quizzically over his
shoulder and coming back when it was obvious I wasn’t going to move.

“You don’t smell anything?” I asked. He followed my gaze to the tree, sniffed round it a
couple of times, then looked back up at me with his head cocked in confusion. “I’ll take that
as a no.” ROOT nin, apparently, were better at covering their tracks than ANBU were.
“Here.” I pointed out the marks for him, my hand hovering just above them without touching.
“These are seals. This one says open, these ones are meant to keep the entrance hidden. This
one says identify, and the one it’s linked to is alarm. It’s the same as the one we saw by the
hospital.”

His ears went back, and he moved to put himself between me and the tree. I wasn’t sure if he
knew that it was a ROOT secret passage into Konoha or if he just remembered my reaction to
the one we’d seen before, but either way, he didn’t like it and he didn’t like the fact that we
were standing so close to it.

I bit my lip. I sympathised, but I also needed a way in, and, “We might be able to open this.”
The identify-alarm combo was the problem. It depended what, exactly, it identified, and who
it alarmed if they failed the check. I nudged Urushi aside and moved closer to look. “Don’t
worry,” I told him, tracing the shape of the seal with my finger. “I’m not going to -”

It flashed blue, a single, glowing pulse over the identify seal. In my other hand, the seal that
marked Kakashi’s mask as Hound, active ANBU operative flashed back, and was echoed by
the barest flicker of the alarm that I would’ve missed if I hadn’t had my sharingan on it. The
ground fell away beneath me, the roots rising up to provide cover; I had one disorientating
second of falling before I hit the ground in a crouch and rolled away, then the hole sealed up
above me and cut off Urushi’s frantic bark.

I slammed a camouflage henge over myself so hard I could feel it as a physical wall of
chakra. I was in a ROOT tunnel. Urushi was stuck the other side of the door and Kakashi’s
mask had activated the identification seal and tripped the alarm and I was in a ROOT tunnel.

“Holy fuck,” I hissed, every muscle tense. When I said I might be able to open it, I mean as a
last resort, not - could I open it again? Get out? Were there seals this side of it? No, not that I
could see. Bail via snake-summon, get Karin to pull me free so we could escape? It’d mean
giving up on the plan but the plan had barely started and it had already gone wrong, because
that’s what plans did, that’s what happened when you acted instead of waiting -

I shook my head, forcibly abandoning that train of thought. “Not escape,” I told myself.
Bailing now wouldn’t just ruin this attempt, it would alert Danzo that I’d been here and ruin
any future attempts as well. “You can’t be weak, you can’t keep trying to escape. You have to
remember.”

I needed to think. The alarm was - not good, but I hadn’t fallen into an instant death trap, so
not irrevocably fatal. Yet. Please. There had to be a way to survive this. There had to - the
tunnel was too visible. Danzo was a paranoid bastard; with two major doujutsu clans
waltzing around - one, one major doujutsu clan and me - he’d never leave ROOT somewhere
so easy to find. I wouldn’t if I were him, I’d, I’d, fuck should I have already bolted how the
hell was a camouflage henge going to help when the wall behind me was a smooth lime-
plastered white - I’d disguise it as a normal ANBU tunnel. Yes. That. Nothing suspicious
here, no sir, just a tunnel. You wouldn’t know it, it goes to a different school. Different
division of ANBU. That’s what I’d do; the tree wasn’t secure enough by itself, and killing
anyone who trespassed by accident was a surefire way to start raising suspicions. But if the
tree triggered a decoy, and if an ANBU mask opened a blank tunnel but tripped the alarm to
hide the real entrance that only a ROOT mask could access, then, then there was a chance I
might be ok.
It was a ropey, hastily cobbled together sort of chance, but it was the best I had. If I’d
gambled correctly and Danzo cared more for subterfuge than for silencing witnesses, it could
work. Maybe. No, more than maybe - silencing witnesses was only viable if you silenced
them all at once, and if I’d been part of a squad and others had seen me enter the tunnel
there’d be unavoidable questions if I never made it out. Danzo wouldn’t kill an intruder
unless he was sure they were a threat to him personally. Him or Konoha. Unclear how much
he differentiated between the two. How he’d tell the difference, I didn’t know, which meant
that I really needed to move; Hound had got me in but I very much was a threat to Konoha at
the moment and on the off chance the alarm did more than hide a second entrance, I really
needed to be somewhere not getting caught.

I took a hurried stock of what I had. “No Urushi. He’ll be fine, he’ll go back to the others.
I’ve got - I don’t know your name. Snake. Still with me, Snake?” I lifted a hand, skimming a
very determinedly steady finger over her scales to check. She was still with me. Didn’t react,
and hadn’t reacted to anything so far, but she was still with me. “Good. That’s good. And -
I’ve got a way in. The plan is still going, it just looks different to how it did before. I can do
different. It’ll be great. I love different.”

I stopped the pep talk there before it could get any more ridiculous. Psyching myself up was
one thing; dawdling when I didn’t know if death was approaching or not was idiotic. At least
if I was moving I could run away from it if I had to. First things first; I deactivated my
sharingan and dismissed the henge - which almost physically hurt, without my illusions I was
naked and vulnerable and I hated it - so I could pull my chakra as far inside me as it would
go. Creepy void, Karin said, creepy void I could do. What was the point of my soul being
attached wrong if I couldn’t use it to literally ghost past the village’s defences.

Their chakra-sensing ones, at least.

The snake finally reacted, shifting her coils uneasily as she poked her head out from under
my collar.

“I’m fine,” I told her, going to pat her head reassuringly before I caught myself and stopped.
She wasn’t Urushi. Or my fish, or any other animate or inanimate entity I instinctively talked
to and grounded myself with. “I’m being sneaky, is all. I’ll stop once we’re definitely through
the barrier.”

Her tongue flicked out to taste the air, then she slowly tucked her head away again. With no
background in snake body language to tell if that was a good sign or not, I decided to leave
her to it.

“Alright tunnel,” I muttered, turning towards it and pressing Kakashi’s mask to my face. I
didn’t want him involved, but I wanted to be seen as an Uchiha in ROOT territory even less.
“Let’s see where you lead.”

The answer to that was: to a series of twists and turns that were purposefully designed to
disorientate anyone running through them. If I wasn’t so on edge, and if it hadn’t been Danzo
behind it, I’d’ve been impressed; with everything from a very slightly slanted floor to
encourage you to bend to the left as you ran to a deliberately repeating crack-pattern on the
wall to make you think you were going in circles, the whole thing was masterfully done and
almost impossible to maneuver through. Sporadic and overly bright lights made for shadows
that I had no night vision to see into, and the glare off the floor was disorientating. Without
the sharingan I couldn’t tell, but I suspected they had an irregular flicker pattern as well -
something was making my eyes strain enough to give me a headache, and the combination of
that plus the hidden unevenness made me nearly stumble before I adjusted to take it into
account. I was fairly certain that the centre of the village was to my right and that I was
following a path that cut underneath the river, but it was equally likely that I was going
backwards and was somewhere in the middle of the mountain instead.

Well, not equally likely. Even without the sharingan I was used to noticing small details, I
was pretty sure I’d accounted for most of the tricks that were meant to throw my sense of
direction off. But only pretty sure. Getting cocky against Danzo of all people sounded like a
monumentally stupid idea.

Less than a minute into the tunnels, someone slid smoothly into keeping pace alongside me. I
kept running, my steps mechanically even and my heartbeat so measured it barely sounded
human. My mouth was dry. I was struck by the sudden fear that I’d forget how to breathe and
start randomly choking, and my instinctive swallow did very little to help.

They were about my height. They wore a nondescript black uniform and a nondescript white
mask. They had a black tanto on their back with white bandages wrapped around the handle.
The monochrome scheme continued; their hair was black and their skin was white, their
sandals were black and the ties for their weapon pouch were white, the floor was black and
the walls of the tunnel were white and all it needed to do was bleed red and I’d be looping in
a nightmare -

“I’m completing a mission assigned by one of Danzo-sama’s agents unable to complete it
themself,” I said, my voice so steady I didn’t recognise it as mine.

They said nothing. Should I keep talking. Liars babbled, but only because lying made people
nervous. Was I even lying. I honestly didn’t know if Itachi was ROOT or not. Did ROOT
agents ever give other people missions or had I inadvertently damned myself by claiming that
someone had. I wanted to swallow again. I couldn’t remember how.

There was a ringing in my ears.

The other person didn’t say a word.

They veered right, suddenly, down a fork in the tunnel that was carefully lit to blend into the
shadows and look like it didn’t exist. My footsteps were matched precisely enough to theirs
that I followed without even realising it, and by the time I’d caught up to what was
happening, the bottom had fallen out of my stomach. They were going to lead me to Danzo. I
could’ve run, or fought, or uncurled my chakra from the tight ball I’d suppressed it to and
tried to see if a signal would reach Karin from this far underground - except I couldn’t.

The Hokage was an enemy I could hate and strike back at. Danzo was an inevitability, and
my only hope had been to avoid his notice. I’d gambled wrong.

I’d lost.
Between one step and the next, my escort vanished. Ahead, the tunnel lifted, connecting to
what I assumed was another door in the ceiling. More tunnel continued straight on as well,
but I’d clearly been led to the door. I didn’t know why I’d been left to go through it by myself
or what would be waiting if I tried to escape. It didn’t matter. I slowed to a stop, looked up at
the door, and easily saw the seals I needed to use it. Were they there because the ROOT agent
had done something to activate them, or was the previous door I’d gone through only ever
meant to be one way? It made no difference. One shakily-traced identification seal later, and
it opened; I closed my eyes, bent my knees, and leapt through it.

And landed in the loose soil at the base of the beech tree behind the hospital.

I stared uncomprehendingly. Why was I at the beech tree. What was the significance of the -
Reality hit me in a sudden, dizzying rush, my pulse thudding deafeningly loud in my ears and
making me stagger back from the sound of it. I abandoned suppressing my chakra to reapply
my henge and reached blindly for something to kawarimi with, instinct driving me up for the
safety of height - there was a pot plant in one of the hospital windows, a small one, that
worked. I landed on the narrow ledge, scrabbling back as though the extra few inches
between me and the tree would help.

“What the fuck,” I gasped. “What the -” I broke off to cough, choking on nothing for a
second until I remembered how breathing worked. “That didn’t happen. What was that. How
did - what the fuck. Is this a test? Genjutsu. It’s fake, I - kai. Kai. There’s no way. What the
actual fuck, I thought I was dead.”

But I wasn’t, I wasn’t - I had no idea what happened. Was I now on a sanctioned mission to
kill the Sandaime? Or, I’d never said what the mission was, how would anyone - I’d never
been so sure I was finished in my life, including the time I legitimately drowned and died.
Fucking hell, I wasn’t ready for Danzo yet. How. How.

I didn’t know. I doubted I was going to know. Waltzing back into the tunnel to ask the ROOT
nin what they’d been thinking was, somehow, not very high on the list of things I wanted to
do.

None of this was high on the list of things I wanted to do. For the first time it struck me how
easily everything could go wrong, not in a vaguely sardonic ‘oh yeah I’m screwed if I mess
this up’ kind of way, but in a visceral, nausea-inducing acknowledgement of my own
mortality. I was a genin.

“Genin’s not good enough,” I said, more to convince myself than because I believed it. “You
have to be strong. Being strong means freeing Itachi from Konoha and making him see how
fucked-up everything is. There isn’t time to doubt.”

If I got out of here, I was never coming back to Konoha ever again. It was a promise. Maybe
not a particularly revolutionary one, but it made me feel better, and I held onto it for the few
moments it took to calm down.

The pot plant I’d swapped with was one of a set. Three little cacti, now two, in cheerful
coloured pots that I recognised from the Yamanaka flower shop. I’d never bought any myself,
but they were popular hospital gifts for people with longer stays - cut flowers had a
  depressing habit of wilting, it wasn’t considered polite to remind someone how long they’d
  been stuck inside.

  “Sorry for stealing your friend,” I told them, leaning over to see if it’d broken when I
  swapped with it. Maybe. I wasn’t going to go down to check - it was right at the base of the
  beech tree - but the ‘pots’ were little metal buckets and it might’ve survived the fall. “You
  look good as a pair, though. If it doesn’t make it, I think you’ll do fine without.”

  I shook my head. Stage one was complete: I’d broken into Konoha. I had a job to do, and
  hiding by the hospital wasn’t going to help me complete it. I crouched, glancing around me to
  check for anyone watching - and paused.

  I’d swapped blindly, reaching for any window with something to swap with, but somehow I’d
  ended up outside Chouji’s room. His bed was against the opposite wall, easily visible through
  the window. I squinted; most of him was covered by the blanket, but from what I could see of
  his face, he looked good. Much closer to his old self than he had been when he first went into
  hospital. It was disorientating, to realise that life in Konoha had progressed despite the fact
  that I hadn’t been there to see it, but I was glad that he was getting better.

  “Sorry,” I said quietly. “I’m not going to say goodbye. I’m more a leave-in-the-middle-of-
  the-night kind of person, goodbyes really aren’t my style.” I hesitated, trying to get the words
  right even though he wasn’t going to hear them. “Don’t blame me too much? You can blame
  me a little, I’m the one that chose to do this, but. I have reasons. Can’t tell you any right now,
  but I have them.”

  I trailed off. This was exactly why I didn’t do goodbyes, how was anyone supposed to know
  what to say? “Call Shikamaru a bitch for me,” I went for, carefully nudging the closest cactus
  further back on the windowsill so it wasn’t so much at risk. “And, I don’t know. Add more
  fish to Yakiniku’s menu? I like squid, but variety is also nice. See you later, Chouji.”

  Talking to him reminded me that this was the last time I was going to be in Konoha. I was on
  a schedule, but it was a while yet ‘till dawn, and I’d complained enough about leaving the
  camp without proper supplies - it would be a missed opportunity not to go via my house and
  stock up. I’d only been missing nin a week, no one would’ve touched my stuff. I scanned the
  skyline for any patrols, eyed the beech tree nervously and decided to leave it a wide berth as I
  went past, and checked my henge was firmly anchored in place.

  Time to go home. It’d been a while since I last fed the fish.

   The route home was soothing in its familiarity. I stuck by the river, leaving it just before I
   reached the Uchiha district and triple checking I hadn’t been followed before hopping over
   the wall and in. The fence to the back garden was the same as ever, and on the other side, I
   was hit with the smell of the honeysuckle and the faint sound of moths’ wings as they
   hovered around the flowers. It was interspersed with the running water and sporadic tunk of
   the sozu fountain, the bamboo tube knocking against its stone base as it rocked forward under
   the weight of the water collecting inside.

   surface of the pond rippled as water passed through the filter, breaking the moon’s reflection
   into dancing ribbon-shards of light. Over on the side the cluster of lotuses was thriving, the

   The flowers were closed now - they’d open again in the morning - but I could still see the
   faint hint of pink in their petals, paler at the base and darker towards the tips.

   sense.”

So I was going to make them doubt him.

It happened all the time. Spy spends too long undercover with the enemy, spy becomes an

but my brother was off limits and if I did, the kyuubi wouldn’t let him die.

His mouth went tight, a flat expression that made the lines of his face stand out sharply in the
moonlight. “Who?” I didn’t answer. “It doesn’t matter. I’m still coming with you.”

“No.” I shook my head, but he stepped forward again, directly into the fucking sword - I
hurriedly turned the blade so the flat of it was against his throat instead of the edge and it
wasn’t going to hurt him, but that left me with no way to stop him walking towards me. I
backed up another step, a shorter one than I’d’ve liked. I was rapidly running out of space
before I’d hit the window. “No. You can’t. This is mine, not yours - and you’re going to be
the hero you can’t leave -” I reached out to hold him at arm’s length him but I had Itachi’s
mask in one hand and the sword in the other, and all I managed to do was awkwardly smoosh
my fingers against his shirt with the mask trapped between us.

“Hero? You mean Hokage?” He made a frustrated sound, rocking onto the balls of his feet in
agitation and still managing to move closer. “I wanted to be Hokage before I had a team.
Why would I need anyone else to recognise me when I have you?”

He wasn’t listening.

“You don’t have me. Maybe you had me, when I was scared and needed help and you were
there, but right now you -”
“And now I’m meant to believe you’re not scared?” His shoulders went back, the frown
subtly shifting until it was almost one of his inspirational poses. I let go of his shirt and
leaned away from him, not bothering to hide my scowl. I’d never liked being inspired-at. I
wasn’t going to be a stray lost soul to be rescued with a kind word and an uplifting speech. I
didn’t need rescuing, and I couldn’t hold myself to the standard of goodness that Naruto’s
optimism demanded, so he should save himself the effort and find someone else to focus on.
“I’m scared,” he said. Bully for him. I hope he enjoyed it. “I’m scared that if you go, you
won’t come back. I’m scared that someone’s going to take your eyes. I’m scared that
something’s wrong, but that you’ll keep it inside and deal with it by yourself until it breaks
you.”

“Aren’t you selfless. Do you want a medal?”

“And you say you don’t want help,” he continued, “but that’s not the way it works. It’s not
me helping you, it’s - it’s us doing things together, and your problems are my problems so I’ll
face them with you like you do with me -”

“I didn’t ask you to!”

“You don’t have to!” He shook his head, his inspiration turning frustrated. “I don’t ask you to
stick up for me against literally everyone, but you do. I didn’t ask you to make me see that I
mattered but you did, the only thing I ever ask you is to let me love you and you -”

“Don’t want you to,” I finished for him, all but baring my teeth on the words. “You were
temporary, Uzumaki, you were always meant to be temporary and I’m sorry if you
misunderstood -”

He bared his teeth back. His were sharper than mine. “Don’t put that on me, bastard. I didn’t
misunderstand anything. If you meant it to be temporary then you’re the one who screwed up
because you’re crap at hiding how much you care.”

I needed a hand. I needed - why were my hands full of a mask and a weapon I couldn’t use.
The tanto took longer to sheath; I pressed the mask onto my face instead. “Then let me make
it perfectly clear,” I said, reaching into my weapon pouch for a shuriken. Naruto leant back
warily, but refused to drop into a defensive position. I grit my teeth; yes, he had a healing
factor, but how the hell was he meant to survive if he couldn’t tell when someone was
genuinely going to stab him. What kind of stupid idiot was he. “You do not have me. You
don’t love me, I don’t have time for you, and if you try anyway then the only person you’re
going to hurt is yourself and I accept no responsibility for it.”

He glared. If there was ever a picture definition of defiance, he was it, and it was an effort not
to lash out and punch him just to make him stop. “Tell me why.”

“I don’t have to explain myself -”

“Sasuke. Tell me why.”

I shot him the filthiest look I knew how to, fingers clenching around the shuriken. “I don’t
have time,” I repeated. “I’m not some tragic victim planting flowers and slowly healing. I’m
not - I’m Uchiha, not a damsel in distress, I have to be strong now because I’m going to kill
the Hokage and I can’t let you stop me -”

“You’re what?”

Fuck. Fucking - “Oh,” I said sweetly, sheathing the tanto in a casual movement to free up my
other hand. “Did I forget to mention that? That’s why I came back to Konoha. It was nothing
to do with you.” Ouch. Technically true, but also much harsher than I meant to be because I
wasn’t paying attention to my words, I was relying on the mask to hide where I was looking
while I distracted Naruto with the shurikens I was now holding in both hands -

“This isn’t you,” he said. “This - you’re being controlled, or someone’s threatening you. You
don’t want to do this. I know you.”

I paused. On the other side of the window, my chakra rested on a pebble, ready to kawarimi
as soon as I needed to. We were inching closer to dawn, the last thing I wanted was a drawn
out battle that would alert the entire village to the fact that I was here. There was still a
chance Naruto could raise the alarm, but. My only other option was to take him out with an
injury so severe even the kyuubi would take a while to bounce him back from it, and that
wasn’t an option.

Unless he was right. Unless this wasn’t what I wanted. If my brother wasn’t an issue, if it was
just Kakashi, if things could go back to how they’d been when Team Seven was still all
together, if if if.

I scowled, shoving the thought aside. I’d come too far not to see it through to the end, and
Kakashi wasn’t an Uchiha. Naruto was wrong. Itachi was wrong. The Hokage was wrong.
And I was sick of people telling me who I was meant to be.

“Trust me,” I said flatly. “For the first time in my life I’m not being threatened. I’m doing
exactly what I want to do.”

“You’re lying.” He sounded - I didn’t know. A lot. Whatever emotion he sounded of, he
sounded of it a lot. “You can’t just expect me to believe -”

I switched. Landed on the gravel, and immediately ducked and switched again as a dozen
clones appeared in my path. I didn’t think they’d seen me - they were roughly evenly spaced,
fanning out from the house in a cone of vision that drastically increased as Naruto leapt out
the window after me. It was a search technique, not an attack, and as fast as each clone was
forming more copies to widen the search range it still wasn’t enough to beat my stealth. Two
more kawarimis, a camouflage henge, and a scent-blocker genjutsu layered over the top; I
could run the Uchiha district blindfolded and he’d only ever visited one part of it, and I
turned towards the village proper when I was sure I’d lost him down the back streets.

He was wrong. He was wrong, and it wasn’t my fault, and I didn’t care about him so it wasn’t
going to hurt. But I hadn’t lied. The only reason I’d never acted against Konoha before was
because I was too scared to. I hadn’t changed. I’d always hated them, I’d always - who did he
even know. Someone full of secrets, that’s who. He was wrong, and the person he thought he
knew wasn’t real because even if parts of that person were honest the whole image they
projected didn’t exist and if I suddenly, overwhelmingly wished it did - tough.

Tough.

Naruto was wrong. It didn’t matter if he believed me or not, I had a job to do. The Hokage
wasn’t going to kill himself.



The Hokage Tower was in the centre of the village. Tall, and immediately identifiable, but
that wasn’t where I was headed. The Hokage residence was just a bit further out, next to the
academy; not every Hokage spent every night there, but it was a known bone of contention
between Asuma and his dad that the Sandaime never slept anywhere else. Dedication to the
role or neglect of familial duties, I wasn’t there to decide, just to take advantage. The building
was round, large enough to potentially house an inner room on each floor that wouldn’t have
any windows, and tiered, each floor slightly smaller than the one below. In daylight it was
very obviously fire themed, with red paint on the walls, orange-glazed terracotta tiles on the
lower roofs that almost shone gold in the sun, and a giant Fire kanji painted on the flat top
roof just in case someone forgot which country we were in.

I landed on the cliff above it, head tilted as I considered my way in. The residence was
walled, but it was a low wall, more of a decorative covered walkway than anything that
would keep intruders out. The roof tiles were covered in seals, written in an excessively
looped cursive that made them impossible for even my sharingan to read. Terracotta wasn’t a
fire country staple, particularly not glazed like that or with those kinds of seals; Uzushio
make? Maybe? Uzushio tiles were in short supply, I didn’t exactly have examples to compare
them to, but I couldn’t think of anywhere else the Shodai would’ve got seal-inlaid glazed tiles
from. Give me enough time and I could maybe decipher what they said, but it made more
sense to assume they’d all either kill me or sound the alarm if I so much as stepped on them,
and just carry on with my life instead.

If they didn’t sound the alarm, Naruto might. Would he? He’d have to know what would
happen to me if I got caught, but could I count on that holding him back? I wasn’t going to
retreat now so I’d have to, but I stayed on high alert all the same.

Apart from the rooves, the walls of the building seemed safe. Safe enough to stand on, at
least, though they’d clearly been designed to be difficult to infiltrate. Rather than a few large
windows it had many small ones, none of them big enough for a ninja to get in through and
all of them secured with solid panes of glass. Kawarimi would’ve dealt with the size
problem, but the glass - I couldn’t go through solid objects. Pipes and electric cables ran
around the outside, clearly added as upgrades after the original house had been built, and
those were what I focussed on. If I could find the hole where they went inside…

I chose a collection of pipes that looked about right for a bathroom. A variety for water and
waste water, but also an old and seemingly disused fuel pipe from when baths used to be
heated in the tub on demand, and a more recent set of insulated pipes that presumably carried
hot water from a central heating tank. Bathrooms meant steam. The windows didn’t open, but
steam needed a way out or the room would be unbearably mouldy - there. Vent. Tucked away
where it wasn’t immediately visible, and bolted down in a way that would be impossible to
work loose without the proper tools. Except, I didn’t need to work it loose. I just needed to
see through it.

“Just think,” I muttered, moving up towards it. “He puts up with living in a house where he
can’t open the windows for security reasons for literal decades, and someone manages to
break in anyway. How sad for him. All that sacrifice for nothing, however will he cope.” I
squinted; there were no convenient plants to steal a leaf from and switch with, so face flannel
or weird sponge shaped decoration? Oh. Toilet roll. I defied anyone to notice a single sheet of
toilet paper falling to the ground.

One kawarimi later, and I was inside. I adjusted my henge to account for the different light
patterns and moved silently to the door, straining my ears for anyone in the corridor before I
opened it and scanning for seal alarms at every point. I didn’t know where the Hokage’s
bedroom was, so my best bet was to search as quickly and methodically as I could; it was
risky, yes, but I’d had practice sneaking past guards before and for all their reputation, ANBU
weren’t actually infallible. Black Ops cared more about your willingness to do anything your
Hokage asked than your skill ranking, ninja at Kakashi’s level were rare.

I blinked, running the sound I was hearing back through my brain.

… Ok, my alternative best bet was to follow the snores. I mean, I guess he wasn’t the
youngest he’d ever been and it was a natural part of life, but. Snores?

Twelve minutes later - creeping silently under genjutsu took time, even a genjutsu that
blocked as much sound and smell as I was able to to keep me from being detected - I
confirmed, to my complete bafflement, that the snoring was genuinely the Hokage and not a
decoy set up to distract anyone coming to assassinate him.

I just. I. Really? Maybe protocol had been written when village heads were expected to die in
their prime on a battlefield. It was the only explanation that made sense. Even so, I hesitated,
tucked into the corner of the ceiling and staring at him in confusion. Now that I was actually
here and faced with a sleeping old man instead of a grim war leader, I wasn’t sure how I was
meant to continue. Stab him? Poison? Only idiots cared about a fair fight, but at the same
time, I was avenging my family and my brother. I felt… cheated, a bit, by how simple
everything seemed.

“I was sure my first appointment wasn’t until eight,” the Hokage said, not moving from his
position in the bed. I held myself very, very still. “I appreciate the enthusiasm, though I must
admit my office is better set up for receiving guests.”

I didn’t respond. He opened his eyes and sat up, feet swinging out of bed and hands resting
politely in his lap with no sign of any residual sleepiness. If he had old-man stiffness to go
along with his old-man snores, he didn’t show it, and under the blanket he was wearing the
sort of plain dark outfit that any field ninja would sleep in on a mission. If he’d even had old-
man snores to begin with. They’d stopped with the sort of abruptness that suggested they
might not have been real in the first place, and the sharingan didn’t help me against auditory
genjutsu.
I was reminded, sharply, that Sarutobi Hiruzen had been one of the most feared ninja of his
generation. It wasn’t an accident that he’d survived this long.

“Please,” he said, gesturing at a chair beside his bed that was currently being used to hold his
robes. There was even a shoehorn leant against it to help him put his sandals on without
bending down. Somehow, that didn’t make it any less foreboding. “Won’t you join me? You
wouldn’t have seen them on your way in, but I assure you, my ANBU are early risers.”

Bluff? He was right, I hadn’t seen anyone. I’d rationalised that they were more concerned
with defending points of entry rather than sticking close to the Hokage himself. If he meant
he could call them, would I still have enough time to kill him before they arrived? I had
Karin and her snake to get me out, escaping afterwards should be fine - but if the ANBU
were close enough…

I dropped down to the open floor space. Not the chair, but if the Hokage felt at all at a
disadvantage by sitting on the bed while I stood, it didn’t bother him.

“Dismiss them,” I demanded, dropping my henge. He raised an eyebrow but didn’t seem
surprised to see me, and I grit my teeth and continued as though I had full confidence that I’d
be obeyed: “My brother sent me.” And, unspoken, you don’t want them to hear what I have to
say.

His mild expression didn’t change, but the threat worked; the fingers of his right hand
pressed against his left wrist in a series of movements that I wouldn’t have picked up without
the sharingan. ANBU tap code. I wasn’t fluent, but I caught enough: stand down was one, as
was not a threat, and await further instructions.

I scowled behind my mask. Not a threat my ass. Still, at least it told me that he recognised
Itachi’s uniform and knew who I was, that was something at least.

“Your brother,” he said. “Not who I was expecting, Sasuke-kun. When you disappeared, I
half suspected that Orochimaru had convinced you to join him.”

“He tried to scoop out my eye with a shuriken. Why the fuck does everyone think I’m going
to join him.”

He smiled at me, grandfatherly and approving. “I’m glad to hear it, Sasuke-kun. He’s
charming when he wants to be, you’re wiser than many who’ve fallen for it.”

Sasuke-kun. Sasuke-kun, Sasuke-kun, repeated use of a friendly form of address and not-so
subtle flattery - “His isn’t the only charm I don’t fall for,” I snapped. “Don’t call me Sasuke-
kun. The only thing I am to you is Uchiha.”

“Uchiha, then,” he agreed. He also dropped the grandfather act, facing me as an equal
instead. His shoulders weren’t bowed, but even so he couldn’t fully hide the exhaustion in
them, and there was an edge of grief and regret to his expression. “You’re here to talk about
your clan.”
I didn’t trust it. There was no way a Hokage would treat a runaway genin as an equal, even if
I was representing my family. It was another act, and the regret was as fake as anything else.

“Talk. Sure. Let’s go with that.” The thing about acting was that it only worked if your act
was believable. Audience participation. It was a thing, and the same applied to genjutsu. That
was where most illusions failed - you make them too prescriptive, tell people to accept too
many changes to their surroundings that they know are false, and the whole premise falls
apart. “You killed us. Is that a good starting place?”

But, and this was the tricky thing; let them fill in the blanks themselves, and they’re much
more likely to believe you - but if you move outside what they know, they’re much more
likely to get it wrong.

“I did.”

I scowled, shifting back on my heels. “That’s it? I did - you’re just going to admit it?”

Sure, ask them to accept that an empty room is empty, everyone knows what that looks like.
But ask them to accept that you stabbed them through the neck and they died? Very few
people are familiar with the feeling. Their consciousness comes up with an approximation
based on what they remember from other wounds, presents it to their nervous system, and
their nervous system asks them if they’re having a laugh because what the fuck is this. You
can’t kill people with genjutsu by making them imagine it. They aren’t that creative. It won’t
work. Even Tsukuyomi failed to provide enough evidence to override a body’s stubborn
belief that it was alive, and it created a world that was entirely under the user’s control.

“There’s no future in dishonesty,” the Hokage said, tilting his head towards me. “I’m not
trying to lie to you, Uchiha-kun.”

“Just Uchiha. Uchiha-sama if you really must.”

“Your clan are dead. I was the one to make the call,” - lie - “and I was the one who had to
choose if the lives of one family outweighed the lives of the entire village.” He closed his
eyes, too long for a blink, and when he opened them every year of his tenure as Hokage was
weighing down on him. “It was not a choice I made lightly. If there was a way to save both, I
would have taken it, but the Uchiha made sure that was not an option.”

“Bullshit,” I sneered. “If there were ways to save both then you were the one who spent
decades refusing to acknowledge them. I know the reasons for the coup, I know about the
years leading up to it - this isn’t your narrative and you can’t control it. You didn’t choose the
lives of the village, you chose the village itself. You chose a power structure you were in
charge of and a system that benefited you and you pretend you did it to stop people dying but
you have no proof that that’s what would have happened either way.”

He frowned. “The coup would’ve torn Konoha apart -”

“So? Konoha’s wrong. Konoha’s so fucking wrong on so many levels, anyone could poke a
hole in it and watch everything come falling out and the only reason they don’t is because no
one’s ever done it before and they’re scared to be the first. Of course they’re scared to be the
first. You know that’s the only thing holding them back, why the fuck would you allow
anyone to be the first? So you have to get rid of dissenters before anyone can see that they
aren’t alone or else your house of cards gets set on fucking fire -” He tried to say something; I
didn’t stop. “And you know the worst thing? It’s not even your house of cards. You didn’t
give the order. Danzo did. You’re fighting for a crown you don’t even get to wear, and you
still sit there like you’re in charge and tell me you made the fucking call.”

“Danzo,” he repeated. He looked stricken. He looked old, so very, very old, he looked - I
didn’t care how he looked. “What did Itachi tell you? Uchiha, what do you know?”

And see, the thing is. I didn’t trust other people’s imaginations. That was why I preferred
detailed genjutsu, why I chose what they saw and didn’t leave it up to chance and why I
preferred subtle changes to sweeping, reality-defying constructions. The Hokage was
indulging me. I was a genjutsu and stealth specialist with a few battle-tricks up my sleeve; if I
was a credible threat, he’d never have sent his ANBU away. Genjutsu wasn’t dangerous by
itself because genjutsu couldn’t kill anyone because no one knew what it was like to die - to
permanently, with full, awful realisation of your own mortality end and never restart again.
No one knew it well enough to recreate it.

I did.

I looked the God of Shinobi in the eye, and said, “Drown.”

And he did.

His eyes went wide. That was a mistake; he was underwater, the salt would sting them. At
first he tried to brush it off and just ignore the illusion, but the current caught him. Dragged
him. Not down, just across; I could see his muscles tensing as he tried instinctively to fight it.
Then - back. Dragged him back. Away from the shore. He’d got used to the change of scene
now, and was feeling around the edges of the genjutsu with his chakra to see where he could
pick it apart. Against someone who hadn’t lived it, maybe, but there weren’t any loose
threads he could lean on. Five days travelling to Konoha from the marshes, five days to
remember every detail and put it together into a reality he couldn’t get out of, five days
pouring all the anger and all the nightmares into something my family would be proud of.
The current pulled him back because he’d turned to swim against it, because he thought he
was strong enough, and now the muscle ache was setting in. Now he was starting to tire. Now
he was starting to panic, because the current was stronger than he was, and the shore was
getting further and further away.

He flared his chakra. The ANBU probably felt it. I didn’t care.

Panic worked against him. He slipped under, and it felt like the current dragged him down. It
didn’t. It just pulled him back, back and back and back with no reprieve - but when he went
under he panicked and lost control. His heart was beating too fast. His eyes were open,
because we’re visual creatures and we get scared of the dark behind our eyelids, but all he
saw was the sea. He scraped his shoulder against the rocky floor, turned and tried to push off
from it, and couldn’t find where it was.
He dislocated his thumb. Any other genjutsu, the pain would’ve snapped him out of it. It
didn’t.

He couldn’t find the surface. He couldn’t find the floor. He couldn’t find any direction, and
now fear overrode any sense of reason. He flailed. He wasted energy and oxygen trying to
escape and all he did was exhaust himself. His chest burned. His brain was telling him to get
out, repeating it on loop like a desperate mantra that would save his life, but his lungs were
straining from the force of not breathing and his scrabbling fingers were finding nothing but
more water wherever they turned.

He slammed his hand down on the bed, black lines spreading out from it in every direction. I
stepped to the side and walked three feet up the wall to avoid them; when he pulsed chakra
down them he left lightning-burn marks on the legs of his furniture but I was out of reach.

He clamped his teeth shut, against the water that wanted to come in, against the used breath
that wanted to go out, against the weight in his ears that felt like the sea was drilling into his
skull -

He stamped his foot, more of a spasm than a controlled gesture, and curving blades of wind
shot out of the ceiling and the floor to meet in the middle. They were so dense with chakra
the outlines of them glowed with it; I kawarimid with his pillow and watched as it got ripped
apart between them.

The instinct to breathe was too strong to ignore. He opened his mouth. Bubbles exploded
from it and for a fraction of a second the release of pressure felt like a miracle, then his chest
expanded again and the water came rushing in.

“Enma,” he mouthed, lifting his dislocated thumb to his mouth with a shaky hand. His other
hand was clutching the mattress for support, but even with it to hold him up he was listing
dangerously to the side. I reached out and pushed his thumb away.

He choked. The urge to cough fought with the urge to inhale. The salt water burnt everything.
His chest was breaking and his lungs were swallowing lava. His head felt like it was going to
explode.

He collapsed.

He drowned.

The genjutsu held for another few moments, then the threads of it snapped. Illusions don’t
work on corpses. I checked his pulse mechanically, then followed up by holding a kunai over
his mouth to see if any condensation formed on the metal from his breath. It didn’t. I’d done
what countless people had tried and failed to do, what even Danzo had had to put on hold; the
Hokage was dead.

Long live the Hokage.

I took a deep, shuddering breath, shaking off the far too vivid experience of maintaining the
genjutsu and assuring myself that I wasn’t the one who had died - this time - and took my
  mask off, dropping it next to his body on the bed. I half expected him to sit up again, or roll
  over and start snoring. Part of me couldn’t actually believe that it had worked. It’d been a
  crazy plan from the start and I’d had doubts that I could even go through with it, but I did.
  ANBU Weasel was done. The Hokage didn’t own my brother any more. I was done. I was
  done.

  From the other side of the room, Orochimaru gave a slow, drawn-out clap.

  “Sasuke-chan,” he said, “You continue to be a delight.”

   Orochimaru.

   I flicked my eyes up to him, but didn’t move. Processing the Hokage’s death would have to
   wait - just then, I needed to focus on getting out. The original plan of signalling Karin to
   summon me via the snake was still my best bet overall, but I didn’t know how long it would
   take her to notice me and I didn’t want to spend any longer around Orochimaru than I had to.

   “You’re like a little knife in the back,” he continued, picking his way through the mess the
   Hokage’s wind blades had left over the floor. “Underwhelming and ignorable, right up until
   you kill someone because they didn’t see you coming. I love it.”

   “I prefer shurikens to knives,” I said. There was only one way in or out of the room. It might
   have been designed that way to be easier to defend, but a box with one opening was a
   dangerous trap if I wasn’t careful. I edged along the wall towards it, scowling and keeping
   my attention on Orochimaru to cover up what I was doing. “And I’m not ignorable. You have
   no idea how strong I am.”

   “Strong enough to handle the S-rank bounty they’ll put on you for killing a kage?” He shook
   his head at me, gently chiding, and retrieved Itachi’s mask with a disappointed downturn of
   his mouth. “I can fix this one for you, but you need to be more careful. How can I ever let
   you out by yourself if you insist on making mistakes like this?”

   “Let me out -” I bit my tongue on the swear words that wanted to follow that. By his amused
   smile, he heard them anyway.

   “I don’t want to keep you cooped up forever, Sasuke-chan. If you leave this room you’ll be
   out of range of my suppressant seal. Much as I appreciate how you dispassionately stared
   Hiruzen down until he died, it wasn’t the quietest way he could’ve gone.”

   It took me a moment to work out what he was saying - there was no change of tone between
   statements to give his threat any context. I stared, watching him blankly as he vanished the
   mask into some unseen pocket (the mask, did he have any idea what it represented or how
   much I hated him stealing it) and took out a kunai to slit the Hokage’s throat. It wasn’t
   necessary - he was very clearly dead - but if it made him feel better, I wasn’t going to stop
   him.

   “You… hid me?” I asked, trying to wrap my head around it. I didn’t know enough about
   suppressant seals to be sure, but in theory, I guessed, they could have blocked any ANBU
   from sensing the Hokage’s attempts to fight me.

   “Of course. You’re no use to me if they execute you.”
I - no. Moving past that. If I was inside a suppressant seal, I couldn’t signal Karin. ANBU

“Well.” What did you say when someone accused you like that? “Well, it’s true. And neither
of you have clones, so if you want to do something about it, you need to scoot.”

“Leaving you free to escape while we do so,” Shino finished for me.
“Bombs, Shino. Big ones. Lots of dead people.”

He nodded, turning expectantly to Shikamaru. When Shikamaru just hesitated, he prompted,
“One missing nin can’t take priority over the many civilians and allies who could be affected

“I know,” Shikamaru snapped. “If she’s telling the truth, we have to go. But either she’s

What. What were the mangoes. Why were there mangoes. “Sorry to disappoint,” I snipped,

“Just - fine. You know what, fine.” He reached into his weapon pouch and withdrew a kunai,
spinning it in his hand to a backwards hold.

I did the same and came up with a shuriken.

“If you attempt to make me knock myself out with this shuriken I swear -”

He gripped the kunai tighter in frustration, and carefully maneuvered his hand so I’d drop my

The Hokage was dead. Whatever was happening between Orochimaru and the ANBU,

Nor did you carry on with your plan to brain your shadow-bound friend-turned-missing nin

Flames spilled out over my hands, aggressive and dangerously wild. The firefly jutsu was

I didn’t have time to be diplomatic.

He didn’t like it, but he was intelligent enough, at least, to know when to concede. He

We are not our fathers. My father did everything he could to keep the clan together. He didn’t
want to fight. He searched desperately for another explanation, another way out, and when he
couldn’t find one - he died. The death Itachi had shown me in his Tsukuyomi was staged, but

crushing defeat, it didn’t matter; they’d given up, and they’d died, and Konoha won.

If I hadn’t had more memories than I was meant to have, the truth of Konoha’s actions would
have died when my father did. Itachi was never going to tell. If anyone else in Konoha knew,
they’d never done anything about it, but my dad was hardly one to share the things the clan

What good did secrets do if you died with them.

“The other one is Danzo,” I said, lifting my head and making eye-contact with Shino’s
glasses. “Be careful. He’s been using a hidden division of ANBU called ROOT to run things

“If you were aware you’d be dead,” I shot back. “Whatever you think you know is only a

“I’m aware of him,” he repeated. “Thank you for the warning. Are you here to murder

I grit my teeth. Had it been a mistake to tell him? He was making himself my ally, but he had
