authority to form alliances in the first place. Hell, he wasn’t even him. Did alliances count if
they were agreed with a clone made up of thousands of symbiotic invertebrates? Had he
connected the Hokage’s death to me being the one to kill him? How did he know of Danzo in
the first place - and when he said that the Aburame allied with the Uchiha, was he speaking
for himself or had I missed something about his entire clan?

I had approximately eleven minutes left until dawn. Questions would have to wait.

“To rescue him,” I corrected. “You missed that part of the conversation, but the hospital’s
going to explode. So are various other places. I can’t warn anyone because I’m not meant to
be here but Shikamaru and Shino - um, original Shino - know, they’re trying to get people to
safety.” At a guess, or maybe they were trying to get someone to dismantle the seals. I had no
idea where the seals actually were, though they’d have to be hidden pretty well to have
escaped notice so far. Could seals be picked up by the byakugan? Could they be disguised as
something else, or be so condensed down they were basically invisible until they activated?

I shook my head. Now wasn’t the time to get distracted.

“Then I will assist them,” Shino said, already beginning to dissolve. “If that was the threat to

“Yeah, that’s - ok. Um. Bye, then.”

I squinted after the kikaichu as they - and the ones that had been left in the cloud to keep
watch - dispersed into the village, presumably to go back to Shino. There was something
inherently weird about someone talking about themselves in the first person and then being
made up of countless separate creatures. Did Shino gain the clone’s memories like Naruto
would if a clone dispelled? Had the clone even dispelled, given that it had reformed itself out
of a cloud once already? How had it been able to talk in the first place?

But again: getting distracted could wait. Whatever else Shino and Shikamaru were doing, I
still needed to get Chouji out. I turned away from the kikaichu, leaving them to warn
whoever they saw fit, and made for the window with a single-minded determination.

   Chouji was awake when I climbed soundlessly onto the windowsill. I’d’ve been worried if he
   wasn’t given how deafeningly loud the klaxon was, but hospital patients were expected to
   stay put unless the village was under direct attack. Which it was. Someone should probably
   update the distress code. Someone who wasn’t me, I had different priorities to focus on.

   I scanned the room, checking if any of Shino’s kikaichu had stayed behind, and only dropped
   my henge when I was sure that Chouji was alone. It didn’t take him long to notice me once I
   did.

   “Sasuke?” he asked, standing up in surprise.

   “Me,” I agreed. The lock on the window barely counted as a lock, just a hook on the inside to
   keep it shut. Ninjas; a bad lock was the same as no lock, and a good one was just a challenge
   for bored patients on bed rest. Easier - cheaper - to not have one at all, and to open the
   window all I had to do was slide one of my thinner shuriken between the glass and the frame
   and lift the hook out of place. “We need to go. The hospital’s a target, it’s not safe to stay.”

   His gaze darted between me and the village behind me. “Go where?”

   “Anywhere that isn’t here.” I checked the sun, and shifted agitatedly on my heels at how
   close dawn was. “Now, Chouji. Come on.”

   “I’m coming,” he promised. He also moved slowly over to the bed, careful not to overtax his
   stiff muscles as he collected his things from the bedside table.

   I nearly screamed.

   “Hey, what happened to your cat?”

   “My cat?” I repeated in disbelief. “Since when have I ever had a cat? And can we talk about
   imaginary pets later when imminent death isn’t literally inches below the horizon?”

   “The brown one,” he continued, entirely unphased. “Tabby? I’m not sure on cat colours. The
   one you gave me to hold when that genin threatened us.”

   What the fuck. “Gaara? You mean when - that was Tora. I know you know Tora, everyone
   knows Tora because she escapes every fecking day. She’s an inspiration to us all. Get.”
The stiffness vanished, as did any interest he had in the small bag he’d supposedly been
packing. “Sorry, sorry, I wasn’t sure it was you.”

“Plus ten for caution, negative four thousand for timing,” I grumped, somewhat mollified by
his explanation. “The hospital’s on an explosive seal, we need to not be here. Preferably
yesterday, now will suffice.”

“Did the evacuation alarm not work? Or is -” he tilted his head in a general, non-specific
direction to indicate the klaxon that was still wailing throughout the village. “I thought that
one was for the Hokage?”

“It is. The Sandaime’s dead, Orochimaru’s here, lots of death is about to occur but you’re not
going to be part of it. How much chakra do you have access to at the moment?”

“None of my techniques,” he answered, and started withdrawing back into the room. “There’s
an alarm point in the corridor. If the hospital’s going to blow up we need to let people know.”

“Wait, there isn’t time -” I reached for him, but he was surprisingly quick, and unsurprisingly
not happy with the idea of leaving the other patients and staff to die.

“We can’t not try,” he insisted.

I bit off my instinctive response to that. I was a missing nin. My priorities were to save
Chouji, save myself, and run. Stopping to play hero really didn’t factor into any part of that,
and if I was sensible I’d either ignore the way Chouji was stubbornly aiming for the door and
abandon him to it, or get him out by force and not care about anyone else.

Except.

“I’ll do it,” I said, dropping into the room. “You go. There’s a tree just below us - don’t touch
the trunk, but if you’ve not got much chakra the branches are an easier way down than wall-
walking.”

“I can come with you,” he started. I scowled at him, physically turning him round and
pushing him towards the window.

“Don’t test me,” I warned. “You said you had no techniques, that makes you a rescue-ee not a
rescuer. Get to safety or so fucking help me, I’m going to knock you unconcious and carry
you there. Clear?”

“Clear,” he repeated, with a faint smile. “And… Sasuke? You’ll tell me after what’s going
on?”

“Dawn’s ten minutes away,” I said instead of answering the question. “Scram, Chouji.”

He nodded, and after a final look back at me, lifted himself out onto the windowsill, and left.
I stayed staring after him for too long, then shook myself and went to the door. There wasn’t
going to be an after. He’d hear about it from the others, see the burn scar I’d left Shikamaru
with, and draw his own conclusions. And if I wanted him to remember me as the person who
listened to him and tried to help the other people in the hospital, well, that was on me. He was
my first friend - for five years, my only friend - and… and, I don’t know. I didn’t want him to
hate me like everyone else would. I just. I’d burnt a lot of bridges, I wanted to be able to kid
myself that I’d kept one alive.

I also wanted to save him, save me, and run, so in light of that I reapplied my henge and
padded silently into the corridor. The alarm point was by the stairwell. I didn’t meet anyone
on my way to it - I didn’t expect to, either - but I did hear sounds coming from a couple of the
rooms I passed. The alarm itself was a simple seal inked on a piece of chakra-paper and stuck
to the wall, with an extensive list of fines outlined underneath for setting it off outside an
emergency. If I was lucky, people would evacuate via the windows, but I kept my attention
on the occupied rooms and the door to the stairwell just in case while I channeled chakra to
my fingers and held them against the seal to activate it.

The seal didn’t activate. Not that one, at least. The paper it was written on dissolved. My
chakra flooded into a second, hidden matrix and down through the floor; I snatched my hand
back and turned to run -

And the building detonated around me.

Interlude: Dead Hokage on the Hokage mountain with his village spread out before him

The hospital went first. A chain of smaller explosions, spreading both up and down from the
fourth floor; they took out load-bearing walls, smashed glass, and acted as flash-bombs to
disorientate anyone still inside. In the seconds it took them to reach the foundation, the
hospital became an unstable death trap. One final explosion as the largest, ground-level seal
went off, and the whole building listed to the side and collapsed.

From the top of the tallest stone hair-spike on the Sandaime’s mountain head, Orochimaru
raised an eyebrow and watched.

“Tut tut, Sasuke-chan,” he said, clicking his tongue against his teeth in disapproval. “Greed is
an ugly trait. We’ll need to teach you to accept what you’re given, you’ll be difficult if you
get used to asking for more.”

Dawn was still below the horizon, though not by much. The sky in the east was a pale-
washed blue-green, fading to an orange glow; the few clouds were dark silhouettes softly
outlined in pink. A few minutes, perhaps, until the sun finally appeared. The first wave of
responders to the attack on the Hokage had been successfully driven off - even ANBU, it
seemed, could work out when they needed to regroup and wait for backup - and the morning
chill carried a feeling of calm and anticipation that Orochimaru was loathe to interrupt.

Well. It did at the top of the Hokage monument, at least. Down in the village the combination
of the klaxon and the explosion had incited a panicked alertness that left the streets swarming
with ninja, but that only added to his general air of satisfaction.

“I wish you could see it, Sensei,” he said, reaching out to rest a hand on the doton pillar he’d
impaled the Sandaime’s corpse against. “I made a set of barrier seals specially for you so you
wouldn’t be able to help them, just stand here and watch them fall.” He hummed, tilting his
head to the side. “Although. I wanted to show you the Edo Tensei too, there might not’ve
been time for sightseeing.”

A flare of chakra by the village gates made him narrow his eyes. He’d assumed Sasuke
would be at the hospital to collect her Akimichi herself. It wasn’t impossible that he’d
misjudged how she’d act - she’d surprised him before, it was one of the things he appreciated
about her - but he didn’t think… Ah. The chakra flared again, an indiscriminate rage of
killing intent that only a bijuu could produce. In the shadow of it, barely discernible at this
distance but recogniseable from its familiarity, came the whisper-scale feel of a snake being
summoned, one of the mid-sized ones that were large enough to fight.

Karin. And the jinchuuriki Sasuke insisted on carting around with her, but he was of lesser
value. Bijuu chakra was just so crude. A blunt and unrefined instrument, difficult to work
with and producing lacklustre results when Orochimaru tried. Granted, living chakra
constructs were an interesting concept, and the way they could reform after their physical
form was destroyed was useful as inspiration if nothing else - but the reality of them was a
frustrating waste of potential that he didn’t care to bother with again. The sharingan’s abilities
to manipulate death, Sasuke as living evidence that souls could be permanently reattached,
Karin’s chakra and the vitality it carried within it; these were far better avenues of research.

But: research was for a later date. “I put so much effort into planning this for you, it seems a
shame not to enjoy it now it’s here,” he said, adjusting Hiruzen’s head so his sightless, ruined
eyes were looking over the village. “Dawn is close enough. Sasuke-chan’s little group is
making quite a scene, I’d hate to be upstaged.”

Jiraiya landed on the mountain with a sharp tap of his wooden sandals. Behind him, ANBU
and jounin fanned out, creating a thick ring of people cutting Orochimaru off from any
escape. Backup had arrived.

Orochimaru’s mouth thinned.

“Jiraiya,” he acknowledged, voice soured with annoyance. “How tedious of you to drop by.
Did you come to watch the show?”

In answer, Jiraiya widened his stance. He didn’t - yet - summon any of his toads, but from the
way his eyes darted first to the other ninja around them then to the open space behind the
Hokage monument, it was clear why he was holding back.

“Come to get in the way,” Orochimaru amended distastefully. “You’ve never been able to
beat me one on one, what’s the point in trying now?”

“Retrieve Sarutobi-sama,” Jiraiya instructed the ANBU next to him. She nodded, hands
already tapping out staccato commands to her squad as she calculated a strategy. To the
jounin on his other side, Jiraiya said, “Protect the village. His widest-reaching area jutsu are
mud and water. Once he’s beyond the village limits, make sure he can’t come back.”

“Ignoring me? Childish. I thought Sensei was the one who turned blind eyes to people, not
you.”
Jiraiya’s expression hardened. So did his hair, the long ponytail solidifying into needle-spikes
in preparation for the fight. “You had all the attention in the world,” he said. “It still was
never enough.”

The first ray of sunlight lifted over the horizon.

“You still think I wanted attention,” Orochimaru shot back. He slid one foot behind himself,
and pooled chakra in the palm of his right hand. “I’d tell you how wrong you were, but the
words are too long for you to understand.”

Something flashed across Jiraiya’s face - pain, frustration, old wounds never given chance to

“Earth release: swamp of the -”

“Detonate!”

The ground beneath them shattered. Huge chunks of rock were violently wrenched into the
air, followed by a scorching, mushrooming fireball as the incendiary explosions caught. The

visible glowing threads - one to the hospital, though that explosion was already spent; one to

to break through. One to the civilian market, burning through the store rooms dug into the
ground below it where the damp earth kept food supplies cool, one to the centre of the largest
residential district where families were huddled in fear as the klaxon continued to sound.

One after the other in inevitable, horrifying succession, the targets blew up. Whatever meagre
evacuation efforts Shino and Shikamaru had managed to put in place with the short notice
Sasuke had given them, they weren’t enough. People died. People died, and the central
administration of the village fell, and Konoha had tried so hard to keep the war outside her
walls but Orochimaru had always meant them to suffer and if Hiruzen had still been alive
then perhaps he’d even tell him why -

He backflipped out the way of the bullet of flaming toad-oil Jiraiya spat at him, mouth
already opening to bring out his sword to parry. Hiruzen was dead. So was a good portion of
his village, or in the process of becoming, and with the majority of Konoha’s forces still
holding the border between Fire and Rice, the survivors had no chance of keeping
Orochimaru from getting away. Sasuke was either caught in the mess of the hospital or well
on her way to escaping, and for the time being, Orochimaru was inclined to let her. Giving
her cause to follow through with her threat to destroy her eyes would be an undesirable
outcome, and not one that at present he had the means to circumvent. The delay was a
setback, but not an unsurmountable one; better for her to realise - with assistance - how
unforgiving the world was to missing nin and come to him of her own volition than to force
her into a corner she did something foolish to get out of.
In the meantime though, it’d been too long since Orochimaru’d rubbed Jiraiya’s face in how
completely outclassed he was. It seemed a waste to ignore the opportunity when it had so
neatly presented itself.

The aftershocks from the second round of explosions subsided. I huddled in a tightly curled
ball, my limbs tucked underneath me as though my spine were any better at shrugging off
rubble than my legs were. My hands were plastered defensively over my face, palms
covering my eyes and my thumbs digging painfully into my temples. I don’t know what I was
expecting them to do. If I couldn’t see the danger, it didn’t exist? That was. I mean, it wasn’t
the smartest thing I’d ever done.

It still took me far too long to get round to moving them away.

“That,” I said hoarsely, grimacing at the dust in my teeth, “was fucking unpleasant.” I stifled
the urge to cough. My throat was dry and the air felt gritty and coarse against it, but if I
started coughing I’d just irritate it further and I didn’t have any water to soothe it. “Why do I
sound weird. Why do I - if you screwed up my ears Orochimaru, I’m going to end you. Who
rigs a detonation trap to the fucking -” I broke off, concentrating on breathing for a second
and trying to suck my tongue for whatever saliva I could manage. It helped. A fraction. “The
fucking alarm. That’s just. That’s a dick move. Who does that.”

What if I’d actually died? Where would he get his sharingan from then, did he stop to think
of that? Or was I so predictable that he’d somehow known I’d only try to get Chouji out, and
not think of warning anyone else? Which. Was true, kind of, but I didn’t like what it said
about me.

“Focus,” I told myself. I was still in the same awkwardly hunched kneeling position, what
felt like half the building pressing down against my back. The floor beneath me was uneven,
a jagged edge of broken tile digging painfully into my shin. I wasn’t being crushed, but when
I tried to shift my weight to find a more comfortable position the assorted debris above me
shuddered with an alarming groan.

I froze. Maybe my spine wasn’t the strongest shield in the world, but I’d much rather hold the
building up with my shoulders than with my head. If the haphazardly piled debris I was
kneeling on slipped at all I’d go sprawling, and I didn’t want to think about what would
happen to me then.

“So,” I said, barely above a whisper, “So, don’t move then. That’s fine. How hard is that, just
stay in one place. What’s the worst that could - no, nope, don’t ask that, that’s not a thing we
want to know.”

I tried to distract myself by wondering if anyone else had got out. If anyone was trapped like
I was and shouting for help, I couldn’t hear them, but that might have been more to do with
the general fuzziness and background ringing that had taken up residence in my ears than
anything else. Hopefully Chouji had stayed clear. Chouji better have stayed clear. Oh god,
what if Chouji hadn’t stayed clear. This was a shit way to distract myself. Fuck.
Fuck.

I swallowed.

“I would really like, please, to go back three hours and start this day over. Night over.” My
voice was tight. The dust was getting in my eyes and making them sting, but I’d moved my
hands to brace against the ground and support my torso, and I didn’t dare move them back.
“It’s ok, the Hokage doesn’t need to be dead. I can find another way to make Itachi part of the
clan again. One that doesn’t end up trapped in a building that’s waiting to flatten me. A better
way. I can -”

Somewhere to my left, something gave way. I didn’t see it, but I heard it, and felt the sudden
increase in pressure as the weight over my shoulders got noticeably heavier. My heartrate
rocketed, but when nothing else happened I grit my teeth and shook my head.

“I take it back,” I said, face twisting into a grimace. “If I had this night again the only thing
I’d do differently would be to not wake Naruto up so he couldn’t interfere. Dead Hokage is
good Hokage. Chouji’s not an idiot, he wouldn’t run into an explosion. I’m still alive. Bad
thoughts don’t help. No space for bad thoughts. Only space for surviving. Get a grip.”

Frustration, even at myself, was a much safer emotion than misplaced regret. My current
position was precarious at best, but if I turned my head just slightly, I could see an air pocket
under a twisted girder that looked stable enough to aim for. More stable than where I was, at
least, and I reached for a piece of broken wall, took a breath, and switched.

The floor beneath me gave way as I landed. The loose rubble skidded aside and I let out a
startled yelp as I lost balance and everything on top of me came clattering down. Girder not
stable. Bad plan. Bad plan. I switched again, blindly, desperately, scraping my knee raw
against broken concrete in the process. One of the hospital machines fell across my leg and I
kicked it viciously away, sharingan straining in the darkness to see any way out that I could
escape through. All I needed was a crack. What was the point of super-vision and the ability
to magically teleport through the tiniest little spaces if the tiniest little spaces didn’t fucking
exist.

I ended up in a doorway. It wasn’t great - the door had had a glass window in it which was
now in jagged shards on the floor - but the ground didn’t move and the ceiling was obligingly
not falling down. It would do. I allowed myself a moment to curl up against the wooden
frame, legs to my chest, arms around my shins, face buried in the narrow dip between my
knees. There was only one dawn. The explosions had gone off and there weren’t going to be
any more. I still had my air pocket of safety. I was good. I’d find a way out - in a bit. I just. In
a bit.

I’d need another strategy for Itachi anyway. He thought I was worthless. It’s not like he was
going to believe I’d actually done anything if Orochimaru was out there taking credit, and I
was running short of kages to get his attention with. Hell, depending on how overkill
Orochimaru had been, I could be running short of Konoha to get his attention with. Arguably
I should be happy about that given how much I hated the place, but rampant destruction and
indiscriminate murder wasn’t really the goal I was aiming for. It was the administration that
needed to go, not the people.
The building creaked alarmingly.

I tensed, lifting my head and bracing myself. Orochimaru had definitely said all the
explosions would go off at dawn. I’d felt them, dawn had been and gone, so what the hell was
happening now. I strained my hearing; the ringing had receded, thankfully, but it was hard to
tell how much of the fuzziness remained and how much was just sounds being muffled by
everything around me. There was… something happening, either too far away or too small
for me to pick much up. Not more explosions. I didn’t think? Thuds, impacts, like earth-
shaking jutsu being thrown around for the hell of it. Literally earth-shaking, even if only
slightly, which would be a lot less alarming if I was somewhere a lot less shakeable.

“If I die to a battle I’m not even fighting in, I’m going to flip. Fuck!” Down to the left of me,
a whole section of crumbled wall caved in. I flinched, moving automatically into a better
position to dodge from, and kept my eyes trained on it. A stray metal handrail clattered as it
fell by the cave in, and I stared in trepidation, all my senses focussed on the shifting-
scrabbling-whining as the -

Wait.

“Urushi?”

There was a pause, then he barked and the scrabbling picked up in earnest. I choked out a
laugh, skidding away from the pile I’d been sitting on and falling to my knees by the hole he
was making. “Urushi,” I repeated. “Oh my god I love you, you genius dog,
perfect perfect person you’re the best thing to ever happen in my life and I’ll never invade the
village without you ever again.” I moved aside what bits I could, knocking on the wall with
my fist to direct him to areas that were safe to dig at and doing my best to shore up the parts
that weren’t. It was slow progress at first, neither of us built for the brute strength required to
break through, then my steady string of praises and nonsense was interrupted by black seals
spreading through the cracks around one of the larger pieces of wall.

I leaned back defensively, but it only took a second for the blocky, square script to resolve
itself into something I could read. Barrier, it said - or, the gist of it said - and when it had
completely encircled the piece of wall and made sure nothing would collapse around it,
someone punched a hole through the middle of it from the other side.

I switched with the first thing I saw and landed in a messy, achy sprawl.

“You’re amazing,” I said, pushing myself unsteadily to a sitting position and searching for
Urushi. “Have I ever told you how much I - Sakura.”

I held myself still, blinking up at her in surprise. Urushi trotted up next to me, tail wagging,
so I hadn’t been wrong in hearing him. I just, clearly, hadn’t been the only one.

“Honestly?” Sakura said, staring back at me with an expression I didn’t know how to
interpret. “I’m not actually sure you did. You’re bad at telling people things, Sasuke-chan.”

“I always thought it was the other way round,” I said around a suddenly dry mouth. How
much did she know? How much had she worked out for herself? I had no idea what she was
thinking. “I tell people too much. Life would be so much easier if I could keep my mouth
shut.”

Her eyes narrowed. “So it’s true? What you said to Naruto?”

Um. That could encompass a lot of things. “I don’t make a habit of lying?” I hazarded.
“Unless you ask Shikamaru, but there’s your mistake to begin with.”

“That you were going to kill the Hokage. They’re saying Orochimaru did it, but no one’s got
an official report either way.”

Oh. Well, no, there wouldn’t have been an official report yet. The klaxon had stopped, but
that was probably because it got blown up along with half the village. Maybe not quite half.
Because it got blown up along with several key areas that both caused major disruption to the
village’s core structure and carried a hefty body count, but Konoha was a big village. It didn’t
come to half.

Stalling wasn’t helping.

“How did you know I was here?”

She took my avoidance for the answer it was. For a moment she faltered, eyes narrowing,
then widening in disbelief, then blinking shut as she swallowed and clenched her jaw. It
didn’t last - it lasted such a short period I almost wasn’t sure I’d seen it, except my sharingan
didn’t miss things - and a second later, she was back to a clipped practicality. “Shino warned
us you were headed this way. We found Chouji out the front; he told us you were inside, but
until Urushi turned up I didn’t know where.” She grimaced, and added, “Apparently you told
Tsuki not to find you and she took it literally. If Urushi hadn’t -”

Nope. No thank you. I’d had enough emotion for one day. “Yeah, well, he did. What are you
going to do now? Stop me using my eyes so I can’t run away? Seize my muscles and try to
knock me out with my own weapons? Force me to the floor with a sheet of fire then
electrocute me so I can’t stand, that was a good one. I mean, I already dropped a building on
me, I’ve done most of the work for you.”

Chouji came jogging round the corner, though from his angle he wasn’t able to see me.
“Sakura? Did you find her?”

Sakura glanced at me. I couldn’t help it; I shook my head, almost flinching away. I’d said
goodbye to Chouji. I’d said goodbye to him twice and I couldn’t do it again. I didn’t expect
her to listen to me, but without breaking eye contact, she raised her voice.

“Not yet. Try the other side? Tsuki’s tracking survivors.”

“Other side,” he agreed, turning and determinedly heading to help.

I stared. I… hadn’t anticipated that? Unless she didn’t want him to stop her arresting me.
Pulverising me? I still couldn’t read her. She took a step closer and Urushi moved to block
her, hackles up in an uncertain growl. I hesitated, but pushed him aside, and when Sakura
offered her hand, I warily took it and let her pull me to my feet.

“You need to go,” she said flatly.

I blinked.

“Go,” she repeated. “The front gates got attacked. Naruto went that way in case it was
anything to do with you, so choose a different direction, and leave.”

I stepped back, not sure I’d understood her correctly. If I hadn’t, then… I could fight.
Probably. I was bruised and sore and the dull fuzziness in my ears had progressed to an
irritating throb at the base of my skull, but my knee didn’t do more than twinge when I asked
it to take my weight, so. If she changed her mind, I could at least retaliate enough to get
away.

She didn’t seem to change her mind. Urushi pressed himself against my legs, positioning
himself so that if I switched I’d easily take him with me, but I didn’t switch. I’d used a lot of
chakra already and if Sakura was going to let me go, it made more sense to run instead and
conserve energy - except I didn’t run either.

“You aren’t stopping me,” I checked. “This is - if I go, I’m not coming back. I’m a missing
nin, I’m not part of the team anymore.”

“What team?” she shot back. “You’re already a missing nin.” She shook her head, the loose
strands that had escaped her braid sticking to the sweat around her headband. “It’s my job to
keep you alive. Konoha would kill you if they caught you, so I’ll do what I can to make sure
they don’t, but that’s it. Go, and stay gone. You don’t get anything else from me.”

Even then, I didn’t. Somewhere over what remained of the Hokage mountain, someone was
throwing out S-class jutsu like they were part of a festival show. Three guesses who. And I’d
been right earlier that there’d been a seventh bomb; it had been in the Sandaime’s head,
obliterating the entire top half and leaving only a single ear and part of the jawline and cheek
behind. The Shodai and Nidaime weren’t affected - much, the Nidaime seemed to have
gained a large crack across his headpiece that he hadn’t had before - but the Yondaime had
been caught either in the explosion or by the falling chunks of rock that followed it. He was
missing his nose, three of his hair spikes, and a vertical gash out of his lips and chin.

Orochimaru and Jiraiya’s battle on the mountain had drawn in the majority of the village’s
higher ranked ninja for support. They were too far to see clearly even for my sharingan but I
could pick out the black and white ANBU armour, at least. Closer to hand, the genin and
retired ninja who formed the village’s skeleton support were crawling over the wreckage of
the hospital, thankfully too distracted searching for survivors to pay much attention to
anything else. Several were digging out medical equipment and field kits, and one of the
older med nins was dispatching teams to take the supplies to the other bomb sites to treat the
wounded there. As I watched, a chunin I recognised as one of the other teachers at the
academy shunshinned up to him, reporting on the status of the evacuation to the caves and
requesting a doton user in case the explosions had made any of them unsafe.
The med nin rattled off a name, then stopped himself with a curse. Not her. She’s dead. Try
someone else instead.

“Your job,” I repeated hollowly, tearing myself away and focusing back on Sakura again.
“That’s it? You don’t have a job. You’re a genin, same as the rest of us. Why do you have to
be responsible for anyone except yourself?” Unspoken, because I didn’t know how to bring it
up: I just killed the Hokage. Your job isn’t to help me escape.

“Because someone had to be and Kakashi wasn’t there.” She crossed her arms, too stubborn
to turn away even though I could tell she wanted to. Or - maybe I was misreading her.
Stubborn is what I would be, maybe she was just too brave. “I don’t know what you want
from me. I don’t know why you find the concept of friends so hard to understand, why
everything has to be clan or team or whatever other stupid construct you’ve decided defines
how people interact with each other. I don’t know why you freak out when we say we love
you or why you’d rather run away from us than let us help you. I don’t know, and you’ve
made it clear that you don’t want to tell me, so fine: I’ll pretend I didn’t see you, and I won’t
report what you came here to do. But -” She cut herself off, a tight, clipped motion that
involved her twisting her wrist like she wanted her chainsaws out, and when she started again
her voice was steadier. “But that’s it. Don’t expect anything else. Don’t come back. Don’t
assume I’ll help you again. Don’t… just. Don’t. Please.”

The sharingan picked up on facial movements so small, people didn’t know they were
making them. It wasn’t quite a lie detector, but in a way it was, and Sakura meant what she
said. If she was conflicted, she wasn’t letting herself show it. Did she know, I wondered,
where the bombs had gone off? She lived in the residential district. I’d never visited her
house, but I knew which way she walked to go home. I hoped her dad was ok. I hoped
Shikamaru had managed to save people. I hoped Shino’s bugs had got the warnings to the
right places in time. I hoped a lot of things, but hoping didn’t do anything, so I dropped my
hand down and rested my fingers on Urushi’s head to warn him we were about to leave.

“I didn’t join Orochimaru,” I promised her. “I swear. The explosions were nothing to do with
me.” She didn’t answer, but I wasn’t waiting for her to. If Urushi had got in, that meant the
barrier seal was down so the safest way out would be over the wall and rendezvous with the
others in the forest. I turned, mentally debating which section of wall would be easiest, and
prepared to go.

By the gates, just beyond my range of vision, a column of flames erupted up into the sky.
They glowed with the uniform, unnatural red of bijuu chakra, forming a solid mass that
warped and reshaped itself into a grinning fox head. As both Sakura and I stared in horror the
flames condensed, wrapping themselves around the figure that leapt up into the air to meet
them; they formed a cloak, two distinct ears, and a grasping, prehensile tail.

Naruto turned himself in the air and rocketed back down to the ground, chakra-shrouded fist
aimed down and a hail of clones flickering into view alongside him.

“Holy fuck,” I mumbled. “That’s a lot more than claws and fangs.”

“That’s the worst way to keep a secret I’ve ever seen,” Sakura hissed, already turning to run
towards the gate. “What is he thinking.”
  I fell in alongside her automatically, distractedly noticing how she adjusted her pace to match
  mine until I was confident enough in my muscles to push for full speed. “Does he ever think
  when he’s being growly?” I asked rhetorically. “Wait - how do you know what the secret is?
  Did he finally get round to telling someone?”

  She shot me an incredulous look.

  “Yeah, no, fair. Pots and kettles, I’ll shut up.”

  “He didn’t need to tell me,” she said. “I have eyes. So do most people in the village, I can’t
  believe he’d use it where so many people could see.” Nor could I, not unless he was losing
  without it - though admittedly he might be more on edge now than he usually was. I glanced
  behind us, but Orochimaru was still occupied with Jiraiya on the mountain so Naruto wasn’t
  fighting him. They’d progressed to a Manda-Gamabunta face-off, which, from the looks of it,
  would have gone easily in Manda’s favour if there hadn’t been a continuous stream of ANBU
  and jounin wearing him down and getting in the way. We focussed so much on individuals
  and three-man teams that it was hard to remember, sometimes, how powerful a larger group
  could be; Orochimaru’s attacks were still devastating and unstoppable, but Manda seemed to
  have lost a chunk of scales to one of Gamabunta’s flaming-oil bullets and his rage was
  turning him into more of a hindrance than a help.

  Not enough that Orochimaru would lose, but enough to make victory painful, and viciously, I
  hoped Jiraiya made it hurt. But; not our battle, and not the direction we were running
  towards. “Gaara,” I guessed, flicking my eyes down to check with Urushi. He dipped his
  head in acknowledgement, and I balled my hands into fists and fought the urge to curse. “I
  left him and Karin outside. He said he’d attack the gates if shit started exploding but I didn’t
  actually expect it to happen.”

  “Gaara and Karin,” Sakura repeated grimly. “Your two friends from the exam. Joy. What are
  the chances you can talk them down without someone dying?”

  “They’re not the ones going bijuu in public, but sure, why not.” Not more than usual,
  anyway; Gaara didn’t count unless he was actively stepping back for Shukaku to take the
  helm. “You sit on your teammate, I’ll collect mine, we’ll promise to meet up again sometime
  and sayonara into the sunset, it’ll be great. Sunrise. Good grief, why is there a whole rest of
  the day to survive after this.”

  She shot me an exasperated look but didn’t reply; we’d reached the gates, and both shifted to
  battle-alertness in preparation for splitting up the death match ahead.

   Interlude: ANBU Hound, who in his efficiency misses the human element that Kakashi would
   not

   Hound didn’t find Sasuke in Iron. He didn’t expect to; the country was large and the
   mountain ranges cutting through it meant what roads there were were winding and indirect.
   The samurai that lived there had spent generations carving steps into the steep cliffs and
   building bridges across the narrow valleys between them and they guarded these stone
   lifelines with a fervour that would take most ninja by surprise; high passes were flanked by
   watch towers, valleys overlooked by fortified outposts, and the few scattered non-military
   settlements were large and ringed by multiple layers of wall.

   Iron knew it was a sword-wielding country in a land dominated by chakra-powered ninja. It
   took great precautions to be able to stay that way.

   Avoiding the roads was difficult. Many of the mountains were covered in ice, even this far
   into summer, and the constant cycle of meltwater dripping into cracks in the cliffs during the
   day and freezing and expanding overnight meant that lower, warmer areas were at risk of
   avalanches and sudden rockfalls. The wind was bitter and biting, funnelling through and
   around the peaks in a way that drove even the most prepared of ninja to seek shelter to avoid
   it, and no vendor in their right mind would sell survival gear to a pair of children. Even if
   Sasuke had posed as an adult or attempted to steal again she’d be asked for papers and
   authorisation that she wouldn’t know how to fake, and shinobi - even young ones - would
   face a strict punishment if they were caught.

   If Hound had the time, he’d get the papers he needed. Not under his own name, nor in any
   way that could tie him back to Konoha, but samurai were pragmatic and willing to be tolerant
   of hunter nin if they had to be. They’d grant him passage on their roads, give him access to
   any updates they had on Sasuke’s whereabouts, and, once she was caught, escort the both of
   them to the border to leave. If nothing else, it would be useful to know for sure that she’d
   made it through the country without being captured at any point.

   Hound didn’t have the time. Sasuke would not have an easy journey passing through the
   mountains, but he did not anticipate her being captured. She was fast and resourceful; the
   unfamiliar terrain would slow her down, and Gaara’s capabilities were unknown, but Hound’s
   mission had the greatest chances of success if he waited for her at Sound than anywhere else.

   He left Iron as unobtrusively as he’d entered it, running through the night with Uhei keeping
   pace.
Rice. The foothills of Iron, tall and rounded with wide swathes of flooded river deltas cutting
between them on their way to the sea. A poor country, too fertile to be overlooked by the
conquering armies of the past, too weakly defended to drive them off. The marshlands of
northern Fire country used to belong to Rice, as did the stretch of shoreline that now formed
Hot Water’s north coast. The fact that Rice as a country survived at all was down to the
network of tunnels and caves that threaded through it, allowing both ninja and civilians to
wage a guerilla war against the invading armies and make victory too bloody to be worth the
cost.

Sound had adopted the principle to heart. The village - if it could be called that - had no
centre, but instead spread through the underground system like a stringy, patchy virus. Every
base was temporary, every soldier expendable; booby traps were common and suicide
techniques considered the norm.

It took Hound three days to find the information he needed. Only two types of structures
among the many bases Sound operated from were permanent; the prisons, and the
laboratories. Of the prisons, there were two kinds: those that kept dissidents and criminals,
and those that kept Orochimaru’s favoured guests and test subjects.

Hound discarded the first. However much one informant delighted in describing the death
matches to him, he wasn’t interested in petty thugs and c-ranked missing nin competing for a
madman’s favour. He cut her throat to thank her for her time and moved on.

Of the labs, there were many. There were even whispers of a purpose-built island being
planned to house some of the grander equipment that didn’t fit in the old tunnels, though the
plan was on hold until after the war was done. Most labs were small, tailored to specific
experiments or designed around housing specific individuals. Among those that Hound could
find records or rumours for were a boy who could turn into water and a demon prone to
flying into a murderous rage; none seemed designed with a sharingan user in mind. He
abandoned that avenue and tried again.

Gamanuma had claimed that Sasuke was going to Sound in search of Karin. Assuming Gaara
was giving her directions, Hound needed to find the base that the Sound and Sand ninja that
had attacked the camp had been staying in. He found several - the advantage of summoning
your allies by snake-summons was that they didn’t need to share the same starting place - and
investigated each one with ruthless efficiency. Still nothing. No sign of Sasuke, no sign of
Karin; he had confirmation that Karin had been seen in several of the Sound bases, that
Orochimaru had taken a personal interest in her, and that she’d been present on the battlefield
but hadn’t been seen since. He had no further leads, except to keep working methodically
through Sound’s bases until he reached the one he needed.

What if, Kakashi thought, slumped against a wall and pretending to be a newly arrested
prisoner from Mist while Uhei scouted. What if he’d missed her. What if Gamanuma was
wrong. What if Itachi had intercepted her, what if she’d been trapped in the ice in Iron, what
if she’d never been headed to Sound at all. What if he didn’t find her. What if he was wasting
his time and she needed him but he wasn’t there, what if he failed her again.

His mission was to ensure Orochimaru didn’t gain access to the sharingan. His mission could
go hang. He had to keep going with Sound because what other leads did he have? Itachi?
That was suicide. The tablet under the shrine? The nagging feeling every time he played back
the confrontation in the woods that something didn’t add up? Sasuke hadn’t treated Itachi like
an enemy. That’s what hadn’t sat right, and more; Itachi hadn’t treated Sasuke like a target. A
target, an annoyance, an oversight; none of those. There was no reason for Itachi to be Suisei
or for an S-ranked missing nin to be infiltrating a village as ANBU. Not a missing nin as mad
and capricious as Uchiha Itachi was meant to be - if he’d betrayed Konoha for another
village, maybe, if he’d been sent on reconnaissance by a foreign kage, but it didn’t fit.

Itachi was there for Sasuke. It was the only explanation for why he’d broken cover when he
had. He was there for Sasuke, and when he thought she’d died, he’d reacted like he’d lost
everything with her.

And Sasuke had treated him like a friend. Like… like her brother.

She should have hated him for what he did. She should have been afraid. She should have
been angry. Why wasn’t she. What was the alternate explanation, what could Kakashi have
missed that would make this all add up.

Uhei returned. Hound pushed himself to his feet and let himself out of the prison cell he’d
been resting in, refusing to allow himself to be frustrated at the lack of good news Uhei
brought. There were more Sound bases. He had to keep going.



On the fifth day:

“I don’t know her name,” the shinobi said. The musical note on his headband was smeared
with sweat and grime; the arm twisted up behind his back was dislocated at the elbow and
two of his fingers were bloody stumps. “I don’t, I swear - Konoha girl, right? Dark hair, um,
shortish dark hair, all pale, kinda small. I don’t know - she looks like a kid! She just looks
like any girl I don’t know -”

“Eyes,” Hound prompted. His voice was steady. Uhei was standing rigidly opposite him.
They were in a service tunnel, lined with water tanks and thick, creaking pipes that lead to the
kitchens and laundry rooms next door. To his left, the coals in the boiler fire glowed red, and
the fire jutsu the shinobi’d been using to tend to them had left scorch marks on the wall.

This particular shinobi handled the linens and bathing facilities for the more well-kept of
Orochimaru’s guests. He’d never been allowed to talk to them, but he’d seen them,
occasionally. Not enough to know who they were. Enough to know where they were being
kept.

“Eyes.”

“I don’t know what you - weird, weird, I swear please you have to believe me, they’re -
they’ve got some bloodline thing or something, I don't know exactly what. That’s all I know,
I promise, if I knew anything more I’d say but I - please no no no I swear, that’s all I know!”
It was enough. Hound ended the man’s sobs with a kunai through his brainstem and made
sure to hide the body before he went. Now, of all times, was not the time to be sloppy, and if
even Kakashi wondered if Hound was being more ruthless than he had to be -

Failure was not an option. Sasuke didn’t have to know what her safety cost, she only had to
be safe.

He signalled Uhei to stay low and aimed for the place where Sasuke was being kept.

                                             ___

Naruto wasn’t at the gates when we reached them. He had been, and so had Gaara been -
among the debris and wreckage was at least one sand-coffined corpse, and I hid a wince as I
glossed over it - but their fight had pushed them back far enough that they weren’t easily
visible among the trees.

That didn’t mean we didn’t know where they were. Two jinchuuriki beating the crap out of
each other weren’t exactly subtle.

The gates themselves were in ruins. It was like a punch to the gut; all the destruction we’d
seen so far, and somehow when we arrived at the edge of the village, I’d expected to see the
gates standing as tall and impenetrable as they always did. For them to be hanging listlessly
open, one barely holding onto its hinge and the other little more than a splintered cross-bar
with nothing attached - it was wrong. The collapsed roof of the stone frame, the crater where
the floor used to be, all of it was wrong.

There was no point crying about it though. Naruto might have forced Gaara away from the
village, but Karin was still there and my attention went immediately to her. Three Konoha
nin; one down, tensely hunched in a way that said he couldn’t stand, but his hands were in a
ram seal and he was still providing jutsu support. One with his back to us, unfeasibly large
mace held crossways across his body - melee type, I decided, there was no way to form hand
seals around that handle and it would be unwieldy as a ranged weapon - and a Hyuuga, eyes
bulging with byakugan veins and her stance classic for the gentle fist.

They had Karin pinned. She wasn’t hurt, but both she and the vivid green snake she’d
summoned had abandoned the offensive. Against two taijutsu opponents her chain was an
effective flail, keeping them both at a distance, but she had no freedom of movement and if
the ninjutsu user got his act together, she’d have nowhere to escape.

Sakura assessed the scene, dismissed it as not in immediate need of backup, and kept running
straight for Naruto.

Urushi and I swerved sharply to the left. The Konoha nin might not need backup, but Karin
sure as fuck did.

“Sasuke,” Sakura started in frustration, halfway through a hand signal instructing me to
continue primary objective - but she cut herself off with a sharp intake of breath as she
remembered that we weren’t fighting on the same side. I ignored her. The downed chunin
wasn’t going anywhere; I ignored him too, but the mace user was steadily driving Karin back
towards the Hyuuga. Karin’s chain was deadly, but neither she nor the snake were used to
working together and were getting in each other’s way. I was in no shape for taijutsu, I didn’t
have flashy ninjutsu in my repertoire even if I had the chakra to use them, and byakugan
meant my usual form of genjutsu were out; what the fuck was I meant to do with this.

Gamble on mace-man. He was the closer target and, if I was incredibly lucky, would be
hesitant to immediately flatten someone in an ANBU uniform.

“Hi,” I said as cheerily and non-threateningly as I could, appearing beside him with my
sharingan spinning. “Look at me?”

“Kunoichi-san.” He glanced my way, the briefest flicker to check my position and ensure he
wouldn’t catch an ally in a sweeping attack, but it was enough. “Your assistance is -”

“Perfectly timed, I know. Have a genjutsu.”

He stumbled. I tightened my grip on the chakra and reinforced it; I didn’t have time for
anything creative so I kept it simple and informed him, as insistently as I knew how, that the
floor had just exploded beneath his feet.

From personal experience, it’s a disorientating experience.

It also threw him off balance enough that when I followed up the genjutsu with an elbow
strike to the nose he had no time to react. It connected; there was a sickening crunch as the
cartilage broke, and he collapsed to a messy sprawl on the ground.

“Syrup trap!” the wounded ninja behind me spat, literally spat, sending a sheet of slippery
liquid towards my feet. I leapt, spinning in the air to fire a trio of shuriken back at him that
he’d wouldn’t be able to dodge -

And cursed, abandoning my next throw as Sakura appeared between us to block them with
her arm guards.

“What the fuck Sakura!”

“That’s my line,” she bit out. Her fist twitched to the side, and her chainsaws leapt out, the
blades not yet spinning as she kept her hands in front of her. “Did you seriously just -”

“He’s alive, isn’t he?” He should be. Noses were dangerous, but only if you hit them wrong.
Or right, depending on your intention, but I only wanted him out the way. Permanent damage
happened when you sent shards from the break up the nasal cavity and into the brain; the
downwards-angled elbow strike I’d used shouldn’t have done more than activate the nerve
cluster to knock him unconscious, I wasn’t risking his life.

From her expression though, alive wasn’t good enough. I grimaced and backed up until I was
standing with Karin, prudently keeping her between me and the snake reared up threateningly
on her other side. “You good?” I asked lowly. ”What happened, where’s Gaara?”

She shot me a withering look. “I had three opponents. You brought a fourth. Gaara’s fighting
the guy who’s apparently my cousin but is also an actual demon and my summon is scared of
needles. I’m grand.”

“He’s no more demon than Gaara is,” I protested. “Why is your summon scared of needles?”

“They’re spiky,” the snake complained, jabbing his head towards the Hyuuga kunoichi.

Karin’s withering look relocated.

“Enough,” Hyuuga snapped. She shifted uneasily; now that I knew they were there, I could
just see the light glinting off the senbon hidden between her fingers. “Status,” she demanded
of Sakura. Whether she recognised her or recognised her headband, I didn’t know. “You
know them? The red-head attacked the gate just before it exploded. Her partner’s fighting the
Uzumaki boy back there -” she jerked her head behind her to indicate “- and three of my
squad are dead. Who’s the newcomer? With you?”

Sakura’s hard expression didn’t change, but I knew her well enough to see how torn she was.
She’d moved forward so that both the wounded ninja and the one I’d knocked out were
behind her; syrup-trap-man had army-crawled his way to mace-man and was rolling him onto
his side to keep his breathing clear. There was a big difference though between defending an
ally and attacking a friend, and Hyuuga was clearly after a definitive answer. Staying on the
fence wouldn’t work.

I decided to be helpful.

“Catch me in your chain,” I muttered to Karin.

“How in the flying fuck does that -”

“Just catch. Snake -” My mind blanked. Was he poisonous? He was very brightly coloured.
Bright colours were poisonous, weren’t they? But then again, big snake. Big snakes
constricted. “Do snake things and don’t get spiked,” I settled for, and crouched in preparation
to sprint.

Ow. No. Ok, and awkwardly half-stooped in preparation to sprint. My bones were not on
board with crouching.

“Status,” Hyuuga demanded sharply, turning her body to encompass Sakura as a potential
enemy. Sakura straightened, the chainsaws starting to spin at their proper speed.

“Not with me,” she said, clipped and flat. “Missing nin, no kill order.”

“Only passing through,” I promised, and bolted for the gap between them. Karin’s chain shot
out to curve around me; Hyuuga moved to intercept, then hesitated when it was clear I
wouldn’t be able to escape my own partner. I waited until the chain was almost touching my
skin, then switched with her, botching the landing so badly I needed to put a hand out to stop
myself falling as I did.

My bones were not on board with any of this.
Behind me, Karin yelped, slamming the chain to the ground with Hyuuga trapped inside. She
only had her upper half; Hyuuga kicked out with her legs, violently enough that she almost
got loose, then the snake shot forwards with his jaws open to catch her feet and hold them
still.

By swallowing them. Yuck.

“Snakes are disturbing,” I decided, pushing myself up and turning to check on the others.
Mace-man was still unconscious, which was great (also slightly worrying, I didn’t think I’d
hit him that hard) and Sakura was -

Hooking her foot behind my ankles and using her shoulder to help me, forcefully, to the
ground.

I landed hard, biting my lip against the pain and already trying to roll into a backflip. If my
knee came dangerously close to her head during it, well, she shouldn’t have dropped me, but
she was too prepared - and too strong - for it to work. Grappling wasn’t my strong suit. Being
solely comprised of bruise really didn’t help.

“Stay,” she said, kneeling on my sternum hard enough that I could barely breathe.

“Like hell,” I hissed, fighting against her grip to get my hands free for a jutsu. What was my
chakra? Fire? Shit. I didn’t have enough for a fireball, maybe I could light the firefly in her
eye and blind her. I needed to add more fire techniques to my repertoire, how the fuck did I
have so few.

She slapped a paper tag to the ground next to me. “Stay,” she repeated, emphasising the
command by flooding the tag with chakra to activate it. It dissolved into black seal-lines,
spreading out in the same heavy script as she’d used back at the hospital. She gave my
shoulders one last shove to keep me from following her, then sprang back just as the seal
completed; I scrambled to follow, but was blocked by a shimmering, bluish-purple wall of
chakra.

A barrier seal.

“Are you kidding me?” I slammed my fist against it, and immediately pulled it back, shaking
out the odd sensation. It was like very concentrated pins and needles - not necessarily painful,
but not something I wanted to experience again. The barrier was low and square, with crisp
straight edges and sides only just tall enough to cover me. I could awkwardly kneel but not
stand, and kicking at it, though satisfying, didn’t make a dent. “She put me in a box. She put
me in a - this isn’t happening. Sakura, what the fuck.”

She didn’t answer. Why would she answer, she’d neatly tidied me away, like a toy she didn’t
want to use anymore, and turned to focus on Karin instead. Was I allowed to be offended by
this? I was offended. I was outraged. Don’t put people in a box when you don’t want to deal
with them. Rude.

Hyuuga was still trapped in Karin’s chain. The snake was still swallowing, working his way
up from her feet to her knees to her thighs; she wasn’t making it easy for him but she had
increasingly less room to fight. It looked… horrific, actually. The sort of slow, encroaching
terror that no ninja ever wanted to find themselves helpless against, and I was glad that Karin
looked just as off put by what was happening as I did.

At least until Sakura slammed into the chain with her right fist forward and her chainsaw
shrieking against the metal, then she looked alarmed and determined all at once.

“That won’t work!” she yelled over the noise. “It's an Uzumaki chain, idiot. It doesn’t break.”

Sakura pulled back, not even looking at the twisted mess of her blade. “You do though,” she
said, squeezing her fingers together. The saw fell to the floor with a clatter, and her knuckle
spikes came out to replace it. “How are you going to block me if your chain’s tied up?”

She didn’t give Karin time to answer. Her charge was fast, deadly, and full on; Karin leapt
back, dragging Hyuuga and the snake with her and flinging them to the side so she could use
the part of the chain nearer to her body as a shield. Sakura’s punch hit the metal hard enough
that if it had been any normal weapon, it surely would have warped and bent from the force
of it; when it didn’t, she turned into a spinning high kick - Karin blocked it with both
forearms crossed above her head - and pushed off to line up another charge.

She wanted the chain gone. If she was genuinely trying to attack, she’d go underground, but
she wanted Hyuuga free. Karin might not know how Sakura fought but she could still tell
what she was trying to do; Sakura’s attacks were relentless and gaining in speed, and with
only a fraction of her chain available to fight with Karin was losing fast.

I kicked at the barrier again. It didn’t move. The tag was - shit. It had dissolved. How did you
end this damn jutsu if the tag wasn’t there anymore? I looked frantically around myself for
inspiration, and grinned when I realised Urushi was behind me, quietly digging his way
underneath.

“The absolute best,” I told him. Sakura had progressed to using earth jutsu speared through
the chain links to try and render it useless; Karin was able to pull them free so far, but from
Sakura’s intense focus she’d found a strategy she liked. I turned my back on them, shielding
Urushi from view. “How deep does it go? It can’t be a complete box. It wouldn’t have been
able to cut through the earth.”

He shook his head, but didn’t have an answer yet and kept digging. I fished in my weapons
pouch for something to help, then changed my mind and drew the sword instead. The blade
was decently sturdy, and long enough that if I worked it straight down the inside of the
barrier and used my weight on it like a lever, I should be able to… There. Just. Just, just -
fuck. It slipped. But it had definitely gone underneath something, so I repositioned it and tried
again.

Sakura slammed her fist into the ground, knuckle-spikes first. A beat later, the same knuckle
spikes shot out the ground, each one now waist-high and carved out of solid rock. Karin
dodged, but the chain caught over them; Sakura twisted her wrist and the rock-spikes twisted
with her, tangling the chain further around them, then she wrenched both spikes and chain
back underground. Karin staggered as she was dragged forward; she had maybe two metres
of chain connecting her to where it disappeared into solid rock, and barely enough left free
the other side to keep holding on to the Hyuuga kunoichi.

The snake was above Hyuuga’s waist.

Sakura shook out her hand, and readied another barrier seal.

I dug the sword as far down as I could, relying on the hole Urushi had made the other side to
give the lever somewhere to push to, and -

Mission critical, Sakura tapped against her thigh. Hold position. Mission critical. Wait.

I froze. There was no way that was for me. There was - no. She’d put me in a damn box. But
Hyuuga was clearly distracted, and the two other ninja were too wounded to be of any use -
mace-man had woken up but wasn’t doing well, and syrup-trap-man was currently busy
trying to convince him not to fight people when he couldn’t see straight. Even if she’d seen
Urushi, she wouldn’t be signalling him, and Karin didn’t even know tap code so the only
option left was that Sakura was giving me instructions and expecting me to follow them. In
what scenario, please, did she ever think that was going to work? She was the one who
attacked me!

And yet, I didn’t leave my box. I could. If I forced the sword down it lifted the barrier just
enough to see underneath it, that was all I needed to kawarimi out the other side. At any
point, I could leave, but I held my position and waited.

If this was a trick to keep me from escaping… Fuck I hoped it wasn’t.

Sakura charged. Full shannaro, and I could easily see the moment Karin realised she had
nowhere left to run. Her eyes darted from Sakura to her chain to me, looking for a way out
that would allow her to keep Hyuuga trapped, but there wasn’t one - at the last second she
dispelled the chain, diving aside and reforming it a moment later to wrap around herself and
shield her from Sakura’s blow. Sakura hit her with enough force to drive both her and her
chain back into the wall, cracks fracturing out from the crater of her impact. The black ink
spread from the barrier seal she tagged the chain with, and Karin frantically stretched it out to
keep the barrier as far away from herself as possible. When the purple box snapped into place
it had a good third of the chain inside but Karin, thank fuck, was still free.

So was the Hyuuga. As soon her hands could move she attacked, rolling in the snake’s grip
and driving senbon down towards his eyes. He reared back, as far as he could without losing
his hold on her, and hissed furiously as her weapons skidded over his scales.

“Ryoku!” Karin barked. “Chakra in her palms, don’t let it touch you!”

The snake - Ryoku - attempted to retreat, but Hyuuga was having none of it. She slapped both
palms down against her sides so that they - and the chakra in them - slammed into the corners
of Ryoku’s mouth, tearing through the stretched skin where he’d unhinged his jaw to swallow
her and leaving his lower jaw hanging listless and numb.
Snakes, normally, cannot scream. They don’t have vocal chords. Ryoku was a summon.
Ryoku could speak. Ryoku had vocal chords. Ryoku screamed. He writhed, muscles
contracting as he attempted to disgorge her and back away. He opened his mouth as far open
as he could, the jagged curving fangs in his upper gum clearly exposed - then, either
changing his mind about letting go or doing it by accident as he flailed, he slammed his head
down to the ground and jerked it violently back.

The fangs went into the kunoichi’s stomach, and tore through it as he moved. She doubled
over, curling her knees up instinctively as she flattened her hands over her abdomen and held
everything together, and Ryoku gave one last gurgling hiss as he finally got free. He huddled
back towards Karin, mouth dangling pitifully open, and tried to hide behind her feet.

Sakura swore, abandoning Karin and running to the Hyuuga to help.

“Is anyone a medic?” She had bandages, but stomach wounds were horrible. Bandages didn’t
do much if the wound inside was contaminated. The other two Konoha nin shook their heads
grimly, but Hyuuga choked out a beat of laughter.

“That’d be me,” she said. “Unless you’ve got a mystical palm up your sleeve, get back to the
fight. I’ll survive, missing nin won’t capture themselves.”

Sakura glanced back at Karin. Her chain was trapped, but all she had to do was dispel it again
and she was free. Ryoku - wasn’t a threat. Unless he was a very good actor, at least, and none
of them had noticed Urushi. Me, I was still in my box, sword and escape route very carefully
hidden behind my back.

“I can handle them,” Sakura said, turning to where mace-man was pushing himself to his
feet. “Can you -”

“First aid and a lift,” he offered, twisting the handle of his mace and somehow shrinking the
massive weapon down to a simple long staff that he held out for his partner.

“And a status jutsu,” his partner added, taking the mace and using it as a crutch. “We can get
her somewhere stable. You’re sure you don’t need backup?”

“I can handle it,” Sakura repeated firmly. She rocked back on her heels, watching with an
unreadable expression as the two of them gathered the kunoichi and headed back for the
village. I caught a flash of Hyuuga’s stomach as they went past - it was red and bloody, but
only bloody, and her hands were faintly glowing where they pressed against the wound.

The second they were out of sight, I levered up the barrier seal and kawarimid out from
underneath it. Karin raised her hands in a hesitant fighting position, but I shook my head at
her and focussed on Sakura instead.

What was I meant to say. She’d rescued me from a collapsed building, broken the law to let
me escape, then been put on the spot and forced to pick a side. Had she picked? Or had
reality been a jarring wake-up call that convinced her to turn us in? How was I meant to ask?

I didn’t.
“Naruto and Gaara are still going,” I said bluntly. “If they haven’t stopped now, they aren’t
going to without help.”

She stared at me for a long second, then retracted her knuckle spikes with a quiet schnick.

“Help,” she agreed warily. “Do I want to know what help means to you?”

“Assistance. Aid.” My best, and as worn and tired as the phrase was, my best was all I had
and I was sorry if it wasn’t enough. “It’s in my name, I’m very good at it.”

She looked away. “Sure. We’ll… we’ll help them.” Her eyes landed on Karin, and she
nodded at the barrier trapping her chain. “I’ll get the seal for you.”

Karin took a wary step back. “It’s fine,” she said defensively. “It’s not like you caught me
under there.”

“Your chain’s a chakra construct,” Sakura said, not even pausing as she moved forward. “The
chakra inside the barrier is no longer under your control. If you cancel the technique, you lose
that part of the chain, and the chakra that does return to you will be corrupted and incomplete
- possibly enough to prevent you ever forming it again.” She held her hand over one
translucent chakra wall and drummed her fingers against it in a precise pattern that caused it
to fade away. “Lesson number one: don’t mess with seals, you won’t like it if they go
wrong.”

Karin grimaced, retracting her chain as soon as the barrier allowed her to. “Lesson number
two,” she sniped, “I didn’t ask for a lecture.”

“Don’t. You attacked my village and nearly killed two of my allies. At least two, and who
knows how many you actually killed before I arrived. You’re lucky I haven’t killed you
myself, don’t push it.” She flicked her gaze down, and added, “Dismiss the snake,” then
turned and started walking towards the sounds of the jinchuuriki battle ahead.

Karin lifted her chin, stubbornness in every line of her posture. “What if I -”

“Karin,” I interrupted. Ryoku was keeping low, as out of sight as someone so brightly green
could hope to be. His jaw still hung uselessly open, and he’d resorted to nosing sadly at his
coils as he tried to push it closed.

Karin briefly flicked her gaze to me, then made a hand seal to dismiss him and continued
without pause. “- Wanted to know why? Not saying you could have killed me, but why aren’t
you?”

“For Naruto. Happy?”

She made a face. “My cousin again? You guys realise the Uzumaki clan were huge right, the
chances of us actually being related are tiny.”

Sakura stopped. She turned around, hands balled into fists against her sides, brows drawn low
over her frown. I stopped too, taking a step back and hovering to the side. Angry Sakuras
didn’t happen very often, but they were best avoided when they did. “Let’s be clear,” she
said. “I don’t care about clans. I don’t care about you. If you were drowning in pig shit, I
wouldn’t help you swim. The only reason I’m doing this is that Sasuke, apparently, isn’t
going to leave without you. Consider yourself lucky; she’s more than happy to leave without
me.” I winced. It wasn’t untrue, but also, ow. If Sakura noticed, she ignored it. “Sasuke
leaves, or she’s executed. If she’s executed, god only knows what Naruto will do. He is my
last teammate and he is the only person who matters, so yes, for him, I’ll leave you alive long
enough for you both to fuck off and never come back. If I see you again after that, Uzumaki,
the chakra barrier goes over your head and I really don’t care if it stays attached.
Understood?”

“Understood,” I answered for her, not giving Karin the chance to say anything else. I stepped
up between them, brushing shoulders with Karin in an attempt to convey wordlessly that this
wasn’t worth arguing over and now wasn’t the time to do it even if it was. That, Sakura
definitely noticed, and her already closed body language shuttered further as she took a step
back.

I swallowed. Not my intention. I didn’t mean to - nevermind.

“We should go,” I said instead. “They’ll be sending more people to reinforce the gate.
Jiraiya’s almost driven Orochimaru off, we need to calm the others down before they draw
his attention.” It was even true, mostly, though I doubted Orochimaru had been driven off so
much as he’d got bored and abandoned the fight. Konoha was defeated, the Hokage was
dead, and as amused as he’d been by the thought that Jiraiya couldn’t fix the seal he’d put on
my arm back in the forest of death, he’d never seemed all that interested in confronting him.
As the dust settled and the immediate panic of organising rescue crews faded, Konoha would
start looking for blood - and we needed to very much not be in the firing line.

Sakura nodded wordlessly and crouched to leap for the trees. I checked Urushi was ok to
follow along the ground, shot Karin an apologetic grimace, and leapt after her. We moved
through the branches in silence, but my thoughts were loud in my head.

Why couldn’t I tell her. Why couldn’t I make her see. Why couldn’t I bring her with me. She
was already breaking the law, what was a bit more on top. If they found out what she’d done,
she’d be a criminal anyway, so -

I stopped that train of thought. She was a genin facing off against two missing nin, both with
summons and known, powerful blood limits. If anything, Hyuuga would get blamed for the
mistake, not her; even when you’re wounded you don’t hand responsibility for captives over
to someone else unless you’re certain they can handle it. And if you’re so wounded that you
don’t have a choice - it happened. There were always stronger enemies. Konoha didn’t punish
people for being weak, only for disobeying. All Sakura would have to do was lie and say
we’d overwhelmed her and so long as she was believable, she’d be fine.

Right? Was that the reasoning? She needed to be believable. Warning Shino about Danzo was
already dangerous enough, and I’d only done it because if he was making himself a target he
needed to know who to. I hadn’t told him about Itachi. I hadn’t told anyone about Itachi, not
in Konoha, because - because secrets aren’t secrets if you tell people, and I needed to keep
him safe. I needed to keep them all safe. Right?
  No. Or at least, not entirely. Protect Itachi, fine, but as far as they went I’d been planning to
  leave and I didn’t want them to stop me. It was nothing to do with wanting to keep them safe,
  don’t lie and pretend it was. I’d been scared, and it had been me and my brother against the
  world, and if an enemy was blind enough to treat you as a friend you thanked your luck and
  let them. Why would I ever have told.

  I had the sudden, mad urge to blurt it out as we ran. All of it. She wasn’t asking for it, hadn’t
  demanded an explanation, and maybe that was why, or maybe I was sick of trying to justify
  her as being Konoha and therefore an enemy when the image wasn’t working in my head.
  Maybe I just hated secrets. Maybe if she knew, she’d… what. Maybe she’d what.

  Actions had consequences. People’s lives continued even if I wasn’t there to see. I couldn’t
  untell her, so did I want her to know, or was it better to keep my secrets to myself.

  I didn’t know, and we reached Naruto and Gaara before I managed to decide.
