   “Fucking hell,” Karin mumbled. “The air is on fire and tastes of angry. I hate it.”

   I spared her a glance; she was pale, and her mouth was slightly open as though she was
   struggling to get enough air through her nose. This far into the forest we were among the
   Hashirama trees and the branch beneath us was easily thick enough to catch her if she
   stumbled, but I didn’t think she was that badly affected just yet.

   “Bijuu killing intent,” I summarised for her. “You’re fine.”

   “You’re fine, you’re not breathing murder soup.”

   “Are you going to be a liability?” Sakura cut in with brusque practicality. “If you can’t handle
   the battle -”

   “Worry about yourself,” Karin shot back, straightening and determinedly closing her mouth.
   “You’re squishy and coffinable, you’re more of a liability than I am.”

   Would it be trite to ask them to get along? Maybe, maybe not. Almost certainly pointless
   either way.

   “I can’t see Gaara,” I said, scanning the trees with both sharingan spinning. Hashiramas were
   tall, that was a given, but the way they were created meant that only the very upper sections
   of the canopy had any leaves or smaller branches. In the mid section that we were standing in
   there were thick, moss-covered trunks, connected by a network of long straight branches with
   surprisingly little vegetation in between. It made for a much more open battlefield than you’d
   expect looking from the outside, but it also left plenty of hiding places for those who knew
   how to use them - and though Naruto was a glaringly obvious ball of kyuubi-chakra ahead of
   us, Gaara was nowhere to be found.

   Naruto hadn’t seen us. As I watched, he dropped to the trunk, one hand flung behind him
   with claws digging into the bark and leaving deep scratches to slow his descent as he skidded
   down. The kyuubi cloak moved with him, the edges curling into flames that streamed out
   behind him and the chakra over his hand so solid that his fingers weren’t even touching the
   tree.

   “Ground,” Karin said tersely. I looked where she pointed, gaze skipping over the gouges in
   the soil and the splintered roots until I found - there. He was still himself, thank fuck, though
   his sand was packed tightly enough around him to form a solid shell with Shukaku’s black
   markings clearly visible over the surface of it. It made him broader, and bulkier, fingers too
   long to be anything but claws, but the majority of his sand was in the thick tail he’d curled
   around himself as a shield. I didn’t know if he was holding back on purpose or if without his
gourd he just didn’t have enough sand to form Shukaku fully, but if the damage done to the
forest was any indication it hadn’t hampered his ability to fight.

Naruto was building a rasengan in his other hand.

“We need to separate them,” Sakura said, eyes flicking rapidly between them and the trees.
“Uzumaki, your chain - can you hold Gaara? If Naruto backs off I need Gaara not to
retaliate.”

I’d never seen a rasengan in person before, but the glowing orb of purple chakra - what else
could it be. He was building it fast, gaining speed as he let go of the trunk and started running
down it, and by the time his plummeting charge reached Gaara the rasengan would be fully
formed and ready to tear him apart.

“Sasuke, if Naruto doesn’t listen -”

If Naruto didn’t listen Gaara would die. Ichibi versus Kyuubi, Gaara was better at working
with his bijuu but rasengan wasn’t an attack an enemy was meant to survive. Everything
narrowed as the world sharpened, tuning Sakura out; Naruto wouldn’t listen. Not for
something like this, not when listening would mean giving up and letting us escape. He was
never going to let go, was he, not for anything short of a lethal injury, and I’d never use lethal
force against him like that - except in the back of my mind the thought flickered through: it
wouldn’t be lethal, would it? He had the kyuubi. He had a healing factor. Canon Sasuke had
stuck a chidori through his chest and he’d been fine. If I could kawarimi with someone’s
hand and rip it off at the wrist, if I could tear an iron chain out of solid rock, then a rib? A
lung?

Sakura might have still been talking, but I didn’t hear her. Teamwork was a Konoha thing. I
could do it if I had to - I was good at it if I had to - but when the stakes were this high,
instinct said it was safer to rely on myself. I switched, landing down at the roots, crouched
between them so I had a clear view of Naruto barrelling down the tree to Gaara. I felt almost
light-headed, sharingan so focussed that all I could see were patches of orange and black and
yellow and red that I couldn’t resolve into a person, but clear view meant clear shot, and for a
second I had the insane thought that if lethal force was what I had then the only way to stop
him would be to follow through. I rejected the thought with an almost violent wave of
revulsion. I didn’t do that. I didn’t - even if I did, I didn’t do that against Naruto, what the
everloving fuck. If that came from Itachi’s damn compulsion to stop being so weak, that
could go fuck itself as well. I didn’t care if he’d probably survive it, that kind of unhinged
bloody destruction wasn’t strong and it wasn’t me. I wasn’t going to gamble with Naruto’s
life.

He leapt off the tree, arm drawn back with the rasengan spinning in his palm. Teeth bared,
whiskers dark against his cheeks, and I so very nearly hated him for putting me in this
position where the only way to stop him was to hurt him which I flat out refused to do -

I saw, almost in slow motion, the moment he noticed me there. He frowned, red eyes creasing
as traces of blue swirled in; he turned his head towards me and recognition lit his face.
I wasn’t going to gamble with Naruto’s life. But fuck it, I could gamble with the fact that he
wouldn’t dare risk mine.

I caught Gaara in my kawarimi, spared a scant second to make sure I’d wrapped the threads
carefully enough round him that he wouldn’t get hurt when I traded places with him, and
switched. I didn’t know if I’d have time to switch again once he was safe, just at the moment
I didn’t care so long as he wasn’t in the path of death -

“No,” Gaara said, turning on me with a frustrated growl as he brought the sand-tail up to
shield us both. “I don’t like you doing that.” I stumbled, knees knocking into him and hand
stretched out for balance as I struggled to stay upright after appearing on top of him. Over by
the tree root the sand that had formed the top layer of his armour hung suspended in the air
for a second, then fell to the ground in a cloud of dust; he’d let go of it so I switched with that
instead of him, and now Naruto’s rasengan was headed straight for us both.

“Bastard -!”

I didn’t have chance to react. Gaara pulled me down, tucking us both into a tight ball so his
sand had the smallest area to cover and pouring everything he had into the tail-shield that
wrapped around us. He was between me and Naruto, angled to take the brunt of the attack on
his back; over his shoulder I saw Naruto desperately attempting to redirect his rasengan but
he was moving too fast to get it far enough away.

It slammed into Gaara’s sand, off-centre and skidding down into the ground. A thousand
spinning wind blades, tearing through his shield - Gaara’s grip on me tightened hard enough
to hurt. His tail was shredded. Naruto leapt back, chakra cloak fading away as he stared at me
in horror, but I wasn’t looking - Gaara was bleeding. Right side of his back, above where his
kidney would be, his shirt was in pieces and the skin underneath was a mess of flaking sand
armour and blood.

“You’re ok,” I told him, dropping to my knees so I could support him better as he staggered
forward. “You’re ok, you’re fine - it’s not deep. You’re fine. Look at me, Gaara, you’re fine,
ok?” The remainder of his sand spasmed, Shukaku’s black markings standing out in livid
contrast as his arm started to bulge into a paw. Next to us, Naruto picked himself up from
where he’d landed, eyes rapidly turning blue as he made to approach.

I warned him away with a wordless look. “Gaara, you with me? It’s just a scrape -” It wasn’t,
not quite, but from what I could see it hadn’t gone deep enough to cause any serious damage.
That didn’t make it any less of an injury though and I pressed my forehead against his in an
attempt to distract him from the pain. “It’ll be fine, Karin will heal it. You remember the
graze you got from when we escaped the camp? It’s just like that, like landing in the reeds. It
feels bad but you’re ok, I promise you’re ok.”

He jerked forward, hands coming up to cradle his head and latching onto my shirt when my
shoulder was in the way. The tail was reforming, lashing angrily behind him, and sand was
streaming out the soil to replace what the rasengan had destroyed.

“It hurts,” he rasped.
“I know. I know, but it’ll stop - I need you to be you until it does. Just for a little bit Gaara,
please be you for a little bit, then it’ll stop hurting and you’ll - shit -” his entire arm was now
tanukified, all but crushing me with how tightly he was holding on. I bit my lip to stifle my
reaction, tried to tell Naruto with my eyes that if he took another step closer he’d end us both,
and took a breath to keep going. “You’ll be ok,” I managed, “I won’t let anything happen, I
promise, but I need -” fuck, where was Karin - “I need you to stay you, you can’t let your
mum out Gaara, please.”

“It hurts,” he repeated, but he forced the rippling, bulging sand still and made no move to get
up. That was fine. That was - it was manageable, and Shukaku was slowly reforming the
armour over the bloody mess of his back; it was impossible to tell if they were healing him as
well, but I chose to take it as a good sign. At least until Karin arrived, and I craned my neck
back up to the branches where I’d left her to see if she was on her way.

I was concentrating so hard on her that I nearly jumped when Urushi brushed up against me. I
blinked down at him, only realising then that I’d moved a hand up to Gaara’s hair on instinct
and was trying to flatten it the way Kakashi sometimes did for me.

“Urushi…?”

He looked between me and Gaara, one ear up and head tilted, then took a step forward and
nosed at Gaara’s misshapen, half-bijuu paw.

Gaara flinched, displeasure rumbling out of him in a warning growl.

“It’s ok,” I promised, still running my fingers through his hair. “It’s Urushi. He’s helping.” I
wasn’t sure how, but. Helping. It’s what he did.

“He doesn’t like me.”

“He hasn’t got to know you yet.” I glanced down at Urushi questioningly. I didn’t think
he’d’ve approached if he didn’t like Gaara, at least, but I wasn’t sure I knew what he was
doing.

He licked his nose, tilted his head again, and came to a decision. This time when he stepped
forward he put his paw deliberately on Gaara’s knee, leaning up until his chin was on Gaara’s
shoulder and he could reach Gaara’s cheek to lick it. Which he did. Gently, but firmly, and
when Gaara moved back he just wagged his tail, also gently, and followed.

“What’s he doing.”

I swallowed what was either a hiccough or a beat of relieved laughter. “Kisses,” I said. “Dog
kisses. He’s kissing it better. It’s what you do when someone’s hurt. I told you, he’s helping.”

Gaara stopped moving away. He didn’t untense, and every line of him displayed extreme
reluctance, but he stoically stayed put and suffered through Urushi covering the entire side of
his face in kisses. Slowly, the tanuki-layer over his arm receded, the sand falling to pool in a
restless puddle on the floor. His tail as well - it coiled around us and subsided, almost like it
was melting, until we were kneeling in a deep circle of sand and Gaara was fully human
again.

At some point, Karin and Sakura joined us. Sakura went immediately to stand with Naruto,
while Karin assumed a defensive position next to us. She frowned at where the wound had
been on Gaara’s back, fingers tugging idly on her sleeve, but from her expression there
wasn’t much left for her to heal.

Eventually, Gaara pushed me away. I sat back on my heels, leaning back to give him space.
So did Urushi, circling round to my other side and sitting next to me, tail still quietly
thumping against my leg.

“All good?” I checked.

“No,” he said bluntly. “You were going to put me in a tree again and get hurt. Don’t.”

I blinked. “Um.” Not quite what I’d been asking, but, “Noted. Are you hurt?”

He considered, then stood up, exaggerating the movement to test the effect on his back. “No,”
he said again. He paused, then turned to Urushi and added, “Thank you.”

Urushi sneezed. Maybe it wasn’t rude, maybe it was just a way of saying you’re welcome.
Or, given how pleased with himself he looked and the way he let his tongue loll out in
satisfaction, maybe he was just a sarcastic kind of dog.

“So,” Karin prompted, shifting restlessly in place. She hadn’t dropped out of her defensive
position, and now that Gaara was standing next to her, she seemed more confident than wary
about it. “We done? Mission success, gang back together, time to go?”

Whelp. There went any attempt at delaying the inevitable. I rocked back, following the
motion through to stand up and join them, though I kept my stance loose and deliberately
relaxed as I did so.

“Mission success,” I confirmed, letting my gaze flick over to Naruto and Sakura. “The
Hokage is dead.” Sakura’s expression didn’t change, as closed and unreadable as it had been
since we left the gate. Her shoulders were angled towards Naruto as much as us, and I
wondered if she was ready to stop him if he tried to stop us. I’d done my half in talking Gaara
down and breaking up the fight, so.

It was easier to talk to her than to Naruto.

“I think Orochimaru’s taking credit,” I continued. “But for what difference it makes, the
actual death was me. I didn’t know Orochimaru was there until the whole -” I waved a
general hand back in Konoha’s direction. “That.”

“Bastard,” Naruto started, taking a step towards us. I took a step back, running into Karin as I
did so and still not looking at him. Because I didn’t want to see, but also just - I’d seriously
considered attacking him. More than attacking him. I was built for assassination, not combat,
and my arsenal revolved around taking someone down fast and making sure they stayed that
way. And I’d been a heartbeat away from turning it on Naruto, because he cared too much
about me to watch me walk away.

“Anyway,” I continued, with forced brightness. “That’s all we were here for, so, lovely to
catch up but we should probably dash.”

“Sasuke.”

He never let me walk away. He never left things, he never listened when I tried to warn him
to back off. He pushed, and he kept pushing, and he forced me to face things I didn’t want to
face and sometimes I felt like the only way I knew how to deal with things was to run away
from them or shout them at him and turn it into an argument.

I didn’t want to argue with him. If I was leaving, I didn’t want that to be the last thing we did.

I swallowed.

I’d messed Kakashi up pretty badly when I’d nearly got myself killed on his chidori. Doing
the same to Naruto had been effective, in the end (would it have been if Gaara hadn’t
shielded us? Naruto had been redirecting his rasengan, but at least part of it had still hit) but.
For all my faith that he would’ve pulled through for me, it wasn’t kind.

I owed him an explanation. I could hardly blame him for not listening when I hadn’t given
him anything to listen to, could I.

“I killed the Hokage,” I said, “Because he killed my clan.” I lifted my head, making eye
contact first with Sakura, then Naruto, and refused to let myself stop. “With politics, with
economics, with missions that left us with half the numbers we should have had. And when
that wasn’t enough, he turned my brother against us and sent him to put us down.” My
parents. The clan elders. Ninja. Civilians. Children. “Danzo gave the order, but I killed the
Hokage because his village was the reason why it happened. His village, his corruption, his
entire system that’s rotten to the core. The Uchiha disagreed with Konoha and Konoha would
rather leave them dead than work with them to fix it, and if it can happen to one clan then it
can happen to any. The only reason it won’t happen to the clanless is that they don’t have a
voice to disagree with in the first place.”

Sakura stared at me, wide-eyed and silent, but Naruto shook his head. “He wouldn’t,” he
argued. “Did your brother say he did? Is that why -”

“My brother’s loyal to the Hokage,” I shot back. If it was bitter, well, I was bitter. “He didn’t
tell me anything. He’d rather I drive myself mad trying to avenge something that didn’t even
happen than -” I cut myself off. “I’m Uchiha,” I said instead. “The point of killing the whole
clan was so no one would find out how low Konoha was prepared to go to keep control, but
they failed. Itachi couldn’t kill me. And now,” I spread my hands, a sardonic twist to my
mouth. “I guess lots of people know.”

Naruto hesitated. Not surprising; kinda a big deal, this whole truth thing I’d just thrown at
him. “Who’s Danzo?”
“One of the village elders. Shadow leader of Konoha, has a hidden division of ANBU under
his direct command that no one knows exists, does the dirty work the Hokage can’t be
connected to.” I paused; Danzo loomed huge and terrifying in my mental image of him, but I
didn’t know the full details of everything he’d done. I didn’t know how to impress on them
how much they had to stay away. “He hoards sharingan,” I went for, not bothering to hide the
way my face twisted with disgust. “He also answers to no one and has spent years keeping
his work secret from the entire village. Whatever you do, don’t let him know you’re aware of
him. It’s not a great way to survive.”

“He’s the one you were scared of.” Naruto’s eyes narrowed, darting between each of mine as
he tried to fit the pieces together and understand. “You said everyone was looking at your
sharingan - he’s the one you meant.”

I gave a helpless kind of shrug. “He breaks people. If he wanted my eyes he - I’d either be
dead or not me anymore, there’d be nothing I could do.”

Behind him, Sakura had progressed from horrified realisation to grim calculation, and though
she kept her focus trained on me I could see the way she was running through her
understanding of the village in her head and slotting the new information in. Naruto though
leapt on what I said, standing straighter and almost triumphant as he found what he thought
was the way out.

“Then Danzo’s to blame,” he said. “He’s the reason you’re running, he’s why your brother
killed your family - he’s the one we need to get rid of.”

“Not - I mean, yes, but -”

“Then that’s fine! You have to stay so you can tell people what he did, and when people
know then the new Hokage can deal with him and you won’t be scared anymore. We’ll fix
it.”

I shook my head. He didn’t believe - he couldn’t believe what he was saying. It was blindly
optimistic, in the desperate way of someone who was latching onto anything plausible
because they knew the truth and didn’t want to face it. That was what he was doing, that had
to be what he was doing, but if it wasn’t then where did I even start to explain how far he’d
got it wrong?

“Naruto,” Sakura said, touching his elbow to get his attention. “She can’t stay.”

“But she -”

“She killed the Hokage,” she interrupted bluntly. “Everyone’s going to think she’s working
with Orochimaru. Even if they don’t find out what she did, she’ll still be a war-traitor who
helped blow up the village.”

“But she’s not,” Naruto insisted. He looked over at me, as if waiting for me to confirm my
innocence - in that, at least - but I just gestured to Karin and Gaara on either side of me.
“These two were.” Not traitors, you had to be loyal to Konoha first - and I don’t think any of
the three of us counted for that - but the rest of it. “They were with the main Sound forces
attacking the camp, and people saw them attacking the gate as well. Sorry, Naruto, but there’s
no good outcome for me here.” More pressingly though, because he appeared to have missed

“So, what then?” He shifted his weight forward on the balls of his feet in agitation, hand
gesturing sharply in front of him. His fingers, I noticed, were still claw-tipped. Whether he’d
been pulling on the kyuubi enough that they were now permanent or whether it was another
sign of his frustration, I didn’t know. “We just keep quiet? Don’t say anything, let him get
away with it - let him keep getting away with it? How the hell does that solve anything?”

“We’re genin.”

“And?”

“And what - are you serious? Do you have so much chakra your brain doesn’t work, do you
think you can just talk everything into going your way?”

He crossed his arms. The agitation was settling, any hints of anger now replaced with
stubborn determination, and I had to bite my lip and yank on a loose piece of hair to stop
myself screaming. “Talking to people is your thing,” he pointed out with far too much calm

“Oh, because I’m doing such a fabulous job of it now, aren’t I. You idiot.”

Somehow, this argument didn’t sway him. Why not. Gaara, go back to going bijuu, I need
you to punch him until he sees sense because he’s being impossible and I hate it.

“We’ll be careful,” he said, level and reasonable and completely at odds with the actual
insanity he was spouting. “Doing something doesn’t mean doing everything at once, and it
doesn’t mean doing it by ourselves.”

I opened my mouth to - I don’t know. Insist that he wasn’t getting it. Change my mind and
tell him I’d lied so he’d back down and leave Danzo alone. Convince him that it was too
dangerous to try so he should keep his head down and survive instead.

I stopped.

Wasn’t… wasn’t that what I’d accused the Hokage of doing? Of scaring Konoha into
submission by making everyone think they were tiny and insignificant, standing alone against
an institution they could never hope to defeat?

“Sakura,” I said instead, turning to her in wary question.

“Someone’s got to,” she said quietly. “If you’re sure that’s what’s happening…” She paused,
waiting for me to confirm. The lie was on the edge of my tongue, but - I didn’t say it. That
wasn’t the point of telling them. I nodded instead, hoping I’d managed to hide my pained

“We can’t do that if we don’t survive,” I pointed out, but this appeared to be a trifling detail

“Yeah,” Naruto said, nodding at Sakura and more confident now he had support. “Danzo

He turned back to me and steeled himself, but didn’t let himself waver. “And if you have to
stay away until it’s done and it’s safe to come back, then you have to stay away. We’ll make

I bit my lip. I wanted to believe him. I wanted to trust him. But I’d been carrying the secrets
by myself for so long, how was I meant to leave them with someone else? I’d been hiding
and running and even now, the fact that someone from ROOT had seen me in the tunnels was

“Promise you’ll be careful,” I blurted. “Promise you understand that you can’t do anything if

“Gardening, bastard?” Naruto asked, wrinkling his nose, but his mock offence was betrayed

entire village for you, now you want us to do your plants as well?”

Well, that got a tongue stuck out at him, more to hide my own complicated feelings at how
everything had turned out than anything else. Somewhere between giddy daring and quiet
dread and overwhelming relief, I’d sort them out later. “I like my plants,” I insisted.
“Promise?”

“We promise, Sasuke-chan,” Sakura said. “Where are you going now? What’s the plan?”

I glanced at Gaara and Karin. They’d both stayed quiet so far - Konoha wasn’t their village, I
guess, it was a difficult conversation for them to contribute to - but future plans involved
them and we hadn’t had much chance to discuss before what we’d do.

“Don’t look at me,” Karin said immediately, raising her hands with her palms out. “My plans

Gaara nodded. “Mother wants to refill their sand,” he added. “They’re not fussy where from,

“And that’s it?” I checked. “You don’t mind following my lead?”

“I mean. Sure?” Karin looked between Gaara and me and shrugged. “I reserve the right to

“Ok.” I ducked my head, and tried again, willing my voice not to wobble. “Ok, then. The
Hokage answers to the Daimyo. It’s a little late, I guess, but it might be worth following up to

And no, I wasn’t only saying that because Orochimaru had brought it up. The clan histories
included several references to the royal family - among them the fact that the Daimyo of the
time had witnessed and ratified the original treaty between the Uchiha and the Senju - and
though most ninja treated it as more of a formality that the village served the Daimyo, he,
technically, was in charge. If I was lucky, he was also removed enough that Danzo hadn’t
bothered with him, so I should be ok to test the water without immediately being arrested for

Lucky and clever. This sounded like one of those improvisation situations that Karin
wouldn’t be impressed by.

“We’ll go to the capital,” I decided. “Not straight away; we need sand, and to stay out of Fire
for a bit, and probably some other things.” I didn’t know where Kakashi was, unless he was
still in Sound. If Naruto and Sakura knew the truth, I wanted him to as well, and if - if he had
a different solution to everything then. Then that was a thing that could happen as well.
Whatever that solution was.

Urushi liked Gaara and Karin. Maybe Pakkun would too. If Kakashi was taking long
missions outside the village anyway, it wasn’t like it could hurt anything for us to tag along.

“The capital,” Sakura confirmed with a lopsided but determined smile. “We’ll keep an eye
out for you.”

“You’re a combat specialist,” I scoffed. “Stealth is my thing. You can try, but you won’t see
me ‘till I let you.”

“Combat specialist.” She blinked. “I - yes. I am.” Then, firmer, “I am. And when Naruto’s
Hokage and I’m the strongest person in Konoha, you have to be on the council with me to

I gave her a wry salute for that. I’d almost forgotten the impulsive promise I’d made her back
in the tower after the second stage of the exam, but screw it. Maybe if everything worked out
it would still happen. There was something inherently weird involved with considering a
future that stretched beyond immediate survival or death, and the fact that I was now looking
down a path that could lead to it - I don’t know. Weird. Not necessarily in a bad way, just.
Weird.

I shook the feeling off. The future wouldn’t happen if we spent so long talking about it that
someone came to look, the explosions wouldn’t delay the village forever. I still wasn’t any
better at goodbyes, so I just waved, and turned to catch Gaara and Karin’s eyes to go.

“See you,” I said over my shoulder. “Good luck with your side. Oh - Shino’s on board. I
don’t know what with exactly, but he’s on board with something. And tell Tsuki I said you
were allowed to find me now, she doesn’t have to stay away.”

“Bastard!” I heard footsteps and looked back, just in time for Naruto to run into me and wrap
his arms around me in a hug.

My arms were trapped between our chests so I didn’t get much choice about hugging back,
but I tangled my fingers into his shirt all the same and buried my face in the crook of his
neck. He smelt like sweat and chakra and home, and until he’d hugged me, I hadn’t realised

didn’t have to let him go.

“Come back,” he said into my hair. “I don’t care how long it takes, I’ll keep going until it’s
safe again, but you have to come back.”

“What is this, one of Jiraiya’s trashy novels?” I mumbled. “I’m not departing with tearful
promises to return. Do you have any idea how cliched that is?”

“Sasuke.”

“Drama queen.” I scrunched my nose, but he seemed serious, so I relented, “I’ll do my best. I
can’t guarantee it’s ever good enough, but. I’ll try.”

He didn’t answer, just held me impossibly tighter for a long moment before he let me go.
When he stepped back, his eyes were over-bright and his lips were pulled tight with the effort
of not saying anything. I nodded, blinked away my own over-brightness (I’d used the
sharingan a lot, it dried my eyes out and made them sting if I pushed it too far, that was

“There’s two chakra signatures out that way,” Karin said, jerking her head to the right of us.
“Not close enough to spot us, and not coming fast, but they’re not far out.”

I tore my eyes away from Naruto and Sakura and focussed my attention on her. “The trees are
the fastest way to travel through the forest,” I said, mentally filling in what I knew of the land
immediately surrounding Konoha. “We’ll stick to the branches, but the canopy will be safer if

“Running,” Gaara deadpanned. “My favourite part of being a missing nin. Can we go to
another town after? There’s only pickled cucumber left, we ate all the food that was good.”

“Pickled cucumber are good. You choose the food next time if you’re fussy.”
“Talk while you move,” I prompted them both, underlining my words by leaping for the
nearest branch. I didn’t look back. There wasn’t any point in looking back, and I had too
much else to focus on anyway. Food, but also some way of fixing Gaara’s ruined shirt, if we
got out of Fire country could we stop somewhere with an actual shower and hot water, where
was the nearest sand and was it en route to Kakashi, how the frick did missing nin missions
work - was there a notice board somewhere? Did we have to advertise? I didn’t want to
advertise, I was meant to be being subtle. Also, my ANBU uniform was very practical, but I
lacked socks. That was a fact that needed to change.

I lied. I looked back once, a glance over my shoulder with my sharingan spinning to capture
the image. They were staring after us, standing with the sort of quiet promise that felt like it
should have been one of Naruto’s inspiration poses, but somehow felt both more and less
optimistic than that. Realer. The inspiration poses belonged to stories, to a version of Naruto
who saw the best in the world because he didn’t understand the worst. Like a wild naivety
that shouldn’t work, that’s why I hated them, but when I looked forward again and stored the
image in my memory it didn’t feel naive.

But; socks. Food. Little things. Day to day problems, the sort that were easy to plan for and
that didn’t cause disasters if they went wrong. Beyond them loomed an uncertain future, with
Orochimaru after Karin and me and Suna potentially looking for Gaara, with Itachi’s reaction
when he got the message I’d sent him by killing the Sandaime and Danzo’s response to me
using the ROOT tunnel and claiming to be on a mission assigned indirectly by him. The
fallout of the war - with Konoha so badly damaged, would Suna and Sound press their
advantage? Would the other hidden villages take notice, would the whole continent end up in
conflict? Crisis bred extremists. Would Danzo seize power, or would Tsunade end up the
Hokage again like she had been before?

I didn’t know. It was impossible to know. But I had an armful of dog and two teammates
running either side of me, with two more in Konoha as well. I wasn’t safe, and I hadn’t fixed
everything, but I wasn’t alone and I was lighter than I had been in a long time. Than I’d ever
been, maybe, since before my family died and Itachi abandoned me with them.

The plan had always been to leave. I’d done that part. The next stage was broadly mapped
out, but the details… I’d work them out when I got to them. It wasn’t improvisation, it was
rapid adjustment of strategy to suit unpredictable circumstances, and it was a necessary life
skill to have.

I tuned back in to the conversation Karin and Gaara were having to discover that Gaara had
never seen ice cream in Suna, and rapidly adjusted my strategy to take the new information
into account.

“Mochi,” I told him. “Ice cream mochi. I’ll make it an A-rank mission to find you some.”

“Cold and sweet doesn’t sound A-rank,” he said dubiously. “Is it that important?”

“Is it that - it’s life changing. You don’t even know what you’re missing, but that’s ok. You’re
with us now, things will be better from here.”
“They make chocolate ones,” Karin offered, too light to be anything other than searching for
a reaction.

I wrinkled my nose at her in outrage and obliged.

“They make - chocolate? What is this, heathen food? Fruit, you need the sharpness to
balance the sweet.”

“What if he doesn’t like sharp though? Maybe he likes chocolate.”

“I’ve never had chocolate either,” Gaara admitted, and Karin nearly missed her next step.

“Strawberry,” I insisted, cutting across both of them. “Try strawberry first, it’s pink and not-
sharp and you’ll love it. Strawberry mochi, nap, clothes, life is going to be great.”

                                             - FIN -

Interlude Afterlude

Orochimaru’s laboratory was hidden, but Hound was good at finding things. Uhei was better.
They weren’t yet at the place the Sound nin had said Sasuke was being kept - or, the Konoha
girl with dojutsu was being kept, but the description matched Sasuke well enough - and for
the sake of the mission, Hound should’ve gone past the lab and kept going.

Kakashi didn’t.

It didn’t make sense for Sasuke to go to Sound. Even if she was rescuing a friend, something
wasn’t right. It didn’t make sense for Itachi to act the way he had done, not if he was the
missing nin he’d been made out to be. It didn’t make sense, and Kakashi wanted to know. He
didn’t expect to learn anything about Itachi in Orochimaru’s lab, but about Sasuke, maybe,
why Orochimaru seemed so confident he could recruit her, why Jiraiya had been so ready to
believe she would turn.

The lab was trapped. Uhei waited outside, keeping watch and avoiding tripping any of the
eclectic selection of seals that formed the main alarm system. Kakashi used a jutsu to create
chakra dead-zones around each of his feet and moved silently through the room. He wasn’t
looking for anything in particular, just information, but he found far more than that.

The sharingan. Detailed diagrams, studies of each evolution. The mangekyou. A theorised
further stage beyond the mangekyou. Optical degeneration. The data-transfer cap caused by a
non-Uchiha optical nerve and the inefficient chakra drain resulting from it. Analysis of data
from implanting living sharingan into arm tissue, and enough notes to identify to whom the
arm belonged.

Izanagi. An as yet untested way to reverse death itself, with a side note that Danzo may have
used it already and decided not to share.

Itachi’s mangekyou. The effect it had had on Sasuke, and suggested experiments to find out
how loosely her soul was attached. Detailed preliminary observations of her inability to feel
killing intent, of her stunted height and chakra reserves, of ways to fix both and shape her
into something powerful and strong. A thought that if her body was accustomed to a loose
soul, it may more readily take a foreign one, with a vague outline of a seal design that could
store a person’s consciousness while their mind was occupied by someone else.

Beyond that - a sketch of another sharingan design, accompanied by a one-eyed swirl mask
and a question mark by Madara’s name. A record of a failed attempt to resurrect Madara.
Records of successful attempts to resurrect the first and second Hokage, soured by the
imperfect and temporary nature of their return. A breakdown of the shinigami seal Minato
had used to defeat the kyuubi, and an attempt to isolate the part that defined the soul-sacrifice
and swap it out for another person’s soul instead. A drawing of a boy with orange hair and
piercings, labelled dojutsu-based body switch? and a dissected image of Sasori of the Red
Sand that concluded puppetry was a poor imitation of immortality. Another paper on the
same orange haired boy, this one with a single word written underneath: Uzumaki. A list of
Uzumaki descendants and the possible locations their parents may have fled to, each one
carefully marked. Deceased, unusable, diluted; deceased, unsuitable, Karin. Her mother,
apparently, had been drained of her life force through consecutive high-powered healings.
Preliminary tests to see if Karin was similarly limited showed positive initial results; she’d
brought Sasuke back to full health after Gaara had crushed her beyond her natural ability to
survive.

Orochimaru’s research was meticulous and thorough. It spanned years, tracking the
disappointing dead ends of Akatsuki and the annoyance of endless imperfections that
amounted to unsustainable techniques. It narrowed with terrifying intensity onto the
sharingan as the solution, latching onto Sasuke as the key that would finally break the lock. It
was patient, and persistent; it began in Konoha before Orochimaru was driven out, and the
earliest papers were written as official reports and approved by the Hokage’s seal. It said that
Orochimaru had been tasked by Konoha to find the secret to immortality. It said the
sharingan was the answer. It said Danzo required a steady supply to fuel his Izanagi. It said
that Orochimaru wanted Sasuke, and he wasn’t going to stop.

Kakashi pulled his headband down over his own sharingan, storing the last document in
chakra-enhanced memory, and reset the security seals over the research. He was silent as he
left the lab. He’d been silent entering it. This was a different sort. He aimed for the room
where Sasuke was supposedly being kept, and he stayed silent, in his footsteps, his words, his
thoughts.

He didn’t allow himself to be Hound.

Under the shrine in the Uchiha compound, on the banks of the Naka river, was a tablet. There
were people in Konoha Itachi didn’t want it to reach. When he thought Sasuke died, he acted
like his whole world died with her. There was a man in Akatsuki with an orange mask and a
mangekyou sharingan, and Orochimaru couldn’t raise Madara from the dead.

Kakashi didn’t know what Akatsuki was. Red dawn, but he didn’t recognise the significance.

Sasuke hadn’t treated her brother like an enemy, and after meeting him, she’d run from
Konoha at the first opportunity and killed people on the way out so they’d never take her
back.
  Kakashi didn’t allow himself to be Hound because Hound prioritised the mission, and just
  then, Kakashi didn’t know if that was right. He didn’t know what Akatsuki was, but the red-
  black cloaks Orochimaru had drawn had been distinctive, and Sasori at least was high profile
  enough to track. Itachi had been his responsibility once. ANBU Weasel, thirteen years old
  and peace-loving, the youngest member of Hound’s squad and the one he failed the most.

  He disabled four separate seals on Sasuke’s door and used a thread of chakra to pick the final
  lock. The door clicked open; in the back of his mind Kakashi planned a route that would take
  them out through Iron, at least until he had more of a lead on Akatsuki’s - on Itachi’s -
  location. He slipped into the room under henge, Uhei at his heels, already scanning it for any
  sign of -

  “Um,” Hyuuga Hinata said, staring at him through mis-matched implanted eyes. “Um! Sorry,
  I don’t - um, I can’t see you very well. Do you need me for another test?”
